{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, changed since the previous version, 7,773 characters)
Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.9% gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.3% gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. The counterpoint is that 14.1% growth on a $109,158M FY2025 base is $15,391M of incremental annual revenue at a 76.3% margin, more gross profit than most software companies generate in total. [S5, S6]

### What one device earns

Apple stopped disclosing unit shipments, so the most defensible unit is the active device. The table divides trailing-twelve-month flows by Apple's own installed-base statement; because that base is an earnings-call figure rather than a filed one, every line is an estimate.

| Line item | Per unit — per active device, per year | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $186.7 | $466,823M TTM ÷ 2,500M devices | S6, S73 |
| of which Services | $48.2 | $120,478M TTM ÷ 2,500M | S6, S73 |
| Gross profit | $90.8 | 48.7% blended gross margin | S6 |
| Selling, general and administrative | ($11.7) | $29,363M TTM | S6 |
| Research and development | ($17.2) | $42,901M TTM | S6 |
| Operating profit | $61.9 | $154,859M TTM | S6 |
| Gross profit ÷ selling cost | 7.8x a year | $90.8 ÷ $11.7 | S6 |
| Cash payback on acquisition | immediate | cash conversion cycle −56.8 days | S5, S6 |

The waterfall ends where most hardware businesses begin: there is no customer-acquisition payback period to compute, because Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays its assemblers. Payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M produced a cash conversion cycle of −56.8 days at 27 June 2026, against +39.2 days at Alphabet; each new device is cash-positive on day one. That advantage is not a scale economy a rival can buy with capital — it is the accounting consequence of owning the customer and outsourcing the factory. [S6, S73]

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

| Offer | Price or take rate | Margin or peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (upfront hardware) | implied ASP $941 ($245,540M TTM ÷ 261M estimated units) | products gross margin 39.9% | S6, S74 |
| App Store (commission, ex-EU) | 15-30%; the 27% link-out commission was ruled prohibitive | services gross margin 76.3% | S6, S69 |
| App Store (EU, from 2026-10-01) | 26% in-app purchase, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission | EU band 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere | S77, S78 |
| Safari default search | 36% of Safari search advertising; $20B in 2022 | 16.6% of TTM services revenue | S70 |
| Subscriptions and cloud | recurring, bundled at the device sale | services 76.3% vs Microsoft 67.9% in FY2026 | S6, S49 |
| Handset peer — Samsung devices (DX) | — | KRW 0.8tn operating loss in Q3 2026 | S75 |

### The cost side has turned

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% a year earlier, and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, and Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%. Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin, and concedes that price increases "may also reduce demand" — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed. [S17, S68]

### What this means for the watchlist

The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value. That structure justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court, and much of the rest faces a memory cycle that turns faster than Apple can re-price handsets. At $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the market capitalisation is $5,072B, or 39.3x trailing EPS of $8.72; the price already assumes the annuity survives intact and that memory costs are passed through. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. [S6, S7]

::: evidence
**The services annuity is what the multiple buys, and it is a smaller share of revenue than it was a year ago.**

Services produced $120,478M of trailing-twelve-month revenue — 25.8% of the total but 40.3% of gross profit and 2.1x company R&D — while its revenue share fell to 25.2% in the nine months to 27 June 2026 as iPhone revenue grew 22.4% against services growth of 14.1% (S5, S6, S17). Two tolls inside that line, the App Store commission and the Safari search licence worth 16.6% of services revenue on a 2022 court figure, are both under active legal challenge (S69, S70).
:::"}],"isError":false}

### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Services, at a 76.3% gross margin, are 40.3% of the gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue; products are not. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% on product mix and tariff refunds, and the 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of its $2.02 EPS to them. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S17, S68]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 quarterly EPS (S17); products gross margin of 39.9% compares with 36.9%, and memory prices rose 146% with the 10-Q warning that cost pressure will intensify (S6, S68). Two hundred basis points off trailing gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, or 6.0% of $8.72.
:::

### Cash conversion is real, but a liability accrual did the lifting

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M while net income rose $16,920M: non-cash add-backs added $1,956M more and working capital $16,366M more. The dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities, +$10,016M against −$15,161M a year earlier. Other non-current liabilities rose $13,531M to $55,080M while other current liabilities fell $4,128M to $62,259M, a combined $9,403M build that reconciles to the cash line within $613M; the prior year carries the ~$15.8B Irish State Aid settlement (cash taxes paid of $37,332M against a $15,381M provision), with the $15,552M added in FY2024 within $250M of the $15.8B payable. The line's clean history is $3,031M in FY2023, −$248M in FY2024 and $4,724M in FY2025, a $2,502M average, so the $14,101M it puts into trailing free cash flow is the soft spot. Replacing it with the $2,502M average gives $125,084M, or 0.97x conversion, a 2.5% free-cash-flow yield and 40.5x price to free cash flow; zeroing the line gives $122,582M and its best clean year $127,306M, so the defensible band is $122.6-127.3B, with $125.1B the midpoint; anything below $122.6B subtracts more than the line contains. The $13,270M of gross intangibles added against investing "other" of only $1,780M is consistent with the $13,531M build being deferred consideration — an unpaid purchase, which would make $123,152M the figure, inside the band. Deferred revenue is no cushion: 3.2% of trailing revenue, with only $7,260M of nine-month revenue out of the opening balance. [S5, S6]

ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine, and the reported ROIC of 320.6% is an artefact of $146.5B of cash and negative working capital that shrink invested capital to $45,347M. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) Apple's market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn and its enterprise value $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that valuation needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding for a company whose revenue compounded at 5.0% a year from FY2021. Forward, 35.2x against a twelve-month average of 35.7x, is still a premium to everyone else. Apple pays 39.5x trailing earnings against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x, a 57% premium only Microsoft at 23.6x comes near. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity, both without peer in the group — not on growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls it [S7, S6, S97, S14].

The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, with iPhone up 21.7% and Greater China up 22.4%, with the September quarter guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it, from 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises; Samsung's mobile division lost money for the same reason. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. The $25.2bn year-on-year swing overstates it, because the prior-year line absorbed the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement in the year to September 2025. Netting the line to zero, to its $2.5bn three-year average or to its best clean year of $4.7bn gives normalised FCF of $122.6-127.3bn, $125.1bn central — 0.95-0.99x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and 39.5-41.0x P/FCF (40.2x at the midpoint on the $5,029.6bn market value, 40.5x diluted), still ahead of Microsoft's 1.5% and Alphabet's 0.6%. The $122.6bn floor treats the whole build as deferred consideration for the $13.3bn of gross intangibles added, which would make that cash an unpaid purchase; on the $13.5bn non-current build alone the figure is $123.2bn and 41.2x diluted. Shareholders have received $438.6bn of repurchases and $75.0bn of dividends in the five fiscal years to FY2025, plus $82.2bn and $15.6bn in the twelve months to June 2026; nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73.9bn cover 72.4% of normalised nine-month free cash flow, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025. No equity has been raised and total debt fell from $124.7bn to $84.3bn [S5, S6, S1].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.0bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus the guided $112.7bn fourth quarter), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin, a 17.5% tax rate and capital expenditure 0.2 points above depreciation. The market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and each 50bp on the rate moves value by 15-18%. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 4 by Product Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,963 characters)
Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model. In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple spent $34.04bn on research and development (+33%), $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn) and $62.1bn buying back its own shares, while services grew 14% to $91.73bn at a 76.3% gross margin. The allocation is unambiguous: the balance sheet funds shareholders, the income statement funds AI. [S6]

### Capital returns come before capital projects

FY2025 set the pattern — $89.3bn of buybacks, $15.4bn of dividends, a new $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.26, against $34.55bn of R&D, up 10%. R&D is now growing three times faster than that, yet none of the increase goes into owned infrastructure. Returning cash while renting intelligence keeps return on equity high and removes the risk of stranded datacentres, but it also means Apple has no AI asset that a competitor cannot rent on similar terms. If features fail to lift average selling price, the R&D step-up is a pure margin cost, and the buyback is what keeps earnings per share intact. The investor gets a capital-return story with an AI expense line, not an AI investment cycle. [S5]

### Tariff insurance is being bought with margin

Apple assembled 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, up from 36 million, taking India to 25% of the 220-230 million made globally; Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron now build every iPhone 17 model there, including the Pro and Pro Max. The strategy is insurance against tariffs and China concentration, and it is working on volume. It is not free: assembly and components still cost more in India than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expired on 2026-03-31, with Apple and peers lobbying New Delhi for a further round. India is also becoming a demand market — sales above $9bn, six stores and Apple Pay planned for 2026. The hedge is real; the margin benefit is not yet. [S115]

### Services funds the strategy; regulation taxes it

Services is the profit engine, and its growth is concentrated where regulation bites: advertising and cloud services drove the 14% increase in the nine months to 2026-06-27, at a gross margin 1.5 times the company average. The Digital Markets Act makes that position contestable. By 2026-03-22 Apple had received 56 interoperability requests under Article 6(7), closing 43 of them and keeping 27 closures confidential, while continuing to challenge the obligations. Each request is engineering time and a potential loss of default status, the mechanism by which services margins are defended. Apple's response has been to comply narrowly and litigate broadly. [S6, S119]

### The AI layer is a partnership, not a programme

The defining strategic choice of the cycle was made on 2026-01-12, when Google confirmed a multi-year deal to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year. Apple paired that with rented Google TPU capacity for its own foundation models rather than building training clusters. The logic is defensible: ship a competitive assistant on time, keep the interface, personal context and the Private Cloud Compute boundary, and let a rival absorb frontier training costs. The price is strategic: the supplier also owns Android, and Apple's own research, while still credible, sits behind a rented frontier. Platform control is preserved at the layer users see; it is ceded at the layer that determines capability. The agreement was confirmed under Tim Cook, who moved to Executive Chairman on 2026-09-01 when John Ternus became chief executive, so execution now sits with Ternus and Federighi's software organisation rather than the negotiators: the contract is continuous, the signatory is not. A supplier that also owns Android has seen Apple slip once, which makes renewal terms the thing to watch — a licence priced per device or per query turns the AI bill into a services-margin item rather than an R&D line. [S111, S98]

| Partner | Scope | Signed or dated | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google (Alphabet) | Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, multi-year | 2026-01-12 | Confirmed by Google | S111 |
| Google Cloud | TPU training capacity for Apple foundation models | 2024, disclosed in Apple's model paper | In use | S118 |
| Foxconn, Tata Electronics, Pegatron | India assembly of the full iPhone line | Ongoing; 55 million units in 2025 | Operating | S115 |
| Klarna | Apple Upgrade device leasing in the U.S. | 2026, with iPhone 18 | Launched | S113 |

### The talent question is the weak link

The partnership was necessary partly because the in-house programme lost people: through 2025 Apple's AI executives and researchers left, mostly for Meta, which paid to recruit them. The leadership answer is now dated: on 2025-12-01 John Giannandrea, senior vice president for Machine Learning and AI Strategy, stepped down ahead of retirement, Amar Subramanya joined as vice president of AI, and Foundation Models, ML research and AI Safety and Evaluation moved into Software Engineering under Craig Federighi, with the rest going to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue. Headcount-related expense is one of the two drivers Apple cites for the R&D increase, so the company is paying more for a team that is smaller at the top than it was two years ago. Apple still publishes competitive inference research, which argues against the strongest version of the decline story, but a research organisation folded into a software group while its flagship assistant runs on a licensed model is a programme in transition, not a moat under construction. [S121, S127]

### Second curves: health and foldables are adjacencies; Vision is not yet one

Health is the most defensible adjacency because it is regulated and sticky: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny, giving owners a reason to upgrade and not to leave. The foldable Duo is the other extension, priced above the Pro Max and manufactured with a hinge that depends on AI-matched assembly and 3D printing rather than on scale alone. Vision Pro has no disclosed revenue, sits inside Wearables and has no confirmed successor: a research option, not a growth curve. The test of an adjacency is whether it earns its capital; health and foldables plausibly do, and the headset does not yet.

### What the next twelve months must prove

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2026 fourth-quarter results, guided to 9-11% revenue growth | 2026-11-02 | Scheduled | Whether iPhone 18 and Duo demand held through launch | S116 |
| Siri AI out of beta, with five more languages | From 2026-10 | Beta in English since 2026-09-14 | That a licensed model can be made to feel like an Apple product | S113 |
| Standard iPhone 18, 18e and Air 2 | Spring 2027, reported | Unlaunched | A two-cycle year and 2nm volume | S112 |
| Duo durability and return data | FY2027 | Not disclosed | Whether the foldable is a franchise or a flagship experiment | S114 |
| Renewal of India production incentives | After the 2026-03-31 expiry | Unresolved in the sources reviewed | The true cost of the China hedge | S115 |
| DMA interoperability decisions and appeals | Ongoing; 56 requests by 2026-03-22 | In progress | Whether services defaults survive regulation | S119 |

The strategy converts AI into growth through the installed base rather than through the model: a better assistant sells phones and protects high-margin services, and those services pay for the R&D the assistant requires. What must be true within twelve months is narrow and checkable. The December 2026 quarter has to show that higher prices did not break demand; Siri has to leave beta and hold quality in languages beyond English; services growth has to stay in double digits against DMA remedies; and gross margin has to absorb memory inflation without the non-recurring tariff refunds that flattered 2026. If all four hold, the company has bought time and the partnership is a bridge. If two fail, the AI expense is funding a feature that does not defend the price.

The signposts that would show the strategy failing are specific: a discount or a lower-capacity model to hold iPhone volume, a second slip in Siri availability, a fall in services growth below the rate of the installed base, or disclosure of a large multi-year model licence whose cost is not offset by hardware price. None of these is visible in the filings reviewed. The strategic risk is not that Apple loses the AI race on capability — it is that the race turns out not to be the thing that sells phones, in which case Apple wins the hardware cycle and the AI spending was a cost of staying in the conversation."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Risk Assessment (risk, revision 8 by Red Team Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,991 characters)
Apple is a high-quality compounder whose price already capitalises a peak margin and a contested services annuity, so the risks that matter destroy the multiple, not the balance sheet, and none is priced at $344.63. At that price on 2026-10-30 the shares trade at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median, and the base DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212. Eight risks follow: two are fatal to the price, the rest execution. The strategic risk is AI defending the price without widening the moat. [S7, S97, S10]

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory cost pushes hardware gross margin below 46% | High, over 60% | EPS -6% per 200bp; -25% to -30% value | Critical | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | Product margin under 37%; DRAM/NAND prices | Enter at $270; wait for the trough | S17, S6, S99, S136 |
| Google search payment cut or banned on appeal | Medium, 20-25% | EPS -10% to -13%; value -15% to -20% | High | 2027, D.C. Circuit No. 26-5023 | Argument schedule; renewal terms | Cap the position | S70, S76, S135 |
| Multiple reverts to the 31.0x four-year mean | Medium-high, 40-60% | -21.5% at 31x; -38% at 24.6x | High | 0-12 months | Ten-year yield above 5%; forward P/E above 40x | No position at $344.63 | S97, S10 |
| EU DMA fee band spreads to other markets | Medium, 20-40% | EU operating income -1% to -2%; -5% if it spreads | Medium | From 2026-10-01 | Services growth below 10%; developer migration | Underwrite 10-12% services | S77, S78, S102 |
| AI cycle fails; Gemini reprices per device | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -5% to -8% | High | FY2027 | Siri beta exit; services margin | Treat AI as a cost line | S111, S6, S137 |
| China demand falls 20% in H2 2026 | Medium, 30-50% | Revenue -3.5%; EPS -5% to -6% | Medium | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | China revenue; Q4 tracker data | Do not capitalise 30% China growth | S96, S84, S87 |
| Cash quality and inventory | Medium, 30-50% | FCF -$1.9bn to $123.2bn, 40.8x; inventory -$3.3bn | Low | 10-K, 2026-11-02 | Other-liabilities note; inventory $11.1bn | Underwrite the $123.2bn case | S6, S5, S17 |
| Governance and key-person | Low, under 20% | Value -5% to -10% | Low | 12-24 months | No named successor; director exits | Board refresh; retention | S134, S133, S141, S11 |
:::

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The 50.1% gross margin carried 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS; because that margin applies to $466.8bn of revenue, one point is $4.7bn of operating income. Memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts fourth-quarter DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter and NAND 15-20% higher; the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38%, memory at 34% against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to about $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel. [S17, S6, S99, S136]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, together a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The Google trial record put the payment at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments; the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 brief asks the D.C. Circuit to strike it, and Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, with the DOJ's cross-appeal, keeps the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value. The EU fee schedule from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ: Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue, and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income. It matters as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### The growth swing factors are AI and China

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capital spending fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books the bill in operating expense; no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation, and X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI survived dismissal. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case holds while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would land in the 76.3% services margin, and whether a licensed assistant sells handsets at $1,199 is the swing factor. China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war: Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, a 4.8-point gain. Greater China was 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue; IDC sees the decline widening to 20% in the second half of 2026, and a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a second layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where production incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs exceed China's, and Section 301 duties replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

At 39.5x, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and 40.2x trailing free cash flow of $125.1bn (39.5-41.0x across the $122.6-127.3bn band, on $5,029.6bn) makes the multiple the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.5%, reversion to the 24.6x FY2022 trough 38%, and the realistic drawdown is $242. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 2 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,877 characters)
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base, the silicon roadmap and the services annuity are real, and FY2026 is a strong trading year: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue rose 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. None of that is in dispute. What is in dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation, 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward. The decision is not whether Apple is a good business — it is — but whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three valuation methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; the bull case at an 8.5% discount rate and a 35% operating margin gives $277; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year average multiple of 31.0 times implies $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth in net operating profit after tax. Those assumptions make the price exactly fair rather than cheap, and the base rate they must beat is modest: revenue compounded 3.3% a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value where this report sees an 18% overvaluation: the median twelve-month target is $338-355, flat to +3% from the close [S142, S144]. Consensus expects iPhone revenue of $252.4bn in FY2026 and $277.4bn in FY2027 and capitalises the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin. The disagreement is specific: that margin included two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned (the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38%, memory 34% of it), and our base case underwrites 47-48%. A 46% margin, which a full memory pass-through implies, takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value to $270 at 29 times — the entry price proposed below, not a discount to it. The non-consensus view is that the market is capitalising a peak margin and a peak multiple at once.

Three scenarios weighted 25/50/25 put the probability-weighted value at $291.5, 15% below the price. Bull ($357, 25%): the AI and foldable cycle extends iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate — 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return, with the upside coming from a multiple that stays elevated. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the search payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline, with intrinsic value of $212-264. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as the DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF bear as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 with the break-up rejected and conduct remedies imposed: the asset survived, but the overhang ran for three years and the resolution did not re-rate the stock — the cloud did, a decade later. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007, peaked near $250bn and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record, 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not [S143, S145, S147]. The rule they teach is that at a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.5 times against 201), owns silicon and a services annuity Nokia never had, and holds $62.2bn of net cash, so the analogy is about duration and multiple, not extinction.

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price, not narrative. A first tranche of 0.75-1.0% of the fund at $270 or below, where a 9% three-year return becomes reachable across 27-34 times exits; a second at $245; the position taken to its 5% cap below $225 or on evidence that FY2027 EPS growth is tracking above 12%. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $242 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety, and the three tranches exist to price that. The strongest counter-evidence is the stock's own record: it returned 27.5% in the twelve months to 30 October 2026, and a sale at 35 times forward would have missed it. The open diligence is the appellate outcome on the search payment and a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, neither of which the register holds. Sell above $380 or above 45 times forward earnings ($441), or if two consecutive quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a services structure that removes the search payment [S6, S7].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 5 by Valuation Analyst, 8,930 characters)
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so a holder's realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. With dividend and gross buyback yielding 1.9% and earnings per share compounding at 8-9%, the arithmetic is adequate only while the 39.5x multiple holds; if it reverts toward the four-year average of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to 1.3% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, and treat $380 and above as a sale [S7, S11, S6].

| Shares outstanding | 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02 | Free float effectively 100% | S11 |
| Largest holders | Vanguard 9.63%; BlackRock 7.10% | Index managers, no controlling or strategic holder | S11 |
| Directors and officers | 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% | Aligned, but immaterial to the register | S11 |
| Index role | Largest in the peer set; the weight itself is not publicly disclosed in the sources here | A structural passive bid, and correlated selling in redemptions | S7 |

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. As the table shows, Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any position a long-only fund would take, so the exit is never closed and market impact is measured in basis points. What cannot be dismissed is price: the buyers on the other side are the same index and active funds the seller competes with, and in a broad de-rating they mark the same multiple down together.

| Buyback yield, net of $13.7bn stock compensation | 1.36% | S6, S7 |
| Total shareholder yield | 1.94% | S6, S7 |
| EPS growth, FY2021 to TTM / FY2026E to FY2029E | 9.2% / 8.0% | S1, S6 |
| Of the historic growth, from a falling share count | 2.7 points a year | S1, S6 |
| Three-year return, multiple unchanged | 9.9% a year | S7, S97 |
| Three-year return, multiple reverts to 31.0x | 1.3% a year | S7, S97 |

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: a 1.9% yield plus 8% earnings growth is a high-single-digit compounding machine, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does much of the work in that growth, and at 39.5x it buys a 2.5% earnings yield per dollar spent, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value at this level. That is not a scandal; it is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 39.5x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month average of 35.7x. A reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x costs 21.5% of the price, or 7.7% a year over three years, which swallows the entire shareholder yield and most of the earnings growth. That is how a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount applied to cash flows arriving after 2035 is materially higher than it was when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

| Dividend | Apple Inc. | $0.27 a quarter, raised annually | Quarterly, with an annual increase each May | High | S17 |
| Strategic acquisition | No buyer large enough: the four largest peers are all smaller than Apple | Antitrust review in the US, EU, China and UK would follow any bid | Not foreseeable | Negligible | S14, S15, S108, S110 |
| Break-up or activist | None identified | Sum of the parts is $177-238 a share against a $5,029.6bn market value | No campaign disclosed | Negligible | S6, S17 |

The precedents are all capital returns, because that is the only exit a company of this size has ever offered its holders. They also show the cost of buying back stock at the top: the FY2024 and FY2025 programmes together spent $185.6bn at 34-38x earnings, and those shares would have been retired 20-30% cheaper at the FY2023 multiple. An investor buying today at 39.5x makes the same choice management made, at a higher price [S4, S5].

The sell discipline follows from that table, which assumes FY2029E EPS of $11.45, $3.55 of dividends and exit multiples of 27x to 34x. A long-only fund earns its 9% hurdle from $270, not from $344; the shares are a hold only for a holder who owns them at a lower basis, and a buy only on a de-rating or on evidence that FY2027-28 earnings growth is running above 12% rather than the 9.9% consensus assumes for iPhone revenue. The conditions that would make me raise the entry price are specific and observable: services growing above 10% with the Google payment intact, gross margin held above 48% through the memory cycle, and a buyback authorisation above $100bn. The conditions that force a sale are equally specific: services growth below 8% for two quarters, gross margin below 46%, normalised free cash flow conversion below 0.9x net income, a buyback cut, or any remedy that removes the Google payment. A multiple above 45x forward, $440, would be a sale on valuation alone [S71, S72, S7].

The bear case sets the drawdown to expect, not just the return. Two independent methods converge on $242: a reversion to Apple's 2022 multiple of 24.6x on FY2027E earnings, and the $243.42 low the shares actually printed within the past twelve months. That is a 30% drawdown, and it is the realistic bad case for a fund holding the shares. The DCF bear of $133 is a different animal — gross margin compression, 2-4% growth and a 9.5% discount rate together — and should be read as the permanent-loss scenario rather than the trading risk. The buyback limits both: the same $82-85bn a year retires 3.0% of the shares at $270 and 3.6% at $240, against 1.7% at today's price, so each leg down raises the forward earnings growth the buyer receives [S7, S6].

The strongest argument against this discipline is that it has been wrong before. Apple has compounded strongly while the technology sector fell in the last month, and a fund that sold on valuation last year would have forgone most of that gain; multiples of this quality have held through a high long-bond yield that most models said would compress them. That is a reason to size modestly and buy on weakness rather than to abandon the arithmetic: the exit route is liquid, the cash return is real and growing, and the only thing between today's price and the fund's required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on the liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on the multiple reversion, which is a forecast rather than an observation. The open diligence question is how much of services revenue the Google payment represents and when the appeal is decided, because neither figure is publicly disclosed in the sources here and both set the floor under the services multiple."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 4 by Regulatory Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,988 characters)
Apple's regulatory exposure, not its ESG record, is what can change a long-only case. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn and Services revenue $109.2bn at a 75.4% gross margin, so App Store commissions and the Google default-search payment sit inside the profit pool carrying the premium multiple [S5]. Fines are not the mechanism; remedies and fee schedules are. Bear case: a 10-15% operating-income tail from losing or repricing search placement and a structurally lower App Store take rate over 2026-2028. A dollar of commission or default rent carries almost no marginal cost, so losing it hits operating income faster than revenue.

### The EU fine is small; the fee schedule is not

On 2025-04-23 the European Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA anti-steering obligation, 0.1% of FY2025 net sales. The material part is the fee schedule: from 2026-10-01 Apple's unified EU terms charge 26% on in-app purchase (down from 30%), 20% on alternative payments, 15% on link-outs and 5% on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web. Apple calls the terms a settlement; EU developer groups contest them. Apple does not disclose EU App Store revenue; at a 75.4% Services margin, each $1bn of commission lost equals $0.75bn of gross profit, and the take rate falls permanently [S78, S77, S5].

### The $20 billion Google payment is the largest policy-sensitive cash flow

Apple does not disclose the Google default-search payment, but the US v. Google trial record put it at $20bn in 2022, or 36% of Google's Safari search revenue: a litigated estimate, not an Apple disclosure. That is 18.3% of FY2025 Services revenue and, if near-pure margin, 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's final judgment of 2025-12-05 preserved non-exclusive payments, banned exclusivity and capped default deals at 12 months; the DOJ and states cross-appealed in February 2026 seeking a payment ban. A lower negotiated rate is more likely than zero, because the payment is worth more as Apple profit than as Google cost; either way it compresses Services growth, and an appellate decision is likely in 2027 [S80, S76, S5].

### US courts are already narrowing the App Store take rate

On 2025-12-11 the Ninth Circuit affirmed that Apple willfully violated the Epic injunction, upheld the steering remedy and limited any fee on linked transactions to Apple's costs; the Supreme Court granted certiorari on 2026-06-30. The DOJ and 16 states and DC have sued Apple for monopolization of "performance smartphones" and "smartphones" since 2024-03-21, seeking equitable relief, not damages; pre-trial litigation has no trial date in Apple's 2026 filings. A willful-violation finding raises the odds of stricter remedies and weakens management's "substantial defenses" posture. US courts can reset App Store economics before the DOJ case reaches trial [S79, S81, S6].

### Tariffs have flipped from cost to refund, not to a new margin level

Q3 FY2026 revenue was $109.4bn and gross margin 50.1%, including 2 percentage points from tariff refunds; EPS of $2.02 included $0.11 from refunds. The underlying margin is 48.1%, against 46.9% for FY2025, when products gross margin fell on tariff costs. The refund follows the Supreme Court's 2026-02-20 ruling striking down certain IEEPA tariffs; Section 232 semiconductor results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariffs on Apple products, but Section 301 duties have since been imposed and more remain possible. For valuation, normalise the margin rather than extrapolate the refund: underwrite 47-48%, not 50% [S17, S5, S6].

### Governance is sound, but the chair is now the former CEO

Governance is not the discount, but the structure changed on 2026-09-01: Tim Cook became Executive Chair, John Ternus became CEO and a ninth director, and Arthur Levinson became Lead Independent Director. The chair is the former CEO, not independent; the independent check now rests on the lead director. The board also waived its guideline against re-election after age 75 for Levinson (75) and Audit Chair Ron Sugar (77), both re-elected in 2026, so refreshment lags the rule. Offsetting that, there is no dual-class stock, four of the 2026 directors were women, the Audit Committee owns privacy and cybersecurity, related-party transactions above $120,000 need its approval, and the 2026 executive-pay vote passed. The gaps are labour and disclosure: 166,000 employees at 2025-09-27, a 10-K concession that supplier code violations "occur from time to time", and no audit metrics; climate claims are unverified. None has changed demand, so ESG is a tail-risk and discount-rate input, not a revenue driver [S56, S11, S138].

### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Services, at a 76.3% gross margin, are 40.3% of the gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue; products are not. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% on product mix and tariff refunds, and the 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of its $2.02 EPS to them. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S17, S68]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 quarterly EPS (S17); products gross margin of 39.9% compares with 36.9%, and memory prices rose 146% with the 10-Q warning that cost pressure will intensify (S6, S68). Two hundred basis points off trailing gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, or 6.0% of $8.72.
:::

### Cash conversion is real, but a liability accrual did the lifting

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M while net income rose $16,920M: non-cash add-backs added $1,956M more and working capital $16,366M more. The dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities, +$10,016M against −$15,161M a year earlier. Other non-current liabilities rose $13,531M to $55,080M while other current liabilities fell $4,128M to $62,259M, a combined $9,403M build that reconciles to the cash line within $613M; the prior year carries the ~$15.8B Irish State Aid settlement (cash taxes paid of $37,332M against a $15,381M provision), with the $15,552M added in FY2024 within $250M of the $15.8B payable. The line's clean history is $3,031M in FY2023, −$248M in FY2024 and $4,724M in FY2025, a $2,502M average, so the $14,101M it puts into trailing free cash flow is the soft spot. Replacing it with the $2,502M average gives $125,084M, or 0.97x conversion, a 2.5% free-cash-flow yield and 40.5x price to free cash flow; zeroing the line gives $122,582M and its best clean year $127,306M, so the defensible band is $122.6-127.3B, with $125.1B the midpoint; anything below $122.6B subtracts more than the line contains. The $13,270M of gross intangibles added against investing "other" of only $1,780M is consistent with the $13,531M build being deferred consideration — an unpaid purchase, which would make $123,152M the figure, inside the band. Deferred revenue is no cushion: 3.2% of trailing revenue, with only $7,260M of nine-month revenue out of the opening balance. [S5, S6]

The composite score describes a good company at a poor price rather than a mediocre one: the quality dimensions score high and the price-related ones low, as the weighted table below shows. That split is the recommendation: Watchlist with a staged entry, not Buy, because the price already pays for the quality, and not Avoid, because the franchise would still compound through most of the downside scenarios.

The composite score is 6.0 out of 10. Valuation scores 2 of 10 and carries the largest weight, 20%. At $344.63 the shares trade at 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward and a peer median of 20.2 times; the trailing multiple is 10.8% above Apple's own twelve-month average of 35.66 times [S97, S146]. The DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212, the bull case $277, the sum of the parts $177-238, and the market price is matched only at a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. The sell side's median target of $338-355 offers flat to +3%, so there is no analyst catalyst to close the gap either.

The quality block is where the score earns its keep. Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Earnings quality scores 7 and the balance sheet 9: normalised free cash flow of $125.1bn, the midpoint of a $122.6-127.3bn band, converts at 0.97 times net income and 0.95 times at the band floor, against 0.50 at Microsoft and 0.08 at Alphabet; net cash is $62,173M, and only $12.4bn of debt matures within a year [S6, S17]. The deduction on earnings quality is deliberate: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, and the FY2026 10-K must settle whether the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities is an unpaid intangible purchase, in which case free cash flow is $123.2bn and the multiple 41.2 times.

Growth and regulation both score low, and together they explain why the recommendation is not merely to wait for a cheaper multiple. Revenue growth has been price and mix rather than volume, so the growth dimension cannot carry the multiple. Regulation is the largest single threat to the services multiple, through the search payment and the European fee schedule, and the catalyst calendar is event-dense and mostly adversarial. The score table below carries the figures and their sources.

The recommendation changes at identifiable points, and the sensitivity table below ranks them. A gross margin at the low end of the base range takes fair value to the first entry tranche, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it. An adverse appellate ruling on the search payment moves the bear case toward the discounted-cash-flow floor. Services growth in single digits removes one tenth of the sum-of-the-parts value. On the other side, a December-quarter guide at the top end with FY2027 memory contracted would justify a higher base multiple that is still below the current price.

Position sizing is zero today and staged thereafter, and the table below carries the mechanics. At the current price the probability-weighted return across the three scenarios is negative, so the Kelly fraction is zero; at the first tranche the odds support a fractional Kelly well above the cap, so the cap binds rather than the calculation. The market regime reinforces patience: an elevated volatility percentile, a ten-year yield at 4.93% and a month of technology underperformance against the index are the profile the regime playbook answers by discounting the target multiple 10-20% and scaling in with limit orders [S9, S10]. The open diligence is the FY2026 10-K detail on working capital and intangibles, a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, and the appellate outcome on the search payment.

Apple Inc., No. 2:24-cv-04055: Docket entries and orders after June 2025: the ruling on Apple's motion to dismiss, the current scheduling order and trial date, and any order defining the remedy theories that remain in the case.. Why: The timing and scope of a US remedy against App Store and device-interoperability rules are the largest long-dated regulatory tail in the investment case; Apple's filings disclose the case but not the schedule or which claims survived dismissal. How: Log in to PACER, open the D.N.J. docket 2:24-cv-04055, download the docket sheet and the motion-to-dismiss and scheduling orders, and attach them.
- U2 (esg, Regulatory Analyst): European Commission DMA case register — DMA.100206 (Apple new business terms) and the Article 6(4) non-compliance proceeding: Any formal decision, commitment decision or closure of the Article 6(4) and Article 5(4) proceedings accepting Apple's 18 August 2026 EU business terms; the non-confidential decision text and the effective fee schedule.. Why: It determines whether the 26%/20%/15%/5% EU fee schedule is a binding settlement or an interim step, and therefore whether EU App Store take-rate erosion is settled or still exposed to further Commission action and fines. How: Search the Commission's DMA case register for DMA.100206 and the Apple non-compliance cases, download the latest decision and press release, and attach them.
- U3 (market, Market Analyst): IDC Worldwide Quarterly Mobile Phone Tracker (regional pivot) or Canalys/Omdia regional smartphone dataset — paid subscription: Smartphone market value in USD and unit shipments by region (Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, Rest of Asia-Pacific) for 2023-2026, with the premium segment (wholesale ASP $600+) split by vendor.. Why: Free releases give global market value ($613B for 2026) and China units only. Without the regional pivot I cannot size the regional TAM or compute Apple's share of each regional market, so the regional growth table relies on Apple's own segment revenue as a proxy and the durability conclusion is weaker for Americas, Europe, Japan and Rest of Asia-Pacific. How: Export the regional market-value pivot from the IDC tracker (or the equivalent Canalys/Omdia workbook) and attach the Excel or PDF to the case file.
- U4 (business_model, Fundamentals Analyst): PACER — US v. Google LLC, D.D.C. No. 1:20-cv-03010 (remedies record and trial exhibits on the Apple default-search agreement): The current Apple–Google Safari default-search agreement terms: the revenue share (36% of Safari search advertising in the 2022 record), the annual amount paid to Apple for the most recent year, and the renewal/termination terms under Judge Mehta's 2025-12-05 final judgment.. Why: Apple discloses no search-licensing revenue. The only public figure is the 2022 payment of $20B, which is 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue and 12.9% of operating income. Whether the 2026 run-rate is $20B or $30B changes the size of the largest single repricing risk in the business model section by half. How: Download the final judgment and the revenue-share exhibits from the D.D.C. docket on PACER (fee per page), or use the Department of Justice antitrust division's public case page for US v. Google, which posts the opinions and trial exhibits without a login.
- U5 (technology_product, Product Analyst): USPTO Patent Center and PatentsView (patent search and grant counts): For Apple Inc. (assignee): granted and pending US patents filed 2023-2026 in foldable hinges/displays, on-device model compression and optical health sensing, with patent numbers, filing and grant dates and status; plus Apple's US grant count for 2025 and 2026.. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 4 by Market Analyst, 8,894 characters)
Apple's markets are large but no longer volume-growth markets: the smartphone unit pool is contracting at the fastest rate on record in 2026 while its dollar value rises, so revenue growth to 2030 must come from holding more than 40% of smartphone value, monetising a record installed base through services, and a foldable and AI-driven upgrade cycle, not from market growth. Apple's revenue compounded at 3.3% from FY2021 to FY2025 ($365.8B to $416.2B) and then accelerated to 16% in the first nine months of FY2026, with iPhone revenue up 22% [S5, S6].

| Measure | Figure | Period | Method and note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Global smartphone units | 1.26B | 2025 | Counterpoint full year, +2% YoY; Omdia 1.25B (+2%) | S92 |
| Global smartphone units | just over 1.0B | 2026E | IDC, -16.7% YoY, steepest annual fall on record | S84 |
| Global smartphone market value (device TAM) | $613B | 2026E | IDC, +6.3% YoY | S84 |
| Global smartphone ASP | $581 | 2026E | IDC, +27.6%; Omdia independently $565 (+21%) | S84, S88 |
| Premium segment (wholesale ASP $600+) | 29% of global units | H1 2026 | Counterpoint; 25% in H1 2025, 20% in H1 2022 | S94 |
| Apple iPhone revenue | $209.6B FY2025; $196.5B 9M FY2026 | FY2025 / 9M FY2026 | Apple filings; +22% in 9M FY2026 | S5, S6 |
| Apple share of smartphone value | 36% FY2025; 42.7% annualised 2026 | FY2025 / 2026 | Calculated: iPhone revenue / (units x ASP); 2026 = $196.5B x 4/3 / $613B | S5, S6, S92, S88 |
| Wearables units | 625M | 2026E | IDC, +1.7%; 2.4% CAGR to 687M by 2030 | S85 |
| Global advertising pool (services) | $1.34T | 2026E | WARC, +11.9% | S89 |

Two independent methods agree that the market is growing in dollars while shrinking in units, and the sizing stacks into three layers. TAM: top-down, IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0B units, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613B because average selling prices jump 27.6% to $581; Omdia independently forecasts ASP rising from $467 in 2025 to $565 in 2026, a 21% increase it calls the largest on record [S84, S88]. SAM: the premium segment (29% of units at $600 or more) plus the iOS installed base for services, where Apple's 65% premium share sets the addressable pool. SOM: Apple's current capture, $466.8B of trailing-twelve-month revenue to June 2026, of which $245.5B is iPhone and $120.5B services. Bottom-up, 1.0B units at $581 imply $581B, within 5% of IDC's value line. The mechanism is a memory cost shock: IDC puts NAND and DRAM costs more than 300% above a year earlier, and the increase is passed through to shelf prices; the market is not expanding, it is being repriced.

Apple's revenue sits where the market is concentrating. Premium handsets reached 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026, up from 25% a year earlier and 20% in H1 2022, and Apple took 65% of those premium units with 9% growth [S94, S92, S84, S5, S6, S88]. Its all-vendor unit share was 20% in 2025, and IDC expects iOS share to reach a record 23.6% in 2026 as Android shipments fall 24.3%. On my calculation Apple captured 36% of global smartphone value in FY2025, $209.6B of iPhone revenue against a $588B market at 1.26B units and a $467 ASP, and annualising nine-month FY2026 iPhone revenue gives $262B, or 42.7% of IDC's $613B 2026 value. Value capture, not unit share, is the franchise an investor is buying.

The durability test is whether that value capture survives a 20-30% price increase, and the evidence is mixed. Apple's product gross margin rose to 40.1% in Q3 FY2026 from 34.5% a year earlier on richer mix and tariff refunds, and revenue grew in every geographic segment in double digits; that is genuine pricing power [S17, S87, S84]. But IDC attributes part of the China strength to buyers pulling purchases forward ahead of Apple's own second-half price increases, and warns China's decline could widen to 20% in H2 2026. The sub-$100 segment, 173M units in 2025, fell nearly 60% in Q2 2026 and emerging markets are forecast down more than 20%. A market that grows in dollars while shrinking in units can flatter Apple for four to six quarters and then mean-revert; the base rate is the 3.3% revenue CAGR of FY2021-FY2025, not the 16% of the last nine months.

Three pools can add revenue to 2030, and only one is large enough to change the trajectory [S84, S6, S83, S89, S85, S95]. Foldables: Apple enters in H2 2026, and IDC expects it to ship more than 17M foldable iPhones by 2027 at an ASP above $2,550, 40% of a category worth more than $45.7B. Services: $120.5B on a trailing-twelve-month basis to June 2026, growing 14.1% in nine months at a 76.3% gross margin, against a global advertising pool of $1.34T in 2026 and an App Store ecosystem Apple says carried $149B of digital goods and services in 2025. Wearables and PC: wearables are a 2.4% CAGR market to 2030 with smartwatches shrinking 3.7% in 2026 while glasses grow 18.1% a year, and the Mac gained share to 9.9% in a PC market down 4.9%. Foldables and services can add; the non-phone device pools, $33.7B of Mac and $35.7B of wearables in FY2025, are too small to carry group growth alone.

| Region | Market size (latest dated) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Americas | Regional value not published; global $613B (2026E) | Apple +11.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; home market; 42.9% of FY2025 revenue | US tariffs (Section 232 and 301); platform antitrust | Samsung, Google, Motorola | S84, S5, S6 |
| Europe | Not published | Apple +16.1% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 26.7% of revenue | DMA take-rate cuts from 2026-10-01; GDPR | Samsung, Xiaomi, Google | S77, S6 |
| Greater China | 66M units in Q2 2026; 134M in H1 2026 | Market -10% in Q3 2026 (Counterpoint), -15.4% (IDC); H2 2026 decline could reach 20%; Apple +30.0% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 19.5% share in Q3 2026 versus Huawei's 21.3%, up 4.8 points YoY | Market access; local champion; data rules | Huawei, OPPO, vivo, Xiaomi, Honor | S139, S140, S87, S6 |
| Japan | Not published | Apple +10.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 6.9% of revenue | Yen weakness; carrier-controlled channel | Samsung, Google, Sharp | S6 |
| Rest of Asia-Pacific | Not published; emerging markets forecast down more than 20% in 2026 | Apple +19.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 8.1% of revenue; India manufacturing and retail expansion | Price sensitivity; tariffs | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, OPPO, Transsion | S84, S6 |

Geography splits the durability question, and policy is a live variable in every region [S6, S87, S77]. Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue but produced 30% growth in the first nine months of FY2026; Europe is 26.7% and grew 16%, the Americas 42.9% and 11%, Japan 6.9% and 10%, and Rest of Asia-Pacific 8.1% and 19%. The China number is the most fragile in size, not share: the market fell 10% in Q3 2026 to the lowest third-quarter level since 2012, yet Apple's share rose 4.8 points to 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, and the top six vendors hold 96%. The EU's DMA terms cut the commission on externally distributed digital transactions to 5% from 1 October 2026. US tariffs moved twice in 2026: the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 20 February 2026 and Section 301 duties were imposed since, while the Section 232 semiconductor review produced no additional tariffs on Apple products on 14 January 2026. Demand is organic consumer replacement, not policy-created: China's subsidies faded in 2026 and India's incentives are supply-side manufacturing support. The budget owner is the consumer or carrier financing plan; the procurement cycle follows the annual September launch; willingness to pay is being tested by the 27.6% ASP increase. What would change the conclusion: services growth above 15% with user growth, a foldable cycle adding IDC's $45.7B category value, or China stabilising after H2 2026. Confidence is high on 2026 data and low on 2027-2030 regional sizing, because regional market values are paywalled and Apple does not disclose units; the open questions are what share of iPhone growth is units versus price, whether services growth is users or price, how much China demand was pulled forward, and how much memory cost Apple can pass through in FY2027.

Components all present and populated (verdict, briefing, efficiency, one-question, takeaways, kpi, timeline, evidence x4, quad, info, risk-matrix, scenarios, analogs, sensitivity). The tool's rule check on version 1 returned no findings; my own N2/N3 spot checks found no unlabelled company-only claim and no unattributed material figure. Gaps that became items: the bull-case collision, the patent table, the sign error, the length ceiling. Not raised because explicitly and adequately stated in the report: the unverifiable BlackRock 13G/A (2023-12-31), the missing regional market values (three of five regions \"not published\": paywalled, U3 open), no named AI P&L owner, no degrees for six executives, no disclosure of the Google payment by Apple.

items.issue: The anchor forecast of the whole valuation, FY2027 EPS of $9.79, has no shown derivation and no source that can produce it. S71 (S&P Global) is an iPhone-revenue preview carrying $56.4bn for the quarter, $252.4bn for FY2026 and $277.4bn for FY2027; the financials section nevertheless cites it for "consensus of $252.4B for FY2026 (+20.4% on FY2025) and $277.4B for FY2027 (+9.9%)" as if it were company revenue, which would put FY2026 revenue below FY2025 and contradicts the same section's $477bn revenue forecast. Separately, $9.79 appears as "implied FY2027 EPS" in the funding table, as the base-case numerator ($284 at 29x) in the thesis and scoring, and as the denominator of the $440 sell trigger, while the open data request records consensus EPS as not obtained. A trailing filing (S6) cannot source a forecast, and no bridge from TTM EPS of $8.72 to $9.79 (+12.3%) is given anywhere.
items.action: Show the bridge: TTM net income and diluted shares to FY2027 EPS, with each assumption (revenue growth, gross margin 47-48%, operating margin 33%, tax 17.5%, share count after buyback) and tag the derived figures as the report's own estimate rather than consensus. items.evidence_request: Primary consensus for AAPL revenue, diluted EPS and free cash flow for FY2027 and FY2028, dated 2026-10-30, to replace or corroborate the $9.79 estimate; and confirmation of the FY2026 iPhone consensus of $252.4bn.

arguments.notes: Product/market-fit questions as put to the section owners. 1) What is the single hardest thing about selling this product now? Answer from the evidence: re-pricing a $1,199 handset into a unit market falling 16.7% while the cost of the bill of materials rises 38% — the report makes this case well but measures demand only after the fact. 2) Who is the budget owner? Consumer, or carrier instalment plan, or developer and subscriber inside services; the memo names all three, evidences none of the channel split. 3) Typical sales cycle? Annual September launch, carrier-controlled channel in Japan, no enterprise cycle discussed; adequate for a consumer business, but the claim that the procurement cycle follows the launch is unevidenced. 4) Why is adoption not faster? Answered well: Siri shipped 23 months after Apple Intelligence and only as an English beta, so the AI upgrade reason arrived late; foldable at $2,550+ ASP is a new price point. 5) What do the lost deals say? Partly answered — China unit share behind Huawei, Xiaomi winning on price-performance, Samsung on foldable head start — but no switching data out of iOS, which is the number that would make the installed-base argument testable. The memo is stronger on why the franchise holds than on what would make a buyer refuse, which is the pass's main finding.

arguments.notes: Stress-test arithmetic, key number by key number. (1) Gross margin 50.1% to 47-48%: 200bp = $9.35bn of gross profit on $466.8bn, $0.52 of EPS after a 17.3% tax rate on 14.75bn shares, 6.0% of $8.72 — the report's figure checks. At 46% ($4.66bn more), EPS $9.79 falls to $9.26, and 29x gives $269 — the entry price is exactly the 46% case, which is why the entry and the margin assumption must be read together. (2) Losing the $20bn payment: 20 × 0.827 / 14.75 = $1.12 of EPS, 12.9% of $8.72 — checks; on a near-pure-margin basis before tax it is $20bn of operating income, 12.9% of $154.9bn, consistent. If the 2026 payment is 25% larger at $25bn, the hit is 16.1% of trailing EPS — still not thesis-breaking at a Watchlist rating but it widens the bear. (3) Revenue 30% lower: at 43% incremental the report gets operating income $95bn and EPS $5.4 (checks: 466.8 × 0.7 = 326.8, a $140.1bn fall, × 0.43 = $60.2bn, leaving $94.7bn; × 0.827 / 14.75 = $5.31). With operating expense held flat the fall passes through at roughly the 33% margin, operating income about $108bn, EPS about $6.05 — the report's stress is the flattering version. (4) Free cash flow 30% lower: $125.1bn × 0.7 = $87.6bn, inside the stated $85.8-89.1bn range, 57.4x on $5,029.6bn — checks; it covers the $82.2bn trailing buyback and not the $97.9bn buyback plus dividend. (5) Multiple reversion: 31.0/39.5 = -21.5%, 24.6/39.5 = -37.7% — checks; the three-year return arithmetic in the exit section (from $270, 5.0-13.3% across 27x-34x exits on FY2029E EPS of $11.45) is consistent with its own assumptions. (6) Probability-weighted value: 0.25 × 357 + 0.50 × 284 + 0.25 × 241 = $291.5, -15.4% on $344.63, and +8.0% at $270 against the tabulated +7.8% — rounding, acceptable. (7) Sum of the parts: services EBIT $62.7bn at 23x = $1,442bn, hardware $92.1bn at 12x = $1,105bn, plus $62.2bn net cash = $2,609bn, $177 a share on 14.72bn shares — checks; the 28x/18x upper case gives $238. (8) Own-history 31.0x on $9.79 = $303 — checks, but inherits the unexplained EPS. Does the thesis survive a 30% worse number? Yes, and asymmetrically: the recommendation is Watchlist with zero position, so a worse number reinforces it; the dangerous error is on the upside, where the 27.5% twelve-month return is the evidence against the discipline, and the report concedes it. What the memo has not stress-tested is the entry ladder itself, which is a single-point bet on $9.79 — item 2 above.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 2 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,877 characters)
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base, the silicon roadmap and the services annuity are real, and FY2026 is a strong trading year: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue rose 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. None of that is in dispute. What is in dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation, 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward. The decision is not whether Apple is a good business — it is — but whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three valuation methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; the bull case at an 8.5% discount rate and a 35% operating margin gives $277; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year average multiple of 31.0 times implies $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth in net operating profit after tax. Those assumptions make the price exactly fair rather than cheap, and the base rate they must beat is modest: revenue compounded 3.3% a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value where this report sees an 18% overvaluation: the median twelve-month target is $338-355, flat to +3% from the close [S142, S144]. Consensus expects iPhone revenue of $252.4bn in FY2026 and $277.4bn in FY2027 and capitalises the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin. The disagreement is specific: that margin included two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned (the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38%, memory 34% of it), and our base case underwrites 47-48%. A 46% margin, which a full memory pass-through implies, takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value to $270 at 29 times — the entry price proposed below, not a discount to it. The non-consensus view is that the market is capitalising a peak margin and a peak multiple at once.

Three scenarios weighted 25/50/25 put the probability-weighted value at $291.5, 15% below the price. Bull ($357, 25%): the AI and foldable cycle extends iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate — 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return, with the upside coming from a multiple that stays elevated. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the search payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline, with intrinsic value of $212-264. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as the DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF bear as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 with the break-up rejected and conduct remedies imposed: the asset survived, but the overhang ran for three years and the resolution did not re-rate the stock — the cloud did, a decade later. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007, peaked near $250bn and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record, 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not [S143, S145, S147]. The rule they teach is that at a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.5 times against 201), owns silicon and a services annuity Nokia never had, and holds $62.2bn of net cash, so the analogy is about duration and multiple, not extinction.

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price, not narrative. A first tranche of 0.75-1.0% of the fund at $270 or below, where a 9% three-year return becomes reachable across 27-34 times exits; a second at $245; the position taken to its 5% cap below $225 or on evidence that FY2027 EPS growth is tracking above 12%. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $242 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety, and the three tranches exist to price that. The strongest counter-evidence is the stock's own record: it returned 27.5% in the twelve months to 30 October 2026, and a sale at 35 times forward would have missed it. The open diligence is the appellate outcome on the search payment and a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, neither of which the register holds. Sell above $380 or above 45 times forward earnings ($441), or if two consecutive quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a services structure that removes the search payment [S6, S7].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation (scoring, revision 6 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,214 characters)
The composite score describes a good company at a poor price rather than a mediocre one: the quality dimensions score high and the price-related ones low, as the weighted table below shows. That split is the recommendation: Watchlist with a staged entry, not Buy, because the price already pays for the quality, and not Avoid, because the franchise would still compound through most of the downside scenarios.

The composite score is 6.0 out of 10. Valuation scores 2 of 10 and carries the largest weight, 20%. At $344.63 the shares trade at 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward and a peer median of 20.2 times; the trailing multiple is 10.8% above Apple's own twelve-month average of 35.66 times [S97, S146]. The DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212, the bull case $277, the sum of the parts $177-238, and the market price is matched only at a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. The sell side's median target of $338-355 offers flat to +3%, so there is no analyst catalyst to close the gap either.

The quality block is where the score earns its keep. Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Earnings quality scores 7 and the balance sheet 9: normalised free cash flow of $125.1bn, the midpoint of a $122.6-127.3bn band, converts at 0.97 times net income and 0.95 times at the band floor, against 0.50 at Microsoft and 0.08 at Alphabet; net cash is $62,173M, and only $12.4bn of debt matures within a year [S6, S17]. Growth and regulation both score low, and together they explain why the recommendation is not merely to wait for a cheaper multiple. Revenue growth has been price and mix rather than volume, so the growth dimension cannot carry the multiple. Regulation is the largest single threat to the services multiple, through the search payment and the European fee schedule, and the catalyst calendar is event-dense and mostly adversarial. The score table below carries the figures and their sources.
