### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.9% in FY2025, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing; the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9%, and the 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of its $2.02 EPS to tariff refunds. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 and memory is now 34% of the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials against 10% a year earlier, and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S17, S68, S99]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and memory is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The refund is 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 quarterly EPS; memory rose 146% and the 10-Q warns cost pressure will intensify (S6, S17, S68). Two hundred basis points off trailing gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of $8.72.
:::

### Cash conversion is real, but a liability accrual did the lifting

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M against a $16,920M rise in net income, and the dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities: +$10,016M against −$15,161M a year earlier, when the Irish State Aid settlement sat in it. Its clean three-year average is $2,502M ($3,031M; −$248M; $4,724M), so the $14,101M it puts into trailing free cash flow is the soft spot. Replacing it with that average gives $125,084M, 0.97x net income; zeroing it gives $122,582M and its best clean year $127,306M, so the band is $122.6-127.3B with $125.1B at the midpoint. The $13,270M of gross intangibles added against investing "other" of $1,780M suggests deferred consideration, putting the figure at $123,152M. [S5, S6]

### The balance sheet is not the risk; the asking price is

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Return on equity | 171.9% | 157.4% | 171.4% | 148.8% | S5, S6 |
| Return on assets | 27.5% | 26.1% | 30.9% | 36.1% | S5, S6 |
| ROIC (equity + debt − cash; distorted) | 1,527% | 1,036% | 479% | 321% | S5, S6 |
| Net cash | 51,011 | 50,021 | 33,763 | 62,173 | S5, S6 |
| Days sales outstanding | 28.1 | 31.2 | 34.9 | 24.5 | S5, S6 |
| Cash conversion cycle (days) | −67.8 | −75.8 | −71.1 | −56.8 | S5, S6 |
| Effective tax rate | 14.7% | 24.1% | 15.6% | 17.3% | S5, S6 |

At 27 June 2026 cash and marketable securities were $146,517M against debt of $84,344M — net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M nine months earlier while $62,094M of stock was retired. FY2025 notes carried $91.3B of principal with $12.4B due within twelve months; leases add $16.8B and purchase obligations $86.3B. Two items need scrutiny: $2,604M of unrealised securities losses, and intangibles up to $25,417M net from $13,301M without the 10-Q saying what was bought. ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine; the 320.6% ROIC is an artefact of cash and negative working capital shrinking invested capital to $45,347M. The measure that survives is cash return on book capital: normalised free cash flow of $125.1B over equity plus debt of $191,864M, 65.2% against 57.3% in FY2025, against a 9-11% cost of equity built from a 4.93% Treasury; the constraint is the price. Nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73,872M are 72.4% of normalised free cash flow. [S5, S6, S7, S10]

### What $9.79 requires

The $284 base case, the $270 entry and the $440 sale trigger all divide by one number: $9.79 of FY2027 EPS, which is $344.63 divided by the 35.21x forward multiple quoted on 2026-10-30, not a figure Apple publishes. [S97]

| FY2027 build to $9.79 | Value | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $520.8bn | iPhone consensus $277.4bn + $243.4bn of services and other hardware; +9.2% on FY2026E $477.1bn | S71, S72 |
| Gross margin | 48.0% | $250.0bn gross profit; 46.9% in FY2025 | S6 |
| Operating expense | $80.0bn | nine months $56.4bn, held to 6.5% growth after 21.9% | S6 |
| Operating income | $170.1bn | 32.7% margin | S6, S71, derived |
| Other income; tax at 17.3% | $1.0bn; $29.6bn | trailing rates | S6 |
| Net income; diluted shares | $141.5bn; 14,450M | 14,715M less 1.8% buyback | S6 |
| EPS | $9.79 | $141.5bn ÷ 14,450M | S97 |

The gross margin carries the bridge: 48.0% is above FY2025's 46.9% and above the 47-48% band the record quarter supports once the refund is stripped, while iPhone revenue grows 9.9% against 8.3% for everything else and products earn 39.9% against services' 76.3%. Each 100 basis points is $0.30 of FY2027 EPS — $9.19 at 46.0%, $10.08 at 49.0% — so the earnings base is a band of $9.19-10.08, not a point. [S6, S71]

### The downside is larger than the up-cycle margin implies

The 30% revenue-fall stress cannot be run at 43%. That rate says $1 of lost revenue costs $0.43 of operating income, but Apple's cost base does not fall with revenue: R&D rose 14.0% in FY2023 while revenue fell 2.8%. On through-cycle margins — revenue 30% lower at $364.6bn, gross margin at the FY2023 trough of 44.1%, operating expense held at $80.0bn — operating income falls to $80.8bn from $170.1bn, a 57% decremental margin, and EPS to $4.68, 52% below what the price implies. At 43% the same stress returns $5.95, overstating stress EPS by 27%; at a 42.0% gross margin EPS is $4.24. At the 24.6x multiple Apple carried out of FY2022 that is $104-115, which is why the $133 cash-flow bear is the permanent-loss anchor rather than a trading drawdown. A 30% fall needs a memory and remedy convergence no filed evidence supports: tail, priced. [S2, S3, S5, S6]

### One share count, one multiple

The 10-Q states 14,608,963 thousand shares outstanding at 27 June 2026, so market value at $344.63 is $5,034bn. The $5,029.6bn used in the valuation and exit work implies 14,594M shares, 15M fewer or 0.1%; the $5,072bn used for the business model is the 14,715M diluted quarterly average, 106M shares and 0.8% more. The multiple is 39.5x either way — price divided by the $8.72 diluted EPS — against 39.0x on trailing net income over the outstanding count; the difference is 0.2 turns. The ladder is a single-point bet because $270 is 27.6x $9.79: on the low end of the band the same $270 is 29.4x, on the high end 26.8x. arguments.markdown:
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base and services annuity are real, and FY2026 is strong: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. What is in dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,072bn market capitalisation, 39.3 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward. The decision is not whether Apple is a good business — it is — but whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three valuation methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; the DCF bull case at an 8.5% discount rate and a 35% operating margin gives $277; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year average multiple of 31.0 times implies $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth in net operating profit after tax. Those assumptions make the price exactly fair rather than cheap; the base rate is modest, with revenue compounding 3.3% a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value; this report sees 18% overvaluation: the median twelve-month target is $338-355, flat to +3% from the close [S142, S144]. Consensus expects iPhone revenue of $252.4bn in FY2026 and $277.4bn in FY2027 and capitalises the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin. The disagreement is specific: that margin included two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned (the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38%, memory 34% of it), and our base case underwrites 47-48%. A 46% margin, which a full memory pass-through implies, takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value to $270 at 29 times — the entry price below, not a discount to it. The non-consensus view is that the market is capitalising a peak margin and multiple at once.

Three scenarios weighted 25/50/25 put the probability-weighted value at $291.5, 15% below the price, and the recommendation rests on that weighted value and the $284 base case, not on the bull. The scenario bull ($357, 25%) — distinct from the $277 DCF bull above — assumes the AI and foldable cycle extends iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate: 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the search payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline, with intrinsic value of $212-264. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as the DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF bear as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 without a break-up: the asset survived, but the overhang ran three years and the settlement did not re-rate the stock — the cloud did, a decade later. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007, peaked near $250bn and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record, 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not [S143, S145, S147]. The rule they teach is that at a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.3 times against 201), owns silicon and a services annuity Nokia never had, and holds $62.2bn of net cash; the analogy is about duration and multiple, not extinction.

The first tranche of 0.75-1.0% of the fund is $270 only on a condition: the 2026-11-02 guide must hold FY2027 EPS at $9.27 or better and gross margin at 47%. That is a 30% drawdown. The DCF bear of $133 is a different animal — gross margin compression, 2-4% growth and a 9.5% discount rate together — and should be read as the permanent-loss scenario rather than the trading risk. The buyback limits both: the same $82-85bn a year retires 2.1% of the shares at $270 and 2.3% at $240, against 1.6% at today's price, so each leg down raises the forward earnings growth the buyer receives [S7, S6].

Apple has compounded while the technology sector fell in the last month, and a fund that sold on valuation last year would have forgone most of that gain; multiples of this quality have held through a high long-bond yield that most models said would compress them. That is a reason to size modestly and buy on weakness rather than to abandon the arithmetic: the exit route is liquid, the cash return is real, and the only thing between today's price and the required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on multiple reversion. The open question is how much of services revenue the Google payment represents and when the appeal is decided; neither is publicly disclosed here and both set the floor under the services multiple.

arguments.markdown:
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base and services annuity are real, and FY2026 is strong: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. What is in dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,072bn market capitalisation, 39.3 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward. The decision is not whether Apple is a good business — it is — but whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three valuation methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; the DCF bull case at an 8.5% discount rate and a 35% operating margin gives $277; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year average multiple of 31.0 times implies $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth in net operating profit after tax. Those assumptions make the price exactly fair rather than cheap; the base rate is modest, with revenue compounding 3.3% a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value; this report sees 18% overvaluation: the median twelve-month target is $338-355, flat to +3% from the close [S142, S144]. Consensus expects iPhone revenue of $252.4bn in FY2026 and $277.4bn in FY2027 and capitalises the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin. The disagreement is specific: that margin included two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned (the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38%, memory 34% of it), and our base case underwrites 47-48%. A 46% margin, which a full memory pass-through implies, takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value to $270 at 29 times — the entry price below, not a discount to it. The non-consensus view is that the market is capitalising a peak margin and multiple at once.

Three scenarios weighted 25/50/25 put the probability-weighted value at $291.5, 15% below the price, and the recommendation rests on that weighted value and the $284 base case, not on the bull. The scenario bull ($357, 25%) — distinct from the $277 DCF bull above — assumes the AI and foldable cycle extends iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate: 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the search payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline, with intrinsic value of $212-264. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as the DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF bear as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 without a break-up: the asset survived, but the overhang ran three years and the settlement did not re-rate the stock — the cloud did, a decade later. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007, peaked near $250bn and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record, 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not [S143, S145, S147]. The rule they teach is that at a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.3x against 201), owns silicon and a services annuity Nokia never had, and holds $62.2bn of net cash; the analogy is about duration and multiple, not extinction.

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price, not narrative. The first tranche of 0.75-1.0% of the fund is $270 only on a condition: the 2026-11-02 guide must hold FY2027 EPS at $9.27 or better and gross margin at 47%. At 27.6 times, $270 is a discount only on the $9.79 base EPS; on $9.27 it is 29.1 times, and on $8.07-8.53, after a 12.9% search-payment cut, 31.7-33.5 times, above the 31.0 times four-year mean. At 27.6 times those lower cases imply $223-235, so if the guide fails the first tranche moves to $235 and the second to $210. The position reaches its 5% cap below $225 or on evidence that FY2027 EPS growth is tracking above 12%. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $242 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety, and the ladder now prices the EPS bridge rather than a single point at $9.79. The counter-evidence is the stock's own record: 27.5% in the twelve months to 30 October 2026; a sale at 35 times forward would have missed it. The open diligence is the appellate outcome on the search payment and a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, neither of which the register holds. Sell above $380 or above 45 times forward earnings ($440), or if two consecutive quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a services structure that removes the search payment [S6, S7].

Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Growth and regulation both score low, and together they explain why the recommendation is not merely to wait for a cheaper multiple. Revenue growth has been price and mix rather than volume, so the growth dimension cannot carry the multiple. arguments.markdown:
Apple's earnings are cash-true and its returns real; what an investor pays $344.63 for is 39.5x a margin that a memory cycle and two legal remedies can move, on FY2027 earnings that require a gross margin above any year before 2026. Trailing free cash flow was $136,683M against net income of $128,930M — 1.06x, or 0.97x on a normalised $125,084M, on capex of 2.2% of revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft and 33.9% at Alphabet. Revenue rose from $383,285M in FY2023 to $466,823M trailing with operating margin up from 29.8% to 33.2%, and the nine months to 27 June 2026 earned a 43.0% incremental operating margin: $21,809M more operating income on $50,662M more revenue. That 43% is an up-cycle rate. [S5, S6]

### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.9% in FY2025, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing; the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9%, and the 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of its $2.02 EPS to tariff refunds. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 and memory is now 34% of the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials against 10% a year earlier, and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S17, S68, S99]

The refund is 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 quarterly EPS; memory rose 146% and the 10-Q warns cost pressure will intensify (S6, S17, S68). Two hundred basis points off trailing gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of $8.72.

### Cash conversion, the balance sheet and one share count

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M against a $16,920M rise in net income, and the dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities: +$10,016M against −$15,161M a year earlier, when the Irish State Aid settlement sat in it. Its clean three-year average is $2,502M ($3,031M; −$248M; $4,724M), so the $14,101M it puts into trailing free cash flow is the soft spot; replacing it with that average gives $125,084M, 0.97x net income, zeroing it gives $122,582M and its best clean year $127,306M, so the band is $122.6-127.3B with $125.1B at the midpoint. At 27 June 2026 cash and marketable securities were $146,517M against debt of $84,344M — net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M nine months earlier while $62,094M of stock was retired; FY2025 notes carried $91.3B of principal with $12.4B due within twelve months, leases add $16.8B and purchase obligations $86.3B, and two items need scrutiny in the $2,604M of unrealised securities losses and intangibles up to $25,417M net from $13,301M with no note saying what was bought. ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine, but the 320.6% ROIC is an artefact of cash and negative working capital shrinking invested capital to $45,347M; the measure that survives is normalised free cash flow of $125.1B over equity plus debt of $191,864M, 65.2% against 57.3% in FY2025 and against a 9-11% cost of equity built on a 4.93% Treasury. Market value at $344.63 is $5,034bn on the 14,608,963 thousand shares outstanding the 10-Q reports, so the $5,029.6bn used in the valuation and exit work is 15M shares (0.1%) light and the $5,072bn used for the business model is 106M shares (0.8%) heavy on the 14,715M diluted average; the multiple is 39.5x on price over $8.72 diluted EPS, 39.0x on net income over the outstanding count. [S5, S6, S7, S10]

### What $9.79 requires

The $284 base case, the $270 entry and the $440 sale trigger all divide by one number: $9.79 of FY2027 EPS, which is $344.63 divided by the 35.21x forward multiple quoted on 2026-10-30, not a figure Apple publishes. Rebuilt from filed and consensus inputs, the build below needs revenue of $520.8bn — consensus iPhone revenue of $277.4bn, up 9.9%, plus $243.4bn of services and other hardware — a 48.0% gross margin, $80.0bn of operating expense and 14,450M diluted shares. That 48.0% is load-bearing: it is above FY2025's 46.9% and above the 47-48% band the record quarter supports once the refund is stripped, while iPhone revenue grows 9.9% against 8.3% for everything else and products earn 39.9% against services' 76.3%; each 100 basis points is $0.30 of FY2027 EPS, so the earnings base is a band of $9.19 at 46.0% to $10.08 at 49.0%, not a point. That makes the ladder a single-point bet, since $270 is 27.6x $9.79 but 29.4x the low end and 26.8x the high end; priced in multiples it becomes $254-278 for the entry, $267-292 for fair value and $414-454 for a sale at 44-48x forward, so three tranches at $278, $266 and $254 hold the multiple inside 27-28x whatever FY2027 delivers, and a 6% lower earnings path turns the 9.9% three-year return at $270 into 7.6%. [S6, S71, S97]

|---|---|---|---|

| Gross margin | 48.0% | $250.0bn gross profit; 46.9% in FY2025 | S6 |

| EPS | $9.79 | $141.5bn ÷ 14,450M | S97 |

### The downside is larger than the up-cycle margin implies

The 30% revenue-fall stress cannot be run at 43%. That rate says $1 of lost revenue costs $0.43 of operating income, but Apple's cost base does not fall with revenue: R&D rose 14.0% in FY2023 while revenue fell 2.8%. On through-cycle margins — revenue 30% lower at $364.6bn, gross margin at the FY2023 trough of 44.1%, operating expense held at $80.0bn — operating income falls to $80.8bn from $170.1bn, a 57% decremental margin, and EPS to $4.68, 52% below what the price implies. At 43% the same stress returns $5.95, overstating stress EPS by 27%, and at a 42.0% gross margin it is $4.24. At the 24.6x multiple Apple carried out of FY2022 that is $104-115, which is why the $133 cash-flow bear is the permanent-loss anchor rather than a trading drawdown; a 30% fall needs a memory and remedy convergence no filed evidence supports, so it belongs in the tail, priced. Apple reports the September quarter on 2 November 2026, guided to 9-11% growth ($111.7-113.7B off $102,466M), with consensus iPhone revenue of $252.4bn for FY2026 and $277.4bn for FY2027. After a 17.3% tax rate, 200 basis points of gross margin is $0.52 of trailing EPS (6.0%), 500 points $1.31 (15.0%), losing the $20B search payment $1.12 (12.9%) and a 10% fall in iPhone revenue $0.55 (6.3%); gross margin moves the outcome most because it applies to all $466,823M of revenue. Earnings quality is not the constraint, the price is, and the diligence that would move it is December-quarter gross-margin guidance, FY2027 memory contracted at fixed prices, and what sits in the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities. Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.9% gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.3% gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. The counterpoint is that 14.1% growth on a $109,158M FY2025 base is $15,391M of incremental annual revenue at a 76.3% margin, more gross profit than most software companies generate in total. [S5, S6]

### What one device earns

Apple stopped disclosing unit shipments, so the most defensible unit is the active device. The table divides trailing-twelve-month flows by Apple's own installed-base statement; because that base is an earnings-call figure rather than a filed one, every line is an estimate.

| Line item | Per unit — per active device, per year | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $186.7 | $466,823M TTM ÷ 2,500M devices | S6, S73 |
| of which Services | $48.2 | $120,478M TTM ÷ 2,500M | S6, S73 |
| Gross profit | $90.8 | 48.7% blended gross margin | S6 |
| Selling, general and administrative | ($11.7) | $29,363M TTM | S6 |
| Research and development | ($17.2) | $42,901M TTM | S6 |
| Operating profit | $61.9 | $154,859M TTM | S6 |
| Gross profit ÷ selling cost | 7.8x a year | $90.8 ÷ $11.7 | S6 |
| Cash payback on acquisition | immediate | cash conversion cycle −56.8 days | S5, S6 |

The waterfall ends where most hardware businesses begin: there is no customer-acquisition payback period to compute, because Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays its assemblers. Payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M produced a cash conversion cycle of −56.8 days at 27 June 2026, against +39.2 days at Alphabet; each new device is cash-positive on day one. That advantage is not a scale economy a rival can buy with capital — it is the accounting consequence of owning the customer and outsourcing the factory. [S6, S73]

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

| Offer | Price or take rate | Margin or peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (upfront hardware) | implied ASP $941 ($245,540M TTM ÷ 261M estimated units) | products gross margin 39.9% | S6, S74 |
| App Store (commission, ex-EU) | 15-30%; the 27% link-out commission was ruled prohibitive | services gross margin 76.3% | S6, S69 |
| App Store (EU, from 2026-10-01) | 26% in-app purchase, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission | EU band 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere | S77, S78 |
| Safari default search | 36% of Safari search advertising; $20B in 2022 | 16.6% of TTM services revenue | S70 |
| Subscriptions and cloud | recurring, bundled at the device sale | services 76.3% vs Microsoft 67.9% in FY2026 | S6, S49 |
| Handset peer — Samsung devices (DX) | — | KRW 0.8tn operating loss in Q3 2026 | S75 |

### The cost side has turned

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% a year earlier, and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, and Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%. Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin, and concedes that price increases "may also reduce demand" — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed. [S17, S68]

### What this means for the watchlist

The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value. That structure justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court, and much of the rest faces a memory cycle that turns faster than Apple can re-price handsets. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? plan.comparison_set: Services gross margin 76.3% against Microsoft's 67.9% in FY2026; products 39.9% against Samsung's mobile division loss in Q3 2026; cash conversion cycle −56.8 days against Alphabet's +39.2; implied iPhone ASP $832-1,060 across unit bases against the $565 market average price.
plan.counter_evidence: The iPhone ASP rise may be a one-off Pro-mix and memory pass-through that reverses when the cycle turns; the App Store and search tolls are being repriced in court and the remedies are not yet fixed; services is still growing 14.1% in absolute dollars.
plan.decision_question: Where does the gross profit actually come from per unit and per device, and which of those pools is being repriced or competed away?
plan.mechanism: Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays assemblers, so each device is cash-positive on day one; the annuity (services at 76.3% gross margin) then monetises the installed base a second time, and its two toll lines are legal constructs rather than product advantages.
plan.prohibited: fierce competition, strong team, well positioned, risks are manageable, huge market, clear business model, high barriers to entry
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple monetises one customer twice — hardware at a 39.9% gross margin paid for before the cost is incurred, and a services annuity at 76.3% — and the annuity, a quarter of revenue and two-fifths of gross profit, is what the multiple buys, but its share of revenue fell in 2026 and two of its tolls are being repriced in court.

rows.implication: Revenue growth is price-led and therefore reversible; the unit base, not the ASP, is the variable to watch because a 10% unit fall at a 39.9% product margin costs $0.55 of EPS.
rows.mechanism: Price and mix rather than volume: carriers and retailers pay before Apple pays its assemblers, so higher ASPs convert straight into cash and gross profit without working capital.
rows.weakens: Apple discloses no units; every per-unit figure rests on a third-party estimate, and the 261M estimate carries low confidence.

rows.benchmark: Services 76.3% gross margin against Microsoft's 67.9% in FY2026
rows.confidence: high — segment gross profit is filed

rows.follow_up: Does services grow above 15% once hardware growth normalises, and what is the split between the App Store, advertising and subscriptions?
rows.implication: The annuity is what the multiple buys, and it already funds the AI build; the risk is that its revenue share fell to 25.2% in the nine months of FY2026 as iPhone grew faster.
rows.mechanism: A high-margin annuity on an installed base whose marginal cost of service is near zero converts installed-base growth into gross profit far faster than hardware does.
rows.weakens: Apple does not split services revenue, so the mix inside the 76.3% margin is not observable.

rows.benchmark: Cash conversion cycle −56.8 days against Alphabet's +39.2 days

rows.follow_up: How much of the payables benefit reverses if suppliers demand shorter terms as memory costs rise?
rows.implication: There is no customer-acquisition payback to underwrite; the investment question is the multiple, not unit profitability.
rows.mechanism: Owning the customer while outsourcing the factory turns working capital into a source of funds, so growth is self-financing.
rows.weakens: The 2.5B active-device base is an earnings-call statement, not a filed figure, and payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M flatter the cycle.

rows.benchmark: App Store 15-30% ex-EU against 5-26% in the EU; Microsoft's 67.9% services margin

rows.implication: Price the annuity at a discount until the remedies are known; a $20B loss is $1.12 of EPS, 12.9%.
rows.mechanism: Both lines are rents on other companies' commerce rather than product advantages, so a court or a regulator can reprice them without Apple losing a customer.
rows.weakens: The remedies ruling kept the Google payments and barred only exclusivity, so the payment may be renegotiated rather than lost.

rows.implication: Every 100 basis points of gross margin is $0.30 of FY2027 EPS, so the margin, not unit volume, sets the value.
rows.mechanism: Component costs pass through the bill of materials faster than handset prices reset, so a hardware-led mix shift compresses margin exactly when revenue grows fastest.
rows.weakens: Apple has historically passed memory costs through via ASP and Pro mix, and Greater China grew 30% in the nine months of FY2026.

### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Services, at a 76.3% gross margin, are 40.3% of the gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue; products are not. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% on product mix and tariff refunds, and the 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of its $2.02 EPS to them. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S17, S68]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 quarterly EPS (S17); products gross margin of 39.9% compares with 36.9%, and memory prices rose 146% with the 10-Q warning that cost pressure will intensify (S6, S68). Two hundred basis points off trailing gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, or 6.0% of $8.72.
:::

### Cash conversion is real, but a liability accrual did the lifting

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M while net income rose $16,920M: non-cash add-backs added $1,956M more and working capital $16,366M more. The dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities, +$10,016M against −$15,161M a year earlier. Other non-current liabilities rose $13,531M to $55,080M while other current liabilities fell $4,128M to $62,259M, a combined $9,403M build that reconciles to the cash line within $613M; the prior year carries the ~$15.8B Irish State Aid settlement (cash taxes paid of $37,332M against a $15,381M provision), with the $15,552M added in FY2024 within $250M of the $15.8B payable. The line's clean history is $3,031M in FY2023, −$248M in FY2024 and $4,724M in FY2025, a $2,502M average, so the $14,101M it puts into trailing free cash flow is the soft spot. Replacing it with the $2,502M average gives $125,084M, or 0.97x conversion, a 2.5% free-cash-flow yield and 40.5x price to free cash flow; zeroing the line gives $122,582M and its best clean year $127,306M, so the defensible band is $122.6-127.3B, with $125.1B the midpoint; anything below $122.6B subtracts more than the line contains. The $13,270M of gross intangibles added against investing "other" of only $1,780M is consistent with the $13,531M build being deferred consideration — an unpaid purchase, which would make $123,152M the figure, inside the band. Deferred revenue is no cushion: 3.2% of trailing revenue, with only $7,260M of nine-month revenue out of the opening balance. [S5, S6]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, 7,773 characters)
Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.9% gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.3% gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. The counterpoint is that 14.1% growth on a $109,158M FY2025 base is $15,391M of incremental annual revenue at a 76.3% margin, more gross profit than most software companies generate in total. [S5, S6]

### What one device earns

Apple stopped disclosing unit shipments, so the most defensible unit is the active device. The table divides trailing-twelve-month flows by Apple's own installed-base statement; because that base is an earnings-call figure rather than a filed one, every line is an estimate.

The waterfall ends where most hardware businesses begin: there is no customer-acquisition payback period to compute, because Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays its assemblers. Payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M produced a cash conversion cycle of −56.8 days at 27 June 2026, against +39.2 days at Alphabet; each new device is cash-positive on day one. That advantage is not a scale economy a rival can buy with capital — it is the accounting consequence of owning the customer and outsourcing the factory. [S6, S73]

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

### The cost side has turned

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% a year earlier, and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin, and concedes that price increases "may also reduce demand" — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed. [S17, S68]

### What this means for the watchlist

The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value. That structure justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court, and much of the rest faces a memory cycle that turns faster than Apple can re-price handsets. At $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the market capitalisation is $5,072B, or 39.3x trailing EPS of $8.72; the price already assumes the annuity survives intact and that memory costs are passed through. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. arguments.markdown:
Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.9% gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.3% gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. Consensus puts iPhone revenue at $252.4bn for FY2026 and $277.4bn for FY2027, a 9.9% step that assumes the price-and-mix cycle repeats without unit growth. [S5, S6, S71]

### What one device earns

Apple stopped disclosing unit shipments, so the most defensible unit is the active device. The table divides trailing-twelve-month flows by Apple's own installed-base statement; because that base is an earnings-call figure rather than a filed one, every line is an estimate.

| Line item | Per unit — per active device, per year | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $186.7 | $466,823M TTM ÷ 2,500M devices | S6, S73 |
| of which Services | $48.2 | $120,478M TTM ÷ 2,500M | S6, S73 |
| Gross profit | $90.8 | 48.7% blended gross margin | S6 |
| Selling, general and administrative | ($11.7) | $29,363M TTM | S6 |
| Research and development | ($17.2) | $42,901M TTM | S6 |
| Operating profit | $61.9 | $154,859M TTM | S6 |
| Gross profit ÷ selling cost | 7.8x a year | $90.8 ÷ $11.7 | S6 |
| Cash payback on acquisition | immediate | cash conversion cycle −56.8 days | S5, S6 |

The waterfall ends where most hardware businesses begin: there is no customer-acquisition payback period to compute, because Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays its assemblers. Payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M produced a cash conversion cycle of −56.8 days at 27 June 2026, against +39.2 days at Alphabet; each new device is cash-positive on day one. The unit count is the weak link, and Apple discloses none: the $941 implied iPhone price rests on a 261M-unit estimate, and on a 20% share of the 1.26B units shipped in 2025 it is $832, while on about 238M units in 2026 (23.6% of IDC's 1.01B) the $252.4bn consensus is $1,060 — a 27% rise that is memory pass-through and Pro mix, not evidence of an upgrade cycle. That advantage is not a scale economy a rival can buy with capital; it is the accounting consequence of owning the customer and outsourcing the factory. [S6, S73, S74, S84, S92, S99]

| Offer | Price or take rate | Margin or peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (upfront hardware) | implied ASP $941 on 261M estimated units; $832-1,060 across unit bases | products gross margin 39.9% | S6, S74, S92 |
| App Store (commission, ex-EU) | 15-30%; the 27% link-out commission was ruled prohibitive | services gross margin 76.3% | S6, S69 |
| App Store (EU, from 2026-10-01) | 26% in-app purchase, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission | EU band 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere | S77, S78 |
| Safari default search | 36% of Safari search advertising; $20B in 2022 | 16.6% of TTM services revenue | S70 |
| Subscriptions and cloud | recurring, bundled at the device sale | services 76.3% vs Microsoft 67.9% in FY2026 | S6, S49 |
| Handset peer — Samsung devices (DX) | — | KRW 0.8tn operating loss in Q3 2026 | S75 |

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

### The cost side has turned, and the multiple is buying a margin

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% a year earlier, and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%, and Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed, and the FY2027 EPS of $9.79 that the $284 base case and the $270 entry divide by requires 48.0%, with each 100 basis points worth $0.30 of that EPS. At $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the market capitalisation is $5,034bn on the 14,608,963 thousand shares outstanding at 27 June 2026 — 39.5x trailing diluted EPS of $8.72 — and that price already assumes the annuity survives intact and that memory costs are passed through. The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value: that justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. [S6, S7, S17, S68]

::: evidence
**The services annuity is what the multiple buys, and it is a smaller share of revenue than it was a year ago.**

Services produced $120,478M of trailing-twelve-month revenue — 25.8% of the total but 40.3% of gross profit and 2.1x company R&D — while its revenue share fell to 25.2% in the nine months to 27 June 2026 as iPhone revenue grew 22.4% against services growth of 14.1% (S5, S6, S17). Two tolls inside that line, the App Store commission and the Safari search licence worth 16.6% of services revenue on a 2022 court figure, are both under active legal challenge (S69, S70).
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 6 by Valuation Analyst, 8,957 characters)
Apple's only exit is the public market and its own buyback, and at $344.63 the shares already discount the scenario bull. No peer is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,071.2bn market value (14,715m diluted shares at $344.63) — so a holder's realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. With dividend and gross buyback yielding 1.9% and earnings per share compounding at 8-9%, the arithmetic is adequate only while the 39.3x multiple holds; if it reverts toward the four-year average of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to 1.3% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, and treat $380 and above as a sale [S7, S11, S6].

| Metric | Value | Implication | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average daily volume | 40.41m shares and $13.84bn (20-day); 41.34m and $13.56bn (3-month) | A $250m position is 1.8% of one day's value traded; $1bn is 7.2% | S7 |
| Shares outstanding | 14,715m diluted at 2026-06-27; the proxy's 14,697.9m basic at 2026-01-02 is 0.1% lower | Free float effectively 100%; one count for the market cap | S6, S11 |
| Largest holders | Vanguard 9.63%; BlackRock 7.10% | Index managers, no controlling or strategic holder | S11 |
| Directors and officers | 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% | Aligned, but immaterial to the register | S11 |

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed: Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any position a long-only fund would take, so the exit is never closed and market impact is measured in basis points. The intended holding period is three years. What cannot be dismissed is price: the buyers on the other side are the same index and active funds the seller competes with, and in a broad de-rating they mark the same multiple down together.

| Component | Rate | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Dividend yield | 0.31% ($1.08 annualised on $344.63) | S17, S7 |
| Buyback yield, gross | 1.62% ($82.2bn repurchased on a $5,071.2bn market value) | S6, S7 |
| Buyback yield, net of $13.7bn stock compensation | 1.35% | S6, S7 |
| Total shareholder yield | 1.93% | S6, S7 |

| Three-year return, multiple reverts to 31.0x | 1.3% a year | S7, S97 |

Two things follow. The operating return is real but modest: a 1.9% yield plus 8% earnings growth is a high-single-digit compounding machine, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. And the buyback does much of the work, buying a 2.5% earnings yield per dollar at 39.3x, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so it supports the price without creating value at this level. That is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital, but an investor paying 39.3x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.3x trailing and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month average of 35.7x. A reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x costs 21.1% of the price, or 7.6% a year over three years, which swallows the entire shareholder yield and most of the earnings growth. With the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount on cash flows after 2035 is materially higher than when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |

| Issuer repurchase | Apple Inc., under its board authorisation | $82.2bn in the twelve months to June 2026; $100bn authorised in May 2025 | Continuous; next authorisation with the May 2027 results | High | S6, S5 |
| Dividend | Apple Inc. | $0.27 a quarter, raised annually | Quarterly, with an annual increase each May | High | S17 |
| Strategic acquisition | No buyer large enough: the four largest peers are all smaller than Apple | Antitrust review in the US, EU, China and UK would follow any bid; a foreign buyer would also face CFIUS national-security review | Not foreseeable | Negligible | S14, S16, S108, S110 |
| Break-up or activist | None identified | Sum of the parts is $177-238 a share against a $5,071.2bn market value | No campaign disclosed | Negligible | S6, S17 |
| Passive flows | S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 index funds | Largest company in the peer set | Quarterly rebalancing | Structural, not a decision | S11 |

No listing or lock-up constraint applies: the shares already trade on NasdaqGS, and only the buyback blackout around results restricts the issuer. The open market is the route that matters, and the price at which it clears is the only variable the holder controls.

The precedents are all capital returns, because that is the only exit a company of this size has ever offered its holders. They also show the cost of buying back stock at the top: the FY2024 and FY2025 programmes together spent $185.6bn at 34-38x earnings, and those shares would have been retired 18-26% cheaper at the FY2023 multiple. | Entry price | Exit at 27x | Exit at 31x | Exit at 34x | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $344.63 (2026-10-30) | -3.2% | 1.3% | 4.5% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $300 | 1.4% | 6.1% | 9.4% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $270 | 5.0% | 9.9% | 13.3% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $240 | 9.2% | 14.3% | 17.9% | S6, S7, S97 |

A long-only fund earns its 9% hurdle from $270, not from $344; the shares are a buy only on a de-rating or on evidence that FY2027-28 earnings growth is running above 12% rather than the 9.9% consensus assumes for iPhone revenue. I would raise the entry price on services growing above 10% with the Google payment intact, gross margin held above 48% through the memory cycle, and a buyback authorisation above $100bn. I would sell on services growth below 8% for two quarters, gross margin below 46%, normalised free cash flow conversion below 0.9x net income, a buyback cut, or any remedy that removes the Google payment. A multiple above 45x forward, $440, would be a sale on valuation alone [S71, S72, S7].

The bear case sets the drawdown to expect, not just the return. Two independent methods converge on $241-243: a reversion to Apple's 2022 multiple of 24.6x on FY2027E earnings gives $241, and the $243.42 low the shares actually printed within the past twelve months is $243. That is a 30% drawdown. The DCF bear of $133 is a different animal — gross margin compression, 2-4% growth and a 9.5% discount rate together — and should be read as the permanent-loss scenario rather than the trading risk. The buyback limits both: the same $82-85bn a year retires 2.1% of the shares at $270 and 2.3% at $240, against 1.6% at today's price, so each leg down raises the forward earnings growth the buyer receives [S7, S6].

The strongest argument against this discipline is that it has been wrong before. Apple has compounded while the technology sector fell in the last month, and a fund that sold on valuation last year would have forgone most of that gain; multiples of this quality have held through a high long-bond yield that most models said would compress them. That is a reason to size modestly and buy on weakness rather than to abandon the arithmetic: the exit route is liquid, the cash return is real, and the only thing between today's price and the required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on multiple reversion. The open question is how much of services revenue the Google payment represents and when the appeal is decided; neither is publicly disclosed here and both set the floor under the services multiple."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 3 by Lead Analyst, 8,996 characters)
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base and services annuity are real, and FY2026 is strong: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. What is in dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,072bn market capitalisation, 39.3 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward. The decision is not whether Apple is a good business — it is — but whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three valuation methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; the DCF bull case at an 8.5% discount rate and a 35% operating margin gives $277; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year average multiple of 31.0 times implies $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth in net operating profit after tax. Those assumptions make the price exactly fair rather than cheap; the base rate is modest, with revenue compounding 3.3% a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value; this report sees 18% overvaluation: the median twelve-month target is $338-355, flat to +3% from the close [S142, S144]. Consensus expects iPhone revenue of $252.4bn in FY2026 and $277.4bn in FY2027 and capitalises the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin. The disagreement is specific: that margin included two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned (the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38%, memory 34% of it), and our base case underwrites 47-48%. A 46% margin, which a full memory pass-through implies, takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value to $270 at 29 times — the entry price below, not a discount to it. The non-consensus view is that the market is capitalising a peak margin and multiple at once.

Three scenarios weighted 25/50/25 put the probability-weighted value at $291.5, 15% below the price, and the recommendation rests on that weighted value and the $284 base case, not on the bull. The scenario bull ($357, 25%) — distinct from the $277 DCF bull above — assumes the AI and foldable cycle extends iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate: 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the search payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline, with intrinsic value of $212-264. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as the DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF bear as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 without a break-up: the asset survived, but the overhang ran three years and the settlement did not re-rate the stock — the cloud did, a decade later. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007, peaked near $250bn and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record, 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not [S143, S145, S147]. The rule they teach is that at a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.3x against 201), owns silicon and a services annuity Nokia never had, and holds $62.2bn of net cash; the analogy is about duration and multiple, not extinction.

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price, not narrative. The first tranche of 0.75-1.0% of the fund is $270 only on a condition: the 2026-11-02 guide must hold FY2027 EPS at $9.27 or better and gross margin at 47%. At 27.6 times, $270 is a discount only on the $9.79 base EPS; on $9.27 it is 29.1 times, and on $8.07-8.53, after a 12.9% search-payment cut, 31.7-33.5 times, above the 31.0 times four-year mean. At 27.6 times those lower cases imply $223-235, so if the guide fails the first tranche moves to $235 and the second to $210. The position reaches its 5% cap below $225 or on evidence that FY2027 EPS growth is tracking above 12%. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $242 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety, and the ladder now prices the EPS bridge rather than a single point at $9.79. The counter-evidence is the stock's own record: 27.5% in the twelve months to 30 October 2026; a sale at 35 times forward would have missed it. The open diligence is the appellate outcome on the search payment and a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, neither of which the register holds. Sell above $380 or above 45 times forward earnings ($440), or if two consecutive quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a services structure that removes the search payment [S6, S7].

Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month while the SPY fell 0.9% — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.97 times net income, 0.95 times at the low end of the normalised band, on capex of 2.2% of revenue; it holds $62,173M of net cash and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48% [S6, S17].

The price is the problem. At 39.3 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings against 18.09 times for the S&P 500, the shares discount a 7.0% cost of equity or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth; the DCF at 9.0% is $212, its 8.5% discount-rate bull is $277 (20% below the close), the sum of the parts is $177-238, and the base scenario is $284, 18% below the close. Two facts would change the call. A gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it; an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear toward the discounted-cash-flow floor. The view is non-consensus on price, not on franchise. The sell side's median target sits at the spot price, so the Street sees fair value where this analysis sees an overvaluation; the difference is the normalised margin and the exit multiple, not the quality of the installed base.

The composite score is 6.0 out of 10. Valuation scores 2 of 10 and carries the largest weight, 20%. The quality block is where the score earns its keep. Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Growth and regulation both score low, and together they explain why the recommendation is not merely to wait for a cheaper multiple. arguments.markdown:
Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.9% gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.3% gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. Consensus puts iPhone revenue at $252.4bn for FY2026 and $277.4bn for FY2027, a 9.9% step that assumes the price-and-mix cycle repeats without unit growth. [S5, S6, S71]

### What one device earns

Apple stopped disclosing unit shipments, so the most defensible unit is the active device. The table divides trailing-twelve-month flows by Apple's own installed-base statement; because that base is an earnings-call figure rather than a filed one, every line is an estimate.

| Line item | Per unit — per active device, per year | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $186.7 | $466,823M TTM ÷ 2,500M devices | S6, S73 |
| of which Services | $48.2 | $120,478M TTM ÷ 2,500M | S6, S73 |
| Gross profit | $90.8 | 48.7% blended gross margin | S6 |
| Selling, general and administrative | ($11.7) | $29,363M TTM | S6 |
| Research and development | ($17.2) | $42,901M TTM | S6 |
| Operating profit | $61.9 | $154,859M TTM | S6 |
| Gross profit ÷ selling cost | 7.8x a year | $90.8 ÷ $11.7 | S6 |
| Cash payback on acquisition | immediate | cash conversion cycle −56.8 days | S5, S6 |

The waterfall ends where most hardware businesses begin: there is no customer-acquisition payback period to compute, because Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays its assemblers. Payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M produced a cash conversion cycle of −56.8 days at 27 June 2026, against +39.2 days at Alphabet; each new device is cash-positive on day one. The unit count is the weak link, and Apple discloses none: the $941 implied iPhone price rests on a 261M-unit estimate, and on a 20% share of the 1.26B units shipped in 2025 it is $832, while on about 238M units in 2026 (23.6% of IDC's 1.01B) the $252.4bn consensus is $1,060 — a 27% rise that is memory pass-through and Pro mix, not evidence of an upgrade cycle. That advantage is not a scale economy a rival can buy with capital; it is the accounting consequence of owning the customer and outsourcing the factory. [S6, S73, S74, S84, S92, S99]

| Offer | Price or take rate | Margin or peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (upfront hardware) | implied ASP $941 on 261M estimated units; $832-1,060 across unit bases | products gross margin 39.9% | S6, S74, S92 |
| App Store (commission, ex-EU) | 15-30%; the 27% link-out commission was ruled prohibitive | services gross margin 76.3% | S6, S69 |
| App Store (EU, from 2026-10-01) | 26% in-app purchase, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission | EU band 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere | S77, S78 |
| Safari default search | 36% of Safari search advertising; $20B in 2022 | 16.6% of TTM services revenue | S70 |
| Subscriptions and cloud | recurring, bundled at the device sale | services 76.3% vs Microsoft 67.9% in FY2026 | S6, S49 |
| Handset peer — Samsung devices (DX) | — | KRW 0.8tn operating loss in Q3 2026 | S75 |

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

### The cost side has turned, and the multiple is buying a margin

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% a year earlier, and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%, and Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed, and the FY2027 EPS of $9.79 that the $284 base case and the $270 entry divide by requires 48.0%, with each 100 basis points worth $0.30 of that EPS. The risk runs both ways: Apple has passed component cycles through before by raising prices and shifting to Pro models, and Greater China grew 30% in the nine months, so margin could hold above 47% rather than break below it, in which case the earnings band and the entry price move up together. At $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the market capitalisation is $5,034bn on the 14,608,963 thousand shares outstanding at 27 June 2026 — 39.5x trailing diluted EPS of $8.72 — and that price already assumes the annuity survives intact and that memory costs are passed through. The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value: that justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. [S6, S7, S17, S68]

::: evidence
**The services annuity is what the multiple buys, and it is a smaller share of revenue than it was a year ago.**

Services produced $120,478M of trailing-twelve-month revenue — 25.8% of the total but 40.3% of gross profit and 2.1x company R&D — while its revenue share fell to 25.2% in the nine months to 27 June 2026 as iPhone revenue grew 22.4% against services growth of 14.1% (S5, S6, S17). Two tolls inside that line, the App Store commission and the Safari search licence worth 16.6% of services revenue on a 2022 court figure, are both under active legal challenge (S69, S70).
:::

Apple is a high-quality compounder whose price already capitalises a peak margin and a contested services annuity, so the risks that matter destroy the multiple, not the balance sheet, and none is priced at $344.63. At that price on 2026-10-30 the shares trade at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median, and the base DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212. Eight risks follow: two are fatal to the price, the rest execution. The strategic risk is AI defending the price without widening the moat. [S7, S97, S10]

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |

| Memory cost pushes hardware gross margin below 46% | High, over 60% | EPS -6% per 200bp; -25% to -30% value | Critical | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | Product margin under 37%; DRAM/NAND prices | Enter at $270 only on the $9.27+ EPS case | S17, S6, S99, S136 |
