rows.finding: IDC forecasts 2026 smartphone shipments at just over 1.0B units (-16.7%, steepest annual fall on record) while market value rises 6.3% to $613B and ASP rises 27.6% to $581.
rows.mechanism: NAND/DRAM costs up more than 300% YoY are passed through to shelf prices, so dollars grow while units fall; the sub-$100 segment (173M units in 2025) fell ~60% in Q2 2026 and emerging markets are forecast down over 20%.
rows.benchmark: 2025: ~1.26B units, +2% (Counterpoint); 2026 value $613B vs bottom-up 1.0B x $581 = $581B.
rows.weakens: Demand destruction and affordability limits mean the value growth is cost-driven, not a healthy cycle; it can reverse when memory normalises in 2028.
rows.implication: Apple revenue growth must come from price/mix and share, not market volume; do not capitalise 2026 growth as a trend.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What share of Apple's FY2026 iPhone growth is units versus price/mix?

rows.finding: Premium handsets (wholesale ASP $600+) reached 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026, up from 25% in H1 2025 and 20% in H1 2022; Apple took 65% of premium units with 9% growth.
rows.mechanism: Rising memory costs push the whole market up-price, mechanically expanding the premium segment and concentrating value in the vendor with the strongest premium brand.
rows.benchmark: Apple global unit share 20% in 2025 (Counterpoint); IDC expects iOS share to reach a record 23.6% in 2026 as Android falls 24.3%.
rows.weakens: The premium-share gain is partly inflation of the price boundary, not Apple winning new buyers at constant prices.
rows.implication: Apple's value capture is durable but cyclical; the franchise is pricing power, and it is being tested by a 20-30% price increase.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Does premium unit growth continue if ASPs rise again in 2027?

rows.finding: Greater China shipments were ~66M units in Q2 2026 (-4.3%, fifth straight decline), with Apple at 18.1% and Huawei at 22.6%; IDC expects the decline to widen to ~20% in H2 2026 and recovery only in 2028-2029.
rows.mechanism: A shrinking pool plus a resurgent local champion means share gains do not compound; Apple's price hold and pull-forward ahead of H2 price rises flattered Q2.
rows.benchmark: Apple Greater China revenue +30% in 9M FY2026 (company filing) against a market down 4.2% in H1 2026.
rows.weakens: The +30% China revenue growth is not a durable market recovery; it is share gain plus timing in a declining market.
rows.implication: Treat China as the swing risk to the growth story; H2 FY2026 and FY2027 comps are the test.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: How much of the China revenue surge was pull-forward ahead of price increases?

rows.finding: Wearables: ~148M units in Q2 2026 (+2.7%); Apple 15.5% share, Xiaomi 11.7%, Huawei 10.9%; 2026 forecast ~625M units (+1.7%) and a 2.4% CAGR to ~687M units by 2030, with smartwatches -3.7% in 2026 and glasses +35.2%.
rows.mechanism: Category mix is shifting toward glasses and rings, where Apple is not the leader; smartwatches and wristbands are shrinking.
rows.benchmark: Apple's share was 21.0% in Q4 2025 and 18.9% in Q3 2025; Huawei leads smartwatches at 18.8% vs Apple 17.2%.
rows.weakens: Wearables cannot be underwritten as a second growth engine to 2030.
rows.implication: Value the wearables segment as a low-growth attachment business, not a re-rating driver.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Will Apple enter AI glasses before 2028, and at what price?

rows.finding: Services pools are large but contested: global advertising $1.34T in 2026 (+11.9%), App Store ecosystem billings ~$1.4T in 2025 of which ~$149B digital goods commissionable, and Apple services revenue $120.5B TTM (+14.1% in 9M FY2026).
rows.mechanism: Apple monetises a small slice of advertising and a large slice of app digital goods; growth comes from installed-base monetisation and price, not from a growing addressable market alone.
rows.benchmark: Spotify has 300M paying subscribers vs Apple Music's estimated 100-108M; Alphabet's total revenue is $471B TTM, nearly four times Apple's services.
rows.weakens: Services growth is partly price- and commission-driven, and the EU DMA cuts the take rate on external distribution to 5% from October 2026.
rows.implication: Services can grow low-to-mid teens for now, but the terminal take rate is regulated downward in Europe.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What is the revenue-per-installed-device trend excluding price increases?

rows.finding: The PC market fell 4.9% to 68.2M units in Q2 2026 while Apple grew Mac shipments 10.1% to 9.9% share, behind Lenovo 24.4%, HP 19.1% and Dell 13.6%.
rows.mechanism: Apple gains share in a shrinking, price-inflating market through new models (MacBook Neo) and vertical integration of silicon.
rows.benchmark: Mac revenue $33.7B in FY2025, 8.1% of Apple revenue; +9% in 9M FY2026.
rows.weakens: Mac is too small to move group growth, and IDC sees a sharp H2 2026 slowdown as price rises bite.
rows.implication: Mac is a share-gainer and margin supporter, not the growth thesis.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does Mac share hold when PC prices rise again in 2027?

rows.finding: Policy changes the market's economics: EU DMA terms from 2026-10-01 cut commissions to 26% for in-app purchase, 20% for alternative payments and 5% for apps distributed outside the App Store; US tariffs moved twice in 2026 (IEEPA tariffs struck down 2026-02-20, Section 301 duties imposed, Section 232 review imposed no additional tariffs on Apple products on 2026-01-14).
rows.mechanism: Regulation lowers the platform take rate in Europe and adds cost volatility in the US, directly changing services gross margin and product cost.
rows.benchmark: Headline App Store commission outside the EU remains 30%/15%; the EU external-distribution rate is 5%.
rows.weakens: The view that Apple's services margin is structurally protected.
rows.implication: Apply a lower terminal take rate to EU services and a tariff risk premium to US hardware cost.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What share of services revenue is EU App Store commission, and how fast will developers shift distribution?

rows.finding: Samsung's MX and Networks division had Q3 2026 revenue of KRW37.7T (+10.55% YoY) but an operating loss of KRW0.6T, its second consecutive quarterly loss, despite flagship and foldable launches.

rows.benchmark: Apple products gross margin 40.1% in Q3 FY2026; Samsung group profit driven by memory, not handsets.
rows.weakens: Samsung's group memory profits subsidise the mobile division, so it can sustain losses longer than a standalone handset maker.
rows.implication: Samsung is the broadest direct competitor but cannot profitably undercut Apple in premium; its mobile losses limit the price war it can sustain.

rows.benchmark: Apple Mac revenue $33.7B FY2025; +9% in 9M FY2026.
rows.weakens: IDC expects a sharp PC slowdown in H2 2026, and Apple raised prices in line with the market.
rows.implication: Mac is a genuine share-gainer against Lenovo/HP/Dell, but at 8% of Apple revenue it cannot change the group trajectory.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does Mac hold share when PC prices rise again in 2027?

rows.finding: Apple's services business ($120.5B TTM, +14.1% in 9M FY2026) competes with Alphabet, whose total revenue reached $471B TTM and grew 23.6% in the first nine months of 2026, and with Spotify at 300M paying subscribers versus Apple Music's estimated 100-108M.
rows.mechanism: Alphabet monetises search and YouTube advertising at global scale, while Apple monetises App Store commissions and subscriptions on iOS only.
rows.benchmark: Apple services revenue $120.5B TTM at 76.3% gross margin; Alphabet revenue $471B TTM and +23.6% in 9M 2026.
rows.weakens: Apple's services gross margin (76.3%) is far above Alphabet's blended margin, so revenue scale understates Apple's profit pool.
rows.implication: Apple is a sub-scale challenger in advertising and a follower in music streaming; services strength is distribution over its own base, not market leadership.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: How much of services growth is users versus price and commission mix?

rows.finding: From 2026-10-01 Apple charges 26% on App Store in-app purchase, 20% on alternative payment processing, 15% on link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed via alternative marketplaces or the web in the EU; it lost its DMA appeal on 2026-07-08 after a EUR500M fine in 2025.
rows.mechanism: DMA-mandated alternative distribution lowers switching costs out of the App Store and gives rival platforms a distribution channel on iOS.
rows.benchmark: EU in-app commission 26% (15% for small business/after year one) versus 5% for external distribution; Apple lost its DMA appeal on 2026-07-08 and was fined EUR500M in 2025.
rows.weakens: The 5% rate applies only to external distribution and the EU is a minority of App Store revenue; global take rates remain 30%/15%.
rows.implication: Regulation is a competitive force that transfers margin from Apple to developers and rivals such as Spotify and Epic, capping services pricing power in Europe.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What share of EU digital-goods developers will move to external distribution at a 5% rate?

plan.decision_question: Is Apple gaining or losing competitive position, product by product and region by region?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple is winning the competition for profit and price while ceding unit share in China: it holds 65% of premium phone units and a 40% product gross margin, but Huawei is taking premium share in a shrinking China market and regulation is capping the services take rate, so its competitive position is strengthening in hardware, holding in services and weakening at the margin in China.
plan.why_different: This section compares rivals per product and region and names the most dangerous competitor; the market section sizes the pools and the financial section owns margins and cash.
plan.mechanism: Apple converts a premium brand and integrated silicon/OS into 65% of premium phone units and 40% product gross margin, while competitors win units at thin or negative margins; regulation and AI attack the platform rent that converts devices into services profit.
plan.comparison_set: Apple 65% of premium units and 23.6% iOS share vs Samsung 19-23% global, Xiaomi 11.5%, Huawei 22.6% in China; Alphabet revenue $471B TTM vs Apple services $120.5B TTM.
plan.counter_evidence: Huawei is taking premium share in a shrinking China market, Android premiumisation and price inflation are compressing Apple's price umbrella, AI assistants could commoditise the OS layer, and DMA cuts the EU take rate to 5% on external distribution.
plan.visual: Per-product competitor table, positioning table and SWOT quad.
plan.prohibited: fierce competition, well positioned, strong team, high barriers to entry, huge market, vague counts, any sentence about report construction

competition.author: Market Analyst
queries: China smartphone market Q3 2026 Apple share Huawei Counterpoint October 2026
IDC China smartphone shipments Q3 2026 Apple 17.8% Huawei 21.1% market down 15.4%
Counterpoint global smartphone shipments grew 2% in 2025 vendor shares
Counterpoint Apple 65% premium smartphone market H1 2026
Samsung Q3 2026 mobile experience division loss revenue
Xiaomi Q2 2026 smartphone gross margin memory costs
EU DMA Apple App Store commission Core Technology Commission 2026 alternative app stores

rows.finding: China Q3 2026 (published October 2026): shipments -10% YoY, lowest Q3 since 2012; Huawei 21.3%, Apple 19.5% and second, up 4.8 points YoY and from sixth a year earlier; Huawei and Apple the only top brands to gain share (40% combined); iPhone 18 Pro series first-three-week sales +23.5% YoY.
rows.mechanism: In a memory-cost contraction, vendors with premium mix and pricing power gain share as the pool shrinks; Apple's gain comes from mix and price-holding, not from a larger market.
rows.benchmark: Q2 2026 Counterpoint/IDC: Apple 18.1% versus Huawei 22.6% in a market down 4.2% in H1 2026 (S87).
rows.weakens: The Q2 2026 figures remain true for that quarter but are no longer the latest reading; any claim of continuing share loss is falsified.
rows.implication: Restate the China risk as a shrinking market with price-led pull-forward, not lost share; the earlier 'deteriorating on share' line is contradicted by newer data.
rows.confidence: high: two independent trackers agree on direction (Apple up, Huawei leading, market down); the magnitude differs (-10% versus -15.4%).
rows.follow_up: How much of Apple's Q3 2026 China gain is pull-forward ahead of the iPhone 18 Pro price increase and the split launch?

rows.finding: IDC Q3 2026 China: market -15.4% YoY; Apple 17.8% share, up from 15.8%, although its shipments fell 4.3%; Huawei 21.1%, shipments +17.3%; IDC expects component costs elevated through much of 2027 and continued significant market declines; iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max +$100 and iPhone Duo from $1,999 on 2026-10-23.
rows.mechanism: Price increases needed to cover memory costs accelerate replacement-cycle extension, so unit pools shrink faster than dollar value; share gains inside a shrinking pool do not protect revenue.
rows.benchmark: Apple's Greater China revenue +30% in 9M FY2026 (S6) against a market down 10-15% in Q3 2026.
rows.weakens: Cuts against the 'Apple is losing China' narrative and against the 'Apple is recovering China' narrative in equal measure.
rows.implication: The risk to underwrite is market size and the durability of price, not Apple's relative position; size positions smaller and watch the H2 2026 decline.
rows.confidence: medium: single house (IDC preliminary), and its decline is 5.4 points steeper than Counterpoint's.
rows.follow_up: Does IDC's steeper decline reflect channel inventory or genuine sell-through?

rows.finding: Apple took 65% of $600-plus phone units in H1 2026 with 9% growth, while premium reached 29% of global units (25% H1 2025, 20% H1 2022); Apple's 42.7% of the $613B 2026 value pool on 23.6% of units.
rows.mechanism: Premium concentration plus installed-base services monetisation lets Apple convert a minority unit position into a majority profit position.
rows.benchmark: Samsung 19% global units 2025 and 23% in Q3 2026; Xiaomi 11.5% in Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: Value capture is flattered by the 27.6% ASP jump, part of which is memory-cost pass-through rather than brand pricing power.
rows.implication: The profit pool is defensible even as units fall; this is the core of a quality-compounder case.
rows.confidence: medium-high: Counterpoint and IDC agree on premium concentration; the value-capture ratio is a calculation from filings and tracker data.
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's premium share measured in revenue rather than units?

rows.finding: Samsung's MX and Networks division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 despite 10.55% revenue growth; Xiaomi's handset gross margin was 8.5% with profit -42.6% in Q2 2026.
rows.mechanism: The memory shock compresses Android OEM margins first, because they lack Apple's mix and silicon/OS integration; they cannot buy share indefinitely.
rows.benchmark: Apple product gross margin 40.1% in Q3 FY2026 versus 34.5% a year earlier (S17).
rows.weakens: Samsung's loss is partly division accounting (MX includes lower-margin mass segments) and could reverse if memory prices normalise.
rows.implication: The nearest Android rivals are financially constrained at the moment Apple is gaining premium share; supports relative-position strength into FY2027.
rows.confidence: medium: company results reported through secondary outlets, not the filings themselves.
rows.follow_up: How much of Samsung's MX loss is memory cost versus mass-segment mix?

rows.finding: EU DMA: from 2026-10-01 Apple charges 26% on in-app purchases, 20% on alternative payment processing, 15% on link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed externally, after a EUR500M DMA fine in 2025.
rows.mechanism: Regulation lowers switching costs out of the App Store, transferring distribution rent to Spotify, Epic and alternative storefronts in a region that is 26.7% of Apple revenue.
rows.benchmark: Spotify 300M paying subscribers versus an estimated 100-108M for Apple Music (S93).
rows.weakens: Developer behaviour under the new fee structure is unobserved; most small developers may still prefer the 15% small-business rate in-app.
rows.implication: Services growth has a regulated ceiling in Europe; price the take-rate risk rather than extrapolating 14% services growth.
rows.confidence: medium-high on the fee schedule; low on the revenue effect, which depends on developer migration.
rows.follow_up: What share of EU App Store billings has moved to external distribution since 2026-10-01?

rows.finding: Status quo: replacement cycles are lengthening; IDC expects China recovery only in 2028-2029 and a smaller, more concentrated market after the memory crisis; the sub-$100 segment (173M units in 2025) fell nearly 60% in Q2 2026.
rows.mechanism: When the cheapest segment disappears, demand is rationed by ability to pay, which favours premium vendors but shrinks the addressable unit base.
rows.benchmark: Base rate: Apple revenue compounded 3.3% FY2021-FY2025 (S5).
rows.weakens: The premium-mix benefit could persist longer than the base rate implies if memory costs stay high through 2027.
rows.implication: Do not capitalise the 16% nine-month FY2026 growth; underwrite a return to high-single-digit growth at best.
rows.confidence: medium: IDC forecast, single house.
rows.follow_up: What replacement-cycle length does IDC assume for 2027-2030?

plan.decision_question: Is Apple gaining or losing competitive position, product by product and region by region, as the smartphone market contracts in units?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple is winning the competition for profit and price and, since Q3 2026, for share in a shrinking China market: it holds 65% of premium phone units and a 40.1% product gross margin, Huawei leads China 21.3% to Apple's 19.5% but Apple gained 4.8 points, and regulation caps the services take rate, so the position is strengthening in hardware, holding in services and exposed to market size rather than to share loss.
plan.why_different: This section maps rival-by-rival and product-by-product position and pricing power; the market section sizes the pools and the regional revenue base, and the risk section prices the failure modes.
plan.mechanism: In a memory-cost shock the market reprices upward and shrinks in units; vendors with premium mix, vertical integration and pricing power gain share and margin while Android OEMs with single-digit margins lose both. Regulation (DMA) then caps the services rent that the hardware position would otherwise monetise.
plan.comparison_set: Samsung (volume leader, loss-making mobile division), Xiaomi (value flagship, 8.5% handset margin), Huawei (China premium leader, HarmonyOS scale), Alphabet (advertising and AI platform), Microsoft (PC and cloud), plus the status quo of longer device life.
plan.counter_evidence: The China share gain is partly price-led pull-forward ahead of iPhone 18 Pro increases and a split launch; the market may shrink 10-15% a year into 2027; Android premiumisation and AI features (Gemini-integrated Pixel, HarmonyOS) could erode iOS differentiation; services growth may be price-driven, with the DMA capping take rates.
plan.visual: Competitor table plus positioning table, with the SWOT quad carrying the profit-versus-share split.
plan.prohibited: fierce competition; well positioned; high barriers to entry; huge market; clear business model; risks are manageable; about/many/various as counts; internal tool, record or bot names; any sentence about how the section is written

queries: Epic Games Ninth Circuit link-out commission ruling 2025
Epic Games Store iOS EU alternative marketplace 2026
OpenAI ChatGPT weekly active users 2026 official

rows.finding: The Ninth Circuit held on 2025-12-11 that Apple's 27% commission on link-outs had a prohibitive effect; from 2026-10-01 Apple charges 26% on in-app purchases, 15% on link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web in the EU.
rows.mechanism: Regulation and litigation set a ceiling on the take rate, converting a rent that was 30% into 5-15%, and the DMA compels Apple to admit rival storefronts in a region that is 26.7% of revenue.
rows.benchmark: The 30% standard commission and the 27% link-out fee that the court found prohibitive.
rows.weakens: No alternative storefront discloses EU share, so the volume loss is unproven; Apple's store remains the default outside the EU.
rows.implication: Price a regulated ceiling on services margin rather than a collapse; the EU is the template to watch for the US and Japan.
rows.confidence: high: court opinion and Apple's own fee schedule.
rows.follow_up: What share of EU developers have moved to external distribution, and at what effective take rate?

rows.finding: ChatGPT reached 900M weekly active users and 50M paying subscribers by 2026-02-27, while Google pays Apple about $20B a year for the Safari default.
rows.mechanism: If assistants intermediate search, the search-licensing rent that costs Apple nothing to earn is at risk before any App Store commission is.
rows.benchmark: Apple's Services revenue of $120.5B trailing twelve months, of which the search payment is the highest-margin component.
rows.weakens: OpenAI does not disclose how much usage displaces search; Apple's services grew 14.1% in nine months, so displacement is not yet visible.
rows.implication: The assistant threat is unpriced in current estimates; size it as an option value on the search rent.
rows.confidence: medium: user figures are company-reported via media, and the displacement is inferred.
rows.follow_up: What share of iOS queries now start in an assistant rather than Safari or Spotlight?

rows.finding: In Q2 2026 Windows personal computing device shipments fell 6.7% while macOS grew 17.4%; Apple held 18.2% of PCD units to Lenovo's 20.1%; Windows on Arm share is not disclosed by Microsoft or IDC.
rows.mechanism: Microsoft's Copilot+ and Windows on Arm programme has not yet converted into share against the Mac; the PC pool is anyway too small to threaten Apple's profit pool.
rows.benchmark: Mac revenue of $33.7B in FY2025 against iPhone's $209.6B.
rows.weakens: Weakens the case that Microsoft is a near-term threat to Apple; the measurable trend runs the other way.
rows.implication: Microsoft belongs in the competitor set but not in the near-term risk case; monitor enterprise Copilot attach instead.
rows.confidence: high: IDC tracker and Microsoft filing.
rows.follow_up: What is Windows on Arm's unit share, and is Microsoft gaining in commercial fleets?

rows.finding: The AI Index puts DeepSeek-R1 level with the top US model in February 2025 and the US lead at 2.7% by March 2026; Apple has licensed Gemini for its next Siri.
rows.mechanism: When frontier capability is available from open weights and multiple vendors, model quality stops being a chargeable differentiator and becomes a purchased input.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own on-device foundation-model papers, which describe small models rather than frontier ones.
rows.weakens: Capability parity at the benchmark level does not equal parity in consumer experience or privacy, which is where Apple sells.
rows.implication: Do not credit Apple Intelligence as a pricing lever; treat the Gemini licence as a services cost line.
rows.confidence: medium: benchmark-based, with commercial impact inferred.
rows.follow_up: What does Apple pay Google for the Gemini licence, and is it expensed in services cost of sales?

rows.finding: Weixin reached 1,418M combined monthly users at 2025-12-31, and Tencent's marketing services grew 19% to RMB145.0B on closed-loop ads into Mini Programs, Mini Shops and Mini Games.
rows.mechanism: Commerce inside a super-app bypasses Apple's billing, so China's distribution rent is set by a company Apple does not compete with on hardware.
rows.benchmark: Apple's China revenue growth of 30% in 9M FY2026 against a market down 10% in Q3 2026.
rows.weakens: Tencent does not say how much mini-programme commerce would otherwise have run through the App Store.
rows.implication: Cap the China services growth assumption below the group services rate.
rows.confidence: medium: primary data, directional inference.
rows.follow_up: How much of China's iOS digital spend runs inside mini-programmes?

rows.finding: Apple's newest foldable-hinge patent family is co-assigned with supplier Hangzhou Amphenol Phoenix; the earlier generation is solely Apple's (US10551880B1 granted 2020-02-04; US12164344B2 granted 2024-12-10).
rows.mechanism: A shared owner in the supply chain means the mechanical advantage over Samsung and Chinese entrants is partially licensable rather than exclusive.
rows.benchmark: Sole ownership of the earlier hinge generation.
rows.weakens: Weakens the claim that Apple's foldable entry creates a defensible hardware moat in 2027.
rows.implication: Value the foldable on category ASP and mix, not on an exclusivity premium.
rows.confidence: high: patent records.
rows.follow_up: Does the co-assignment give the supplier rights to license the hinge to other handset makers?

plan.decision_question: Which competitor takes which of Apple's profit pools, and how much of the profit pool is actually contestable?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's advantage is profit capture in hardware; its distribution rent is the exposed flank.
plan.why_different: Maps each rival to the specific profit pool it attacks with a size, rather than listing competitors; the market section sizes the pool, this one shows who takes which slice and why integration protects hardware but not distribution.
plan.mechanism: Apple's profit pools are hardware gross profit (protected by silicon and OS integration), App Store commission (protected only by switching costs that regulation is dismantling) and search licensing (protected only by the search default that assistants can bypass); each pool is attacked by a different class of competitor, so hardware strength does not defend the other two.
plan.comparison_set: Samsung and Huawei as the hardware benchmark; Xiaomi's 8.5% handset gross margin and Samsung's mobile loss as the margin base rate; Spotify and Epic as the distribution-rent precedents; Microsoft and OpenAI as the assistant-layer benchmark; Apple's FY2021-FY2025 history as the base rate for competitive stability.
plan.counter_evidence: Microsoft's Copilot and Windows on Arm programme has not taken share from the Mac (Windows -6.7% vs macOS +17.4% in Q2 2026), and no alternative storefront discloses EU volume, so the distribution threat is a price effect before it is a volume effect; Apple's services still grew 14.1% in nine months, which is the strongest evidence against an assistant-displacement story so far.
plan.visual: Per-product competitor table plus the substitute-to-profit-pool table and the positioning table.
plan.prohibited: fierce competition; high barriers to entry; well positioned; strong team; clear business model; risks are manageable; recently; about N; unqualified moat

queries: get_valuation_snapshot AAPL vs MSFT, GOOGL (SEC XBRL + Yahoo prices)

rows.finding: AAPL $344.63 at 2026-10-30T20:00Z on NasdaqGS in USD; market cap $5,029.6bn; EV $4,967.4bn; P/E 39.5x TTM, EV/Sales 10.6x, EV/EBITDA 29.6x, EV/EBIT 32.1x, FCF yield 2.7%, P/B 46.8x.
rows.mechanism: The multiple is set on trailing earnings that include a one-off tariff refund and on FCF flattered by working capital; both flatter the denominator and so understate the true multiple.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own fiscal year-end P/E 24.6x (FY2022), 27.9x (FY2023), 37.5x (FY2024), 34.2x (FY2025); EV/Sales 6.1x, 6.9x, 8.8x, 9.1x.
rows.weakens: TTM earnings and FCF are not clean run-rates; part of the 2026 step-up (revenue +16%) may be durable rather than one-off.
rows.implication: Current 39.5x is a 27% premium to the four-year mean of 31.0x and the highest EV/Sales in five years: the price already assumes improvement, so the margin of safety is negative.
rows.confidence: high - SEC XBRL plus timestamped Yahoo quotes
rows.follow_up: What is the FY2027 consensus EPS and revenue, and how much of FY2026 growth is tariff front-running?

rows.finding: Services gross margin 76.0% and products 39.1% on TTM revenue of $120.5bn services and $346.3bn products; consolidated gross margin 48.7% TTM and 50.1% in the June 2026 quarter (including ~2pp of tariff refunds).
rows.mechanism: Every 100bp of mix shift toward services adds roughly 37bp to consolidated gross margin at constant segment margins, which is why a hardware company reports software-like gross margins.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 services gross margin 75.4% ($82.3bn on $109.2bn) versus products 36.8%; consolidated 46.9% in FY2025.
rows.weakens: Apple does not disclose segment operating income, so services profitability is an estimate; the 2pp tariff-refund benefit will not repeat.
rows.implication: The services mix is the single largest support for the multiple; any regulatory or competitive hit to services margins moves the whole valuation, not just one segment.
rows.confidence: high for gross profit by segment (filing); medium for operating profit by segment (estimated allocation)
rows.follow_up: What share of services gross profit comes from App Store commission and from the Google default-search payment?

rows.finding: Nine-month FY2026 operating cash flow $116,996m versus $81,754m a year earlier; of the $35,242m increase, $25,177m is a favourable swing in 'other current and non-current liabilities' (+$10,016m versus -$15,161m) and $2,631m is receivables.
rows.mechanism: Working-capital and accrual timing, not earnings, produced most of the cash-flow step-up, so trailing FCF overstates recurring cash generation.
rows.benchmark: TTM FCF $136.7bn (2.7% yield) versus a working-capital-normalised $111.5bn (2.2% yield, 45x) - my estimate; FY2025 FCF was $98.8bn.
rows.weakens: The 10-Q aggregates the liability line, so the reversal timing is unknown and part may be structural (deferred revenue, accrued taxes).
rows.implication: On normalised FCF the shares are 45x, not 37x; the buyback and the DCF must be run on the lower number.
rows.confidence: medium - the swing is disclosed, its composition is not
rows.follow_up: What sits inside the $25.2bn other-liabilities swing, and does it reverse in FY2027?

rows.finding: June 2026 quarter revenue $109,417m, +16.4% y/y; iPhone $54,252m (+21.7%), Services $30,739m (+12.1%), Greater China $18,816m (+22.4%); diluted EPS $2.02 (+28.7%) including $0.11 from tariff refunds.
rows.mechanism: A hardware upgrade cycle plus a China recovery re-accelerated revenue far above the FY2023-FY2025 trend, which is the fundamental case for a premium multiple.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 revenue growth +6.4%, FY2024 +2.0%, FY2023 -2.8%; TTM revenue $466.8bn (+12.2%).
rows.weakens: One quarter; iPhone and China are the most cyclical lines and the easiest to have been pulled forward by tariff timing.
rows.implication: The growth-to-GDP bear case is contradicted for now; the question is whether 16% is a cycle peak that the 39.5x multiple capitalises as permanent.
rows.confidence: high - company's own 8-K press release
rows.follow_up: What is the iPhone unit versus price/mix split in the June quarter, and what does the September quarter guide to?

rows.finding: Peer multiples at 2026-10-30: Apple 39.5x P/E and 32.1x EV/EBIT; Microsoft 27.3x and 23.6x; Alphabet 14.6x and 21.2x; Meta 21.0x and 19.9x; Amazon 19.4x and 25.5x; Dell 24.7x and 21.0x; HP 11.0x and 9.6x; median of the six 20.2x P/E and 20.5x EV/EBIT.
rows.mechanism: Apple's premium is a quality and duration premium: higher margins and returns than hardware peers, lower growth than the platform peers, and a more concentrated product line than either.
rows.benchmark: Apple trades at a 96% P/E premium and a 57% EV/EBIT premium to the peer median; against Microsoft alone the P/E premium is 45%.
rows.weakens: Alphabet's 14.6x P/E is an outlier that drags the median down; on EV/EBIT the peer set is tighter (19.9x-25.5x) and Apple's premium is 57%.
rows.implication: Even granting Apple the best margin structure in the group, the premium leaves no room for a services regulatory hit or a hardware air pocket.
rows.confidence: high for US peers; low for the global handset comparison
rows.follow_up: Samsung Electronics and Xiaomi multiples were not retrievable - what do they trade at on 2027 consensus?

rows.finding: DCF on FY2026E revenue of $477.0bn (my estimate from nine months' actual plus a $112.7bn fourth quarter), growth of 9%/8%/7%/6%/5%, 33% operating margin, 17.5% tax and capex 3.0% versus D&A 2.8%: equity value $229/share at an 8.5% WACC, $302 at 7.5%, $352 at 7.0%, $193 at 9.5%.
rows.mechanism: Nearly all of the valuation sits in the terminal value, so the answer is driven by the spread between WACC and terminal growth rather than by the near-term forecast.
rows.benchmark: The market price of $344.63 is matched at roughly a 7.0% WACC; my cost of equity from a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta is 9.7%.
rows.weakens: The cost of equity is an assumption; a 7% WACC (which some quality-growth models use) makes the current price fair rather than expensive.
rows.implication: The shares are fairly valued only if the required return is about 7%; at a defensible 9.0-9.5% cost of equity the DCF says $193-$212, a 38-44% downside.
rows.confidence: medium - inputs are disclosed, the discount rate is a judgement
rows.follow_up: What WACC does management's own capital-allocation hurdle imply, and does the buyback clear it at 39.5x?

rows.finding: Sum of the parts: services EBIT of $62.7bn (76.0% gross margin less 40% of corporate opex, an estimate) at 23x = $1,442bn; hardware EBIT of $92.1bn at 12x = $1,105bn; plus $62.2bn net cash = $2,609bn, or $177/share.
rows.mechanism: Applying market multiples to Apple's own segment margins, rather than to its consolidated earnings, strips out the scarcity premium the market pays for a single $5tn liquid compounder.
rows.benchmark: HP at 9.6x EV/EBIT and Dell at 21.0x for hardware; Microsoft at 23.6x and Meta at 19.9x for platform services.
rows.weakens: Segment EBIT is not disclosed, so the allocation of $72.3bn of opex is an assumption; a 60/40 split toward services raises the SOTP to about $194/share, still far below the market.
rows.implication: The market is paying about twice what the parts are worth at peer multiples - the gap is a liquidity and quality premium that can compress without any operating deterioration.
rows.confidence: medium - gross profit is filed, opex allocation is estimated
rows.follow_up: What multiple would a strategic or activist ascribe to services if App Store commission economics were halved?

rows.finding: Capital return: $82.2bn of buybacks and $15.6bn of dividends in the TTM to 2026-06-27, a 1.9% total shareholder yield; diluted shares 16,865m in FY2021 to 14,715m in the June 2026 quarter.
rows.mechanism: Buybacks at 39.5x earnings buy a 2.5% earnings yield, below the 4.93% risk-free rate and well below the cost of equity, so repurchases shrink the share count without creating value at this price.
rows.benchmark: Five-year revenue CAGR 5.0%, net income CAGR 6.4%, diluted EPS CAGR 9.2% - roughly 2.8 points a year of EPS growth came from the shrinking share count, not from operations.
rows.weakens: The buyback is price-sensitive: the same dollar amount retires 3.4% of the shares at $250 versus 1.7% at $345, so a de-rating mechanically raises future EPS growth.
rows.implication: Roughly 30% of historic EPS growth is financial engineering; if the buyback slows or the multiple compresses, the EPS growth that supports the valuation loses a leg.
rows.confidence: high - all figures from the filings

plan.decision_question: What is Apple worth today, and what price makes it an attractive long for a long-only fund?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder: at $344.63 the market capitalises $128.1bn of NOPAT at 38.8x, which requires about 6.9% perpetual growth or a 7.0% cost of capital, so a long-only buyer is accepting a ~7% expected return on a business whose own five-year revenue CAGR is 5.0%.
plan.why_different: This section is the only one that converts the operating story into a price: it owns the arithmetic of what the market is paying, the DCF, the sum of the parts and the entry threshold, and it must state a number at which the shares become a buy.
plan.mechanism: Apple's value is the present value of a slowly compounding cash flow with a very long duration; when the ten-year Treasury is 4.93% and the cost of equity is ~9.5%, the multiple the market pays (39.5x) discounts a 7% return, so the shares de-rate until either the discount rate falls or growth rises. Buybacks recycle cash at a 2.5% earnings yield and therefore support EPS without creating value at this price.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own FY2022-FY2025 year-end multiples (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x; four-year mean 31.0x), US platform peers (MSFT 27.3x, GOOGL 14.6x, META 21.0x, AMZN 19.4x on P/E; 19.9x-25.5x on EV/EBIT), hardware peers (HP 11.0x, Dell 24.7x P/E; 9.6x and 21.0x EV/EBIT) and a 9.0-9.5% cost of equity against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury.
plan.counter_evidence: Growth re-accelerated to +16.4% in the June 2026 quarter with a 50.1% gross margin, so the DCF's 9%-to-5% fade may understate the cycle; a 7% WACC (defensible in some quality-growth models) makes $344.63 fair; and the buyback's price sensitivity cushions any de-rating. Alphabet's 14.6x P/E also drags the peer median down and exaggerates Apple's premium.
plan.visual: Valuation methods table (method, inputs, value per share, weight) plus a WACC x terminal-growth sensitivity grid showing the market price is reached only near a 7% WACC.
plan.prohibited: No 'about 5', no 'strong moat', no 'well positioned', no 'huge', no unlabelled estimates, no claim that the DCF is precise, no repetition of the risk section's regulatory narrative beyond its valuation effect.

rows.benchmark: Prior iPhone 17 cycle and FY2025 iPhone growth; Q3 FY2026 iPhone +22% versus total company +16.4%.
rows.weakens: MacRumors reports Apple raised prices and repriced the iPhone 17 to $899 while memory costs rise, so unit elasticity is untested; the Duo's durability and yield are unproven.
rows.implication: The hardware cycle is not maturing yet; it is being re-priced. Watch Q4 FY2026 (2026-11-02) for whether mix held through launch.
rows.confidence: high — launch and pricing from Apple's own release; revenue from the 10-Q
rows.follow_up: What are Duo first-quarter units and return/warranty rates, and did Pro mix hold in the December 2026 quarter?

rows.finding: The rebuilt Siri shipped on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English only, running on a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed 2026-01-12; Bloomberg reported the model at 1.2 trillion parameters and about $1bn a year (neither company confirmed the price). Apple's own foundation-model papers describe on-device and server models.
rows.mechanism: Apple keeps the interface, personal context and Private Cloud Compute wrapper, but licenses frontier reasoning from a competitor; the differentiation moves from model quality to distribution and privacy architecture.
rows.benchmark: Google owns the model, the TPUs and Android; Apple owns the device and the assistant surface but rents the intelligence.
rows.weakens: A 1.2-trillion-parameter rented model versus a published on-device model shows the hardest queries are outsourced; the beta label two years after Apple Intelligence launched is a delay, not a launch.
rows.implication: Siri is a feature that protects the installed base, not a moat that expands it. Price Apple as a hardware-and-services company with an AI option.
rows.confidence: high on dates and the deal; medium on the $1bn and parameter count (press reports, not company disclosure)
rows.follow_up: When does Siri AI leave beta, what proportion of queries route to Gemini, and what does Apple disclose about the cost?

rows.finding: Apple spent $34.04bn on R&D in the first nine months of FY2026, +33% year on year, while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6.80bn from $9.47bn. Its foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud.
rows.mechanism: Apple is running an opex-heavy AI strategy: pay for models and rented compute rather than build datacentres, which protects free cash flow but caps frontier scale and hands bargaining power to Google.
rows.benchmark: Hyperscalers capitalise AI infrastructure; Apple's nine-month capex is about 2% of revenue while R&D is running at roughly 30% growth.
rows.weakens: The R&D step-up is a real cost: +$8.4bn in nine months, with no separately disclosed AI revenue to offset it, so margin is the place the bill lands.
rows.implication: Free cash flow stays intact and buybacks continue, but there is no proprietary compute moat to underwrite a higher multiple on AI.
rows.confidence: high — both figures are in the 10-Q cash-flow and income statements
rows.follow_up: What share of the R&D increase is AI infrastructure and depreciation, and does Apple intend to keep renting frontier models after the Gemini term?

rows.finding: Silicon stays the deepest in-house layer: A20 Pro in the iPhone 18 Pro on a 2nm process versus A19 on 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line. Products gross margin rose on mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by memory costs.
rows.mechanism: Vertical integration in silicon converts into either margin or performance at fixed price; the modem insourcing removes a Qualcomm royalty and gives Apple control over cellular power and cost.
rows.benchmark: A19 (3nm) to A20 (2nm) is a full node step; the modem shift ends Apple's dependence on an external cellular supplier.
rows.weakens: Component costs are rising: the 10-Q warns of advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints expected to intensify. A node advantage does not protect gross margin when memory prices spike.
rows.implication: Silicon is the moat that is still widening; it supports the products margin line rather than revenue growth.
rows.confidence: medium — 2nm and C2 are press-reported; margins are from the 10-Q
rows.follow_up: What is the C2 versus Qualcomm cost delta per unit, and how much of the FY2027 products margin assumption depends on tariff refunds that may not repeat?

rows.finding: U.S. patent grants fell to 2,722 in 2025 from 3,082 in 2024 (-12%), placing Apple seventh; the foldable Duo's hinge is made with AI-matched parts, confocal laser scanning and 3D-printed photopolymer micro-layers rather than protected by a single blocking patent.
rows.mechanism: The durable IP sits in process know-how and integration, which is harder to design around but also harder to assert; the portfolio is broad rather than deep in any one blocking area.
rows.benchmark: Apple's grant count is declining while U.S. patent activity overall declined; Huawei and TSMC rank ahead of Apple in the same 2025 table.
rows.weakens: A falling grant count is not proof of a weakening moat, but it removes the patent-count argument for one; the hinge know-how must be proven in field reliability.
rows.implication: Underwrite the moat on switching costs and manufacturing yield, not on patent breadth.
rows.confidence: medium — aggregate counts are third-party (IFI) data; individual patent families were not retrieved
rows.follow_up: What is the granted-versus-pending mix in the foldable and on-device-AI families, and are there blocking third-party hinge or display patents?

rows.finding: Health features are shipping and regulated: Apple Watch hypertension notifications were FDA-cleared, with peer-reviewed commentary in Hypertension treating the clearance as a juncture for cuffless screening and questioning accuracy and utility; the feature notifies over a 30-day signal rather than measuring blood pressure.
rows.mechanism: Health adds a regulated, trust-based reason to upgrade a watch every few years and raises the cost of leaving the ecosystem, but it is sold inside a hardware product rather than as a therapy.
rows.benchmark: Apple Watch is described as the most widely adopted consumer health device; the clinical evidence level is a cleared screening notification, not a diagnostic claim.
rows.weakens: Contested clinical value limits pricing power and invites litigation and regulator scrutiny; it is a differentiator, not a new revenue pool.
rows.implication: Wearables and health support the installed base and ASP without changing the growth slope on their own.
rows.confidence: medium — clearance reported by a peer-reviewed journal; the FDA record itself returned no match in the openFDA device search
rows.follow_up: What is the attach and upgrade rate for watches with the hypertension feature, and what does the FDA clearance letter allow Apple to claim?

plan.decision_question: Is Apple's silicon/OS/AI stack a durable moat, or is Apple falling behind in AI while the hardware cycle matures?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer that the next upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it.
plan.why_different: This section judges mechanism and replicability of the technology itself — how the silicon, OS and AI layers work and what can be copied — not market size, valuation or the industry's growth rate.
plan.mechanism: Vertical integration in silicon and OS converts into margin or performance at a fixed price and into switching costs; buying frontier models and renting TPU compute converts a would-be fixed-cost AI moat into a variable cost paid to a competitor, which protects cash flow but leaves the differentiation in hardware, privacy and distribution.
plan.comparison_set: Google (owns Gemini, TPUs and Android), Samsung (licenses Google's stack), Huawei (constrained by domestic process), Microsoft (cloud capex model), and Apple's own prior cycle (iPhone 17, A19 3nm, no foldable).
plan.counter_evidence: AI talent left for Meta through 2025; the Siri rebuild shipped as an English beta in September 2026, two years after Apple Intelligence launched; capex fell while R&D rose; patent grants fell 12%; the Duo's hinge durability is unproven; memory costs threaten products margin.
plan.visual: Performance-metrics table plus the moat table with the replication test (funded team of 50), and the evidence component on the Google dependency.
plan.prohibited: AI leader, seamless ecosystem, strong team, huge market, well positioned, innovative company, best-in-class without a metric, 'many patents', 'about' before a figure, any sentence describing how the section is written.

rows.finding: Average daily volume 40.41m shares ($13.84bn) over 20 days and 41.34m shares ($13.56bn) over three months; price sits 3.5% above the 50-day average of $333.04 and 16.2% above the 200-day of $296.56.
rows.mechanism: A $5tn mega-cap with 40m shares a day traded has an exit that is always open at the screen price; the cost of exit is the spread and any de-rating, not the ability to sell.
rows.benchmark: A $250m position is 0.62% of the 20-day average value traded; a $1bn position is 2.5%.
rows.weakens: Liquidity evaporates in a correlated drawdown - in a market-wide selloff the bid thins and the discount to the last price widens, so ADV overstates achievable exit size in stress.
rows.implication: Liquidity is not a constraint at any plausible position size: the fund can enter and exit in days with negligible market impact, so the exit risk is entirely a price risk, not a liquidity risk.
rows.confidence: high - timestamped market data
rows.follow_up: What position size is the fund contemplating, and does it breach any single-issuer or index-weight limit?

rows.finding: No holder owns control: 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding at 2026-01-02, Vanguard 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10%, the largest holders being index managers; directors and officers hold about 0.06% between them.
rows.mechanism: With no controlling shareholder and a dispersed index base, price is set by flows and by the marginal institutional view of the multiple, not by a strategic buyer or a control contest.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own 12-month low of $243.42 is 29.4% below the current price; the five-year closing low is $125.02.
rows.weakens: Index concentration cuts both ways: forced selling by passive funds in a redemption wave would hit Apple harder than a smaller, less-owned name.
rows.implication: Free float is effectively 100% and the marginal holder is an index or active fund, so the stock's buyer on exit is the same pool the fund sells into - index inclusion has been a structural bid, but it does not raise the price at which the business is worth owning.
rows.confidence: medium - the 52-week low overstates the chance of a full retracement but is the best local base rate
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's current S&P 500 weight, and what happens to passive demand if it is trimmed at a rebalance?

rows.finding: Total shareholder yield 1.9% (dividend 0.3% plus gross buyback 1.6%); net of $13.7bn of stock compensation the buyback yield is 1.36%; EPS grew 9.2% a year from FY2021 to the TTM, of which about 2.8 points a year came from the 12.8% reduction in diluted shares.
rows.mechanism: A long-only fund's return is dividend plus net buyback plus EPS growth plus the change in multiple; Apple supplies only 1.7 points of the first two, so nearly all of the return has to come from earnings growth or from a multiple that does not fall.
rows.benchmark: Trailing EPS CAGR over the five years to FY2021-TTM is 9.2% (S6, S1) versus revenue CAGR of 5.0% and net income CAGR of 6.4%.
rows.weakens: If the multiple expands further, the decomposition understates the return; 2026's 16.4% revenue growth suggests forward EPS growth may exceed 9%.
rows.implication: With a flat multiple the total return is about 10.7% a year (0.3% dividend, 1.4% net buyback, 9% EPS growth) - adequate; the whole question is whether 39.5x is a multiple that holds.
rows.confidence: high for the historic decomposition; medium for the forward multiple assumption
rows.follow_up: What EPS growth does consensus assume for FY2027 and FY2028, and does it require the buyback to keep running above $80bn?

rows.finding: A reversion from 39.5x to 31.0x costs 21.5% of price, about -7.7% a year over three years, which more than offsets the 1.7% shareholder yield and most of a 9% EPS growth rate.
rows.mechanism: Multiple compression is the mechanism by which a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year at 4.93% (+84bp y/y), the discount rate on Apple's terminal cash flows is higher than when the stock traded at 27.9x in FY2023.
rows.benchmark: Apple's fiscal year-end P/E: 24.6x (FY2022), 27.9x (FY2023), 37.5x (FY2024), 34.2x (FY2025); four-year mean 31.0x; AAPL currently 39.5x, a 27% premium to that mean.
rows.weakens: The stock has been 'expensive' versus its own history since FY2024 and has still returned 27.5% over the last twelve months; a mean-reversion model has been wrong for two years.
rows.implication: The asymmetry is the argument for selling into strength: at a five-year-high multiple the upside needs further expansion, while the downside is a reversion that is already observed once within the past four years.
rows.confidence: medium - multiples are certain, their persistence is not
rows.follow_up: What would keep the multiple above 35x for three years - sustained 10%-plus revenue growth, or a fall in the ten-year yield?

rows.finding: No plausible acquirer exists: every company in the peer set is smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market cap, so a takeover would require a buyer larger than any in the sector, plus antitrust clearance in the US, EU, China and UK.
rows.mechanism: The bid side of a $5tn equity is other portfolio managers, not strategics; index funds and buybacks are price-insensitive in direction but not in price, so the exit price is set by the same valuation debate the fund is making.
rows.benchmark: Largest technology peer Microsoft at $3,875.8bn market cap and $3,846.8bn EV; Alphabet $3,461.1bn; Meta $1,582.4bn.
rows.weakens: A sovereign wealth fund or a consortium could in principle bid, but at 39.5x earnings and a $5tn equity cheque the financing does not exist at a premium.
rows.implication: A control premium is not part of the return: the exit is at the market price, which means the fund's realisation depends entirely on the multiple other investors will pay.
rows.confidence: high - the comparison is arithmetic
rows.follow_up: Is there any activist or break-up case that would separate services from hardware, and who would fund a $5tn position?

rows.finding: Apple repurchased $82.2bn of stock in the TTM to 2026-06-27 against $15.6bn of dividends and $111.5bn of working-capital-normalised FCF, so the repurchase is at the limit of internally generated cash.
rows.mechanism: A fixed-dollar repurchase retires more shares as the price falls, so the EPS accretion per dollar rises and the floor under the per-share value is firmer than for a company that does not buy back.
rows.benchmark: $85bn a year is 1.7% of the $5.03tn capitalisation at $344.63, 3.0% at $270 and 3.6% at $240.
rows.weakens: The buyback is discretionary and could be cut in a downturn or redirected to AI capital spending; it also supports EPS, not the multiple, so it cannot prevent a de-rating.
rows.implication: The buyback is a standing, price-sensitive buyer that makes a de-rating self-limiting: each 10% fall in the price adds roughly 0.17 points to the buyback yield, which is why a bear case to $190-240 is more likely to be a long opportunity than a permanent loss.
rows.confidence: high for the arithmetic; medium for the $85bn run-rate
rows.follow_up: Will the May 2027 authorisation exceed the May 2025 $100bn programme, and will Apple fund it from cash or from debt?

rows.finding: On FY2029E EPS of $11.45 (my estimate: FY2026E $9.09 grown 9%/8%/7%), a 27x exit gives $309, a 31x exit $355 and a 34x exit $389; with about $3.50 of dividends over three years the three-year IRR from $344.63 is -3.2%, +1.3% and +4.5%.
rows.mechanism: Buying at a high multiple transfers the future return to the seller: the entry price fixes the IRR once the exit multiple and the earnings path are set, and at 39.5x the arithmetic leaves nothing for the buyer.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own FY2022-FY2025 P/E range of 24.6x-37.5x.
rows.weakens: If EPS grows faster than 9% - the June 2026 quarter grew EPS 28.7% - the IRR rises by roughly the excess growth rate for each year held.
rows.implication: From today's price the three-year return fails the 9% hurdle under every exit multiple below 39.5x; at a $270 entry the same range becomes +5.0% to +13.4% with a 10% central case.
rows.confidence: medium - exit multiples are a scenario assumption
rows.follow_up: What entry price does the fund's own hurdle rate require, and is a three-year or five-year holding period assumed?

rows.finding: No insider purchased a share in the six months to 2026-10-29; 37 sales totalled 590,642 shares and $183.45m, of which 34 transactions ($96.70m) were under Rule 10b5-1 plans; director Arthur Levinson sold $86.74m and Executive Chair Tim Cook $63.85m.
rows.mechanism: Insider behaviour is informative mainly at the extremes - a cluster of discretionary buys after a fall, or discretionary sales near highs; here the mix is plan-driven and uninformative about the multiple.
rows.benchmark: Peer insiders and the absence of open-market purchases across the six-month window.
rows.weakens: Almost all sales were scheduled 10b5-1 sales, and executives of a $5tn company sell for diversification regardless of valuation, so the signal is weak.
rows.implication: Management is not adding at $344; that is weak evidence against a near-term re-rating and consistent with a stock trading above what insiders consider value, though it is not a sell signal on its own.
rows.confidence: medium - plan sales are scheduled in advance and carry little information, discretionary sales carry more
rows.follow_up: Did any of the discretionary sales follow a change in the trading plan, and what is the executives' remaining unvested exposure?

plan.decision_question: For a long-only fund, what is the exit and total-return path, and what would force a sale?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer: with no company large enough to acquire it, the three-year return from $344.63 is -3% to +5% a year if the 39.5x multiple reverts toward its 31.0x four-year average, which sets the sell discipline at a price where the arithmetic clears 9% - roughly $270.
plan.why_different: Every other section asks whether Apple's business improves; this one asks how the fund gets its money back and at what price the risk/reward stops paying, and it must name the buyer or venue rather than list generic options.
plan.mechanism: There is no strategic exit for a $5tn company, so the only realisation routes are the market, Apple's own repurchase and the dividend. Return = dividend (0.31%) + net buyback (1.36%) + EPS growth, minus the annualised cost of any multiple compression; at 39.5x versus a 31.0x four-year mean, compression of about 7-8% a year can cancel the operating return.
plan.comparison_set: The last twelve months' own trading (52-week low $243.42, i.e. 29.4% below the current price), the FY2022-FY2025 multiple range (24.6x-37.5x, mean 31.0x), HP and Dell for hardware, Microsoft and Alphabet for the platform bid, and the 4.93% ten-year Treasury as the opportunity cost of holding a 1.9% shareholder yield.
plan.counter_evidence: A flat 39.5x multiple with 9-10% EPS growth still delivers about 10.7% a year, so the return is adequate while the multiple holds; the buyback is a self-correcting bid that accelerates as the price falls; and the June 2026 quarter's 16.4% revenue growth could keep the multiple elevated for longer than a mean-reversion model assumes.
plan.visual: Exit routes table (route, named buyer or venue, rationale, timing, likelihood, source) plus a return-sensitivity table by entry price and exit multiple.
plan.prohibited: No 'IPO or M&A', no unnamed acquirers, no invented index weight, no claim that a takeover premium is a return source, no repetition of the risk section's regulatory detail, no 'well positioned'.

exit.author: Valuation Analyst
queries: AAPL trading snapshot: average daily volume, 20-day and 3-month liquidity, 52-week range

AAPL valuation snapshot: market cap, P/E history FY2022-FY2025, peer market caps MSFT GOOGL META AMZN
AAPL return sensitivity: entry price x exit multiple 27x/31x/34x on FY2029E EPS $11.45
AAPL consensus iPhone revenue FY2027 $277.4bn (+9.9%) and FY2026 $252.4bn

rows.finding: At $344.63 and 14,715m diluted shares Apple's market value is $5,071.2bn, 1.6% of which the $82.2bn buyback retires; the $5,029.6bn screen figure uses 14,594m cover-page shares and the 39.5x P/E uses $8.72 summed EPS.
rows.mechanism: One share count and one market cap keep the yield, the retirement rate and the multiple on the same basis; mixing them overstates the buyback yield by 0.8% and the P/E by 0.2x.
rows.benchmark: Market cap $5,071.2bn at 14,715m diluted shares vs $5,029.6bn on 14,594m cover-page shares; P/E 39.3x vs feed 39.5x.
rows.weakens: The cover-page count and the diluted count differ by 0.1% and both are point-in-time; buybacks change the count every quarter.
rows.implication: Liquidity and buyback-yield arithmetic must use $5,071.2bn and 14,715m so the exit table reconciles with the funding section and the financials section's $5,072bn.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Confirm the FY2026 10-K cover-page share count.

rows.finding: The multiple is the swing factor: a reversion from 39.3x to the four-year mean of 31.0x costs 21.1% of the price, or 7.6% a year over three years, which swallows the 1.9% shareholder yield and most of the 8-9% EPS growth.
rows.mechanism: Return = shareholder yield + EPS growth + multiple change. At 39.3x the multiple change dominates: -7.6% a year from reversion against +1.9% yield and +8.2% EPS growth nets about 1.3%.
rows.benchmark: Three-year return 9.6% a year at a 39.3x exit vs 1.3% at a 31.0x exit, on FY2029E EPS $11.45 and $3.55 of dividends.
rows.weakens: The multiple has held for years and the stock returned 27.5% in the last twelve months; reversion is a forecast, not an observed fact.
rows.implication: A 9% hurdle is reachable only from a lower entry price or a multiple that does not revert; the exit is liquid but not price-insensitive.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic, medium on the multiple path
rows.follow_up: What would hold the multiple at 35x or above for three years: services mix, buyback, or a lower ten-year yield?

rows.finding: The $82.2bn trailing buyback retires 1.6% of the 14,715m shares at today's $5,071.2bn market value, 2.1% at $270 ($3,973bn) and 2.3% at $240 ($3,532bn).
rows.mechanism: A fixed dollar buyback retires a larger share of the company as the price falls; the retirement rate is the buyback divided by the market capitalisation at that price.
rows.benchmark: Buyback retirement rate 1.6% at $344.63, 2.1% at $270 and 2.3% at $240 on $82.2bn a year.
rows.weakens: Buybacks are discretionary, can be cut in a downturn, and the gross figure overstates net retirement because stock compensation adds $13.7bn of shares.
rows.implication: Each leg down raises the forward EPS growth the buyer receives, which is why the entry ladder is staged by price rather than by narrative.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does the May 2027 authorisation stay at or above $100bn?

rows.finding: No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire Apple: the four largest are all smaller than Apple's $5,071.2bn market value, and any bid would face US, EU, China and UK antitrust review.
rows.mechanism: Acquisition requires a buyer larger than the target; none exists in the sector, so the takeover premium is not part of the return set.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft $3,875.8bn, Alphabet $3,461.1bn, Amazon $2,598.9bn, Meta $1,582.4bn vs Apple $5,071.2bn.
rows.weakens: A break-up or activist route could in theory crystallise the $177-238 sum of the parts, but no campaign is disclosed.
rows.implication: The strategic-acquisition route is negligible; the holder's exit is the open market, the buyback and the dividend.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Is there any sovereign or private-capital vehicle large enough, and would any jurisdiction clear it?

rows.finding: The FY2024 and FY2025 buybacks spent $185.6bn at 34-38x earnings; those shares would have been retired 18-26% cheaper at the FY2023 multiple of 27.9x.
rows.mechanism: Repurchasing above intrinsic value transfers value from continuing holders to sellers; the earnings yield on the $82.2bn spent is 2.5%, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury.
rows.weakens: Buybacks also offset dilution and signal confidence; a mechanistic comparison ignores the cash-return policy's role in supporting the multiple.
rows.implication: Management is buying at the top of its own historical range, as an investor at $344.63 would be; the buyback supports the price but does not create value at this level.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: How much of the buyback is offset by stock compensation ($13.7bn in the TTM)?

plan.decision_question: How does a long-only holder realise value in Apple, at what price does the three-year return clear a 9% hurdle, and what would force an exit?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's only exit is the public market and its own buyback, and at $344.63 the shares already discount the scenario bull, so the holder's return depends on a 39.3x multiple holding rather than on any strategic buyer.
plan.why_different: This section asks how the position becomes cash: who buys, at what multiple and when. It is not a restatement of fair value; it converts the valuation into a sell discipline, a holding period and a drawdown estimate, and it tests the acquisition and listing routes.
plan.mechanism: With no acquirer large enough, realisation comes from the open market, the buyback and the dividend; the return is shareholder yield (1.9%) plus EPS growth (8-9%) plus the change in the multiple, so a reversion from 39.3x to 31.0x subtracts 21.1% of the price and 7.6% a year over three years, overwhelming the cash return.
plan.comparison_set: Peer market caps (MSFT $3,875.8bn, GOOGL $3,461.1bn, AMZN $2,598.9bn, META $1,582.4bn) vs Apple's $5,071.2bn; historical entry-multiple exits 27x/31x/34x; FY2022-25 P/E 24.6-37.5x; scenario values $241/$284/$357 and DCF bull $277.
plan.counter_evidence: The stock returned 27.5% in the twelve months to 2026-10-30 while the technology sector fell 8.3% in the last month; a 35x forward multiple has held through a 4.93% ten-year yield, so multiple reversion is a forecast, not an observation, and a holder could earn a high-single-digit return if the multiple simply persists.
plan.visual: Exit-routes table naming the open market, the issuer, the dividend and the absent strategic buyer, followed by the entry-price x exit-multiple return table and the scenario-range cross-check in the text.
plan.prohibited: Do not call $277 'the bull case' without the DCF qualifier; do not mix $5,029.6bn and $5,071.2bn or 39.5x and 39.3x; no unsourced index multiple or Street target; no buyback retirement rate that is not divided by the 14,715m-share market cap at the stated price.

rows.finding: In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple repurchased $62.1bn of stock, paid $0.27 a quarter in dividends, spent $34.04bn on R&D (+33%) and only $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn). In FY2025 it bought back $89.3bn under a $100bn authorisation and raised the dividend to $0.26.
rows.mechanism: Capital allocation reveals the bet: Apple funds AI from the income statement and returns the balance-sheet capacity to shareholders, treating frontier models as a purchased input rather than an owned platform.
rows.benchmark: FY2025: $89.3bn of buybacks and $15.4bn of dividends against $34.55bn of R&D.
rows.weakens: A 33% R&D increase with falling capex means the marginal AI dollar is opex; if AI features do not lift hardware ASP, that spending is a pure margin drag.
rows.implication: The strategy is shareholder-return first, AI as an operating expense. It supports EPS and limits downside, but it does not build an asset that a competitor cannot rent too.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Will Apple disclose AI-related depreciation or licensing cost separately, and does the buyback pace hold if margin compresses?

rows.finding: Apple assembled about 55m iPhones in India in 2025, up 53% and roughly a quarter of global output, using Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron; Indian assembly and components still cost more than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expire on 2026-03-31.
rows.mechanism: Geographic diversification reduces tariff and concentration risk but trades a mature supply chain for a subsidised, higher-cost one; the strategy is insurance bought with gross margin.
rows.benchmark: India assembled 36m iPhones in 2024; global iPhone output is 220-230m a year; all iPhone 17 models are now built in India.
rows.weakens: The shift is subsidy-dependent and costlier, so it does not improve unit economics; it also invites retaliation risk on the China side that the source does not quantify.
rows.implication: The tariff hedge is working on volume but is not yet a margin tailwind, and it depends on policy that expires within the next twelve months.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Has the subsidy regime been renewed, and what is the landed-cost gap between Indian and Chinese assembly for U.S.-bound units?

rows.finding: Services reached $91.73bn in nine months of FY2026 (+14%) at a 76.3% gross margin, with advertising and cloud services cited as the growth drivers; the EU DMA generated 56 interoperability requests by 2026-03-22, of which 43 were closed and 27 confidentially.
rows.mechanism: Services monetise the installed base at high incremental margin, but the DMA forces Apple to open interfaces and choice screens, which erodes the control that makes those services default.
rows.benchmark: iPhone revenue grew 22% in the same quarter; services gross margin is roughly 1.5 times the company average.
rows.weakens: Growth is concentrated in advertising and cloud, the areas most exposed to platform regulation and to the Google search distribution deal.
rows.implication: Services is the profit engine and the part regulation can tax; the DMA is a recurring engineering and legal cost, not a one-off.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What is the revenue at risk from DMA-driven sideloading and default-choice changes, and how much of advertising growth is search-revenue-share dependent?

rows.finding: Apple confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to use Google Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and about $1bn a year, while its own foundation models are trained on rented Google TPUs and its capex fell year on year.
rows.mechanism: Build-vs-buy resolved in favour of buy for the model and rent for the compute: Apple keeps capital light and ships sooner, at the cost of dependency on the company that also owns Android.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own July 2024 paper disclosing 8,192 TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips, rented through Google Cloud.
rows.weakens: Neither company confirmed the price or exclusivity, and the arrangement could be a bridge while Apple's own models improve — the 2026 Stepped MoE paper shows the research org still shipping efficiency work.
rows.implication: Partnering preserves cash and speed but cedes the frontier layer; the platform control that remains is the interface, the data boundary and the device.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Is the Gemini deal exclusive, what are its term and renewal date, and can Apple switch models without degrading Siri?

rows.finding: On 2026-01-14 the Commerce Department published initial Section 232 semiconductor findings that imposed no additional tariffs on Apple products; after the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, Apple applied for refunds and recognised them as a reduction of products cost of sales, while warning that memory and advanced-semiconductor supply constraints are expected to intensify.
rows.mechanism: Trade policy is being absorbed through the P&L rather than through supply-chain redesign alone; refunds flatter margin while the underlying cost of components rises.
rows.benchmark: The Section 232 investigation opened in 2025; the Supreme Court ruling of 2026-02-20 struck down certain IEEPA tariffs.
rows.weakens: The refund is non-recurring and the 10-Q flags further Section 232, Section 301 or sector tariffs as possible, so the relief may reverse.
rows.implication: Tariff policy is now a swing factor in reported gross margin, which makes one quarter's margin a poor guide to the next.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: How much of the products gross-margin improvement came from one-off tariff refunds, and what Section 301 measures now apply?

rows.finding: Apple reports fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter results on 2026-11-02 having guided to 9-11% revenue growth, with iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max and Duo on sale from 2026-09-18 and the standard iPhone 18 deferred to spring 2027.
rows.mechanism: Splitting the launch moves revenue between quarters and lets Apple sell higher-priced Pro and foldable models into the holiday window while 2nm supply matures for the cheaper models in spring.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 fourth-quarter revenue was $102.5bn, up 8% year on year.
rows.weakens: Guidance of 9-11% is below the 16.4% growth of the June 2026 quarter, which implies deceleration into the launch quarter rather than acceleration.
rows.implication: The next twelve months are checkable quarter by quarter; the launch split means the March 2027 quarter carries a second iPhone cycle that the prior year did not have.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Do Duo units and Pro mix hold through the December quarter, and does services growth stay in double digits against DMA remedies?

plan.decision_question: Does Apple's strategy convert AI and services into growth without ceding platform control?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model.
plan.why_different: This section judges execution and allocation — dated milestones, partners and what must be true in twelve months — rather than the technology's mechanism or the market's size.
plan.mechanism: Apple funds the AI layer from the income statement (R&D and licensing) rather than the balance sheet (datacentres), keeps control of the interface, distribution and privacy layer, and returns the resulting cash through buybacks; platform control is preserved while the frontier-model layer is ceded.
plan.comparison_set: Microsoft and Alphabet (capitalise AI infrastructure), Samsung (follows Apple's price and form factor), Huawei (rebuilds a domestic stack), and Apple's own prior capital-return cycle (FY2025 buybacks $89.3bn).
plan.counter_evidence: R&D is funding rented intelligence rather than owned capability; capex fell; memory costs and tariffs pressure margin; India depends on expiring subsidies; DMA compliance consumes engineering time; Duo durability unproven.
plan.visual: Milestone table with target dates and status, plus the partner table with signing dates.
plan.prohibited: AI leader, well positioned, strong execution, huge opportunity, seamless, 'about' before a figure, any sentence about how the section is written.
