rows.finding: One class of common stock only: 50,400,000,000 shares authorised at $0.00001 par, 14,773,260,000 issued and outstanding at 2025-09-27 and 14,697,926,000 outstanding at 2026-01-02; Vanguard 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10% are the only disclosed 5% holders; all 12 directors and executive officers together hold 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% of the count.
rows.mechanism: One-share-one-vote with a diffuse register means no founder, family or supervoting class can block a bid, dictate capital allocation or install directors; control is exercised through the proxy and the indexed holders, so governance risk shows up as slow board refresh rather than as expropriation.
rows.benchmark: Alphabet, the closest mega-cap peer, still issues Class C stock alongside voting classes (2026 proxy), so a founder-controlled competitor can ignore short-term owners in a way Apple's holders cannot be forced to accept.
rows.weakens: BlackRock's 7.10% is computed from a Schedule 13G/A reflecting holdings at 2023-12-31, so the holder table is partly stale and the true 2026 holder mix is not disclosed.
rows.implication: Clean title and an unblocked exit path support a multi-year holding; the price of that cleanliness is that no insider owns enough to align the board against management's preferences.
rows.confidence: high - figures read from the 10-K balance sheet and the 2026 proxy ownership table.
rows.follow_up: Has BlackRock's stake moved since 2023, and does any activist have a position below 5%?

rows.finding: Eight directors stood in 2026: seven independent plus CEO Cook; independent tenure averages 12.0 years (Levinson since 2000, i.e. 26 years; Jung 2008; Sugar 2010; Wagner 2014), and two of the seven independents (Levinson, 75; Sugar, 77) are at or past the company's own guideline that directors generally may not stand for re-election after 75.
rows.mechanism: A low-turnover board chaired by a 26-year director, with an executive chair who is the outgoing CEO after 2026-09-01, lowers the probability of external pressure on capital allocation, M&A or succession timing; the age guideline is the only formal refresh mechanism and it is being waived for two members.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own stated age-75 guideline (applied to Al Gore after 21 years and James Bell after 9 years in 2024) is the relevant base rate, not an external norm.
rows.weakens: 92% of votes cast supported say-on-pay in 2025 and 7 of 8 directors are independent, so holders are not signalling discontent; the guideline says 'generally', which permits exceptions.
rows.implication: Governance is stable but weakly refreshed; an investor should price a slower correction if AI-era capital allocation goes wrong, and should not pay a governance premium.
rows.confidence: high - names, ages, start years and the guideline are in the 2026 proxy.
rows.follow_up: Did the board formally waive the age guideline for Levinson and Sugar, and who chairs the board after 2027?

rows.finding: FY2025 returned $106.1bn to shareholders ($90.7bn buybacks plus $15.4bn dividends) against free cash flow of $98.8bn, i.e. 107% of FCF, while diluted EPS rose 22.7% against an 8.0% rise in operating income and the effective tax rate fell to 15.6% from 24.1%.
rows.mechanism: Buybacks shrink the denominator (diluted shares fell 6.9% from 15,812,547,000 in FY2023 to 14,714,676,000 in Q3 FY2026) and a lower tax rate lifts the numerator, so reported EPS growth overstates operating growth; the equity behaves partly as a bond-like cash-return instrument.
rows.benchmark: Company's own FY2023-FY2025 buybacks of $263.2bn and its FY2024 effective tax rate of 24.1% provide the counterfactual.
rows.weakens: Q3 FY2026 revenue grew 16% with a 50.1% gross margin including a ~2pp tariff-refund benefit, so operating momentum in FY2026 is genuine and the 'financial engineering' charge is weaker for the current year.
rows.implication: Underwrite the holding on operating growth and cash conversion, not on EPS optics; if buybacks slow, headline EPS growth converges to operating growth.
rows.confidence: high - all figures from the FY2025 statements and the Q3 FY2026 exhibit 99.1.
rows.follow_up: What is the FY2026 buyback pace after the $100bn May 2025 authorisation, and how much of FY2025 EPS growth was tax?

rows.finding: Two Irish subsidiaries' Irish branches received tax opinions in 1991 and 2007 allocating profits; the Commission's 2016-08-30 decision was annulled by the General Court on 2020-07-15 but confirmed by the ECJ on 2024-09-10, producing a one-time $10.2bn net tax charge in Q4 FY2024 and $15.8bn payable to Ireland from escrow.
rows.mechanism: The entity map's profit allocation, not its legal ownership, was the source of the tax advantage; Irish law changed from January 2015 and the ECJ judgment converted a contingent liability into a paid one, so the post-2015 structure is taxed on a permanently less favourable basis.
rows.benchmark: Effective tax rate of 24.1% in FY2024 versus 15.6% in FY2025 shows how much of the reported rate is discrete items rather than structure.
rows.weakens: The FY2025 rate of 15.6% shows the rate can still fall on discrete benefits, so the direction of travel is not monotonic.
rows.implication: The Irish tax leg of the compounding story is over; model a mid-to-high teens effective rate rather than historical single-digit foreign rates, and treat further EU tax integration as a live risk.
rows.confidence: high - the 10-K note states the dates, amounts and offsets.
rows.follow_up: What is the FY2026 effective rate excluding discrete items, and where is residual non-US IP now booked?

rows.finding: The Services line that carries the highest margin (75.4% gross margin in FY2025 versus 36.8% for products) is the one attacked by live proceedings: the DOJ monopolisation suit filed 2024-03-21, a EUR 500m DMA fine and cease-and-desist on 2025-04-23 with a second Article 6(4) file open, and an Epic contempt finding on 2025-04-30 referred to the US Attorney.
rows.mechanism: Remedies target the commission and anti-steering rules that let Apple tax third-party distribution, so they attack the rent, not the product; a structural remedy would compress the 75% margin line while leaving hardware intact.
rows.benchmark: Services gross margin 75.4% against products 36.8% in FY2025 quantifies the rent at stake.
rows.weakens: Services revenue still grew 14.1% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 while these cases were live, so remedies have not yet dented growth.
rows.implication: The highest-margin revenue stream carries the largest legal tail; that, not hardware competition, is the reason to demand a discount to a pure compounder multiple.
rows.confidence: medium-high - case facts are from the 10-K; the revenue effect is inferred from segment growth.
rows.follow_up: What Services revenue is directly exposed to US third-party payment rules, and what is the appeal timetable in the Ninth Circuit?

rows.finding: Twelve months of Form 4s to 2026-10-29 show no purchases and 46 sales of 687,127 shares for $208.0m, led by director Levinson ($86.7m, not under a 10b5-1 plan) and Tim Cook ($80.4m); Cook's disclosed holding of 3,280,295 shares is 0.02% of the company but about $1.09bn at the $332.94 price of his 2026-10-02 sale.
rows.mechanism: At a $3.8trn market capitalisation, percentage ownership is a poor measure of alignment; dollar exposure and unvested RSUs are what bind management, and planned sales under 10b5-1 rules carry little information.
rows.benchmark: The company's own requirement that the CEO hold ten times base salary ($30m against a $3m salary) is the alignment test management sets for itself.
rows.weakens: All but three of the sales were 10b5-1 planned and three were gifts, so the pattern is scheduled diversification, not a signal of inside information.
rows.implication: Alignment is adequate in dollars and weak in votes, so the investor should watch changes in unvested equity and retention terms rather than the percentage table.
rows.confidence: high for the trades; medium for the dollar value of Cook's stake, which is a calculation across two sources.
rows.follow_up: What are the retention and vesting terms offered to Ternus on appointment, and does Cook's executive-chair role carry new equity?

plan.decision_question: Is Apple's legal, ownership and governance structure clean and stable enough to underwrite a multi-year holding?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple is legally and structurally clean enough to hold for years - one share class, one registrant, no VIE and a genuinely unblocked exit - but its governance has barely refreshed in a decade and two of seven independents sit past its own age-75 rule, so the holding should be underwritten on cash generation and clean title rather than on board quality.
plan.why_different: This section owns identity, legal structure, ownership and board mechanics; the business model and unit economics belong to the financial sections, the product roadmap to the product section, and litigation substance to the regulatory section.
plan.mechanism: One share class removes control risk but concentrates governance in a long-tenured board; capital return plus a falling tax rate flattered EPS while the Irish profit-allocation structure that supported the tax rate was closed by the ECJ; the highest-margin revenue line is the one exposed to antitrust remedies.
plan.comparison_set: Alphabet as the multi-class mega-cap peer; Apple's own 2011-2026 record (cumulative TSR +2,162% under Cook) as the base rate for a leadership handover; Apple's stated age-75 board policy applied to its 2024 retirements.
plan.counter_evidence: 92% say-on-pay support, seven of eight directors independent, Q3 FY2026 revenue growth of 16% and gross margin of 50.1%, and a CEO whose disclosed stake is worth about $1.09bn all argue the governance and alignment discount should be small.
plan.visual: KPI table (share structure, float, independence, tenure, capital return, tax rate, iPhone concentration) with the entity table and the dated timeline.
plan.prohibited: clean structure as an assertion without evidence, strong governance, well positioned, stable leadership, huge market, risks are manageable, any sentence about how the report was written

rows.finding: On 2026-04-17 the board appointed John Ternus (50 at appointment) CEO effective 2026-09-01; he joined Apple's product design team in 2001, became a vice president of hardware engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021, and holds a 1997 Penn degree in mechanical engineering and applied mechanics; Cook becomes Executive Chair and Levinson Lead Independent Director.
rows.mechanism: Promoting the hardware engineering head keeps the integrated product model intact but transfers the CEO role from a commercial operator who built the China supply chain and services pricing to an engineer whose record is product development.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own 2011 handover, when an operations executive with 13 years as COO replaced a product founder; and Microsoft's internal CEO succession as the peer base rate for continuity.
rows.weakens: Ternus has run the largest product organisation at Apple for five years, which is broader than the title suggests; internal promotion is also the pattern that worked in 2011.
rows.implication: Continuity is high and the product-integration model is safe, but the skills most tested in 2026-28 (AI platform economics, regulatory negotiation, tariffs) are not the ones on his record, which argues for a wait-for-evidence stance rather than paying a new-CEO premium.
rows.confidence: high - the appointment, effective date, age and Apple career dates are in the 8-K; the degree is from the university newspaper.
rows.follow_up: What operating scope has Ternus had outside hardware engineering, and does his employment agreement disclose a retention award?

rows.finding: On 2025-12-01 Apple announced John Giannandrea, SVP Machine Learning and AI Strategy, was stepping down to advise before retiring in spring 2026; Amar Subramanya joined as VP of AI reporting to Craig Federighi, with Apple Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety moved into the software organisation, and the rest of the AI org split between Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue.
rows.mechanism: AI accountability was spread across a standalone SVP, the software org and the operations org; folding models and safety under Software Engineering shortens the path from model to product but leaves the P&L owner for AI undisclosed.
rows.benchmark: Q3 FY2026 revenue growth of 16% and the July 2026 statement that Siri AI shipped at WWDC26 are the test of whether the reorganisation delivered.
rows.weakens: Apple shipped the all-new Siri AI by WWDC26, so the reorganisation produced a deliverable within seven months; the delay that triggered it is not quantified in any filing.
rows.implication: Treat AI execution as an unresolved item requiring a milestone (shipped Siri AI adoption and a disclosed AI roadmap) before adding to a position.
rows.confidence: high on the reorganisation; medium on whether accountability is now clear, which the company has not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Who now owns Siri roadmap and model strategy, and does Subramanya report to the CEO or only to Federighi?

rows.finding: On 2025-12-06 it was reported that Johny Srouji, SVP Hardware Technologies and the architect of Apple silicon, told Tim Cook he was seriously considering leaving the company; no departure or new role has been disclosed in any filing since.
rows.mechanism: Custom silicon is the mechanism behind both product differentiation and hardware margin; losing the executive who built it threatens a multi-year roadmap that competitors cannot copy quickly.
rows.benchmark: Products gross margin of 36.8% in FY2025 rests on custom silicon and is the line at risk if silicon leadership weakens.
rows.weakens: The report is unconfirmed and Apple has disclosed no change; promoting a hardware engineer to CEO may be exactly the move that retains silicon talent.
rows.implication: This is the single most underpriced key-person risk in the holding; ask for the retention arrangement before sizing a position.
rows.confidence: medium - single media report, denied by nobody and confirmed by nobody; no departure has been disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Has Srouji been given a new title, retention award or CTO role, and who is his designated successor?

rows.finding: Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m (base $3m unchanged since 2016, target cash $6m, target equity $50m, 75% performance-based); the other named executive officers each target about $23m (base $1m, 200% cash target, $20m equity); Parekh's CFO package was $1m base with 175% cash target and $16.75m target equity.
rows.mechanism: Apple pays small annual awards with long vesting (about 4.5 years) and no employment contracts, so retention depends on unvested equity rather than contractual protection; peers use front-loaded mega-grants that make leaving expensive.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft's Nadella at $96.5m reported for FY2025 and Alphabet's Pichai at $10.9m reported for 2025 but with a 2026 target equity award of $210m and a 1.35m-share PSU vesting in February 2026.
rows.weakens: Pay follows performance: 92% say-on-pay in 2025 and a 2,162% cumulative TSR from 2011 to 2025 make the structure defensible, and unvested RSUs are large in absolute terms.
rows.implication: Shareholders get a chief executive paid well below mega-cap peers, which is a real plus, but the same restraint applied to undisclosed SVPs is a poaching risk in the AI labour market.
rows.confidence: high on Apple's numbers; medium on peers, where one figure comes from reporting rather than the proxy itself.
rows.follow_up: What are the 2026 awards to Ternus and to the non-NEO SVPs, and do they include multi-year retention grants?

rows.finding: Apple's Section 16 population is narrow: the Form 4 filers in the twelve months to 2026-10-29 are Cook (now Executive Chair), Ternus, O'Brien, Parekh, Newstead, principal accounting officer Borders and director Levinson; Craig Federighi, Eddy Cue, Johny Srouji and Greg Joswiak do not appear, so their ownership and trades are not publicly disclosed.
rows.mechanism: Non-disclosure of the operating bench means outside holders cannot price succession, retention or internal competition for the CEO role from filings alone.
rows.benchmark: The 2026 proxy names only six named executive officers and four current executives in the ownership table, against a peer group whose CEOs are covered individually in sector research.
rows.weakens: The named group still covers operations, finance, legal and retail, i.e. every function with external reporting exposure, so the disclosure gap is about product and technology leaders rather than the whole bench.
rows.implication: Information asymmetry is material for a people-dependent thesis; the report should carry an explicit disclosure limitation and the investor should seek management access before sizing.
rows.confidence: high - the set of filers and titles comes from the Form 4 list itself.
rows.follow_up: Will Apple designate its AI and silicon leaders as Section 16 officers, and what does the 2027 proxy disclose about their awards?

rows.finding: In roughly eighteen months Apple changed CFO (Parekh, 2025-01-01), COO (Khan, 2025), general counsel (Newstead from 2026-03-01, with Adams moving to government affairs until retirement in late 2026), lost its AI chief (2025-12-01) and its environment chief (Lisa Jackson, announced 2025-12-04), and named a new CEO (2026-09-01).
rows.mechanism: Simultaneous turnover in finance, operations, legal, environment and AI removes institutional knowledge at the moment the company must re-price its services rent and defend antitrust cases.
rows.benchmark: Apple's 2011 transition had one CEO change with no simultaneous CFO, COO, GC or AI-lead change.
rows.weakens: Apple describes each move as a planned transition, the CFO and COO successors were internal, and there is no filing evidence of dispute or dysfunction.
rows.implication: A cluster of senior turnover into a CEO change raises execution risk; it supports a conditions-based entry rather than buying the transition narrative.
rows.confidence: high on dates and roles; the causation between turnover and execution is an interpretation.
rows.follow_up: Which of these roles is now filled by an external hire, and what is the average tenure of the current executive team?

plan.decision_question: Does the leadership team have the depth and incentives to defend the platform through the AI transition?
plan.thesis_sentence: The team is deep in the functions that built the iPhone era - hardware, operations, finance - and thin where the next era is being decided: AI accountability was reorganised in December 2025 into Craig Federighi's software organisation after the Siri delay, the chip chief was reported to be considering leaving, and the new CEO is a hardware engineer who has never run a services or regulatory fight, so the platform is being defended by continuity rather than by a bench built for the transition.
plan.why_different: This section owns the people, their records, pay and succession; product roadmap, financial results and legal substance belong to other sections, and this section treats them only as evidence of what the leaders have and have not run.
plan.mechanism: Apple built its moat on integrated hardware and a distribution rent; the AI transition shifts value to models, data and cloud, where Apple's bench is thinnest. Its pay model (annual, modest, at-will, heavy unvested RSUs) retains people who value stability but leaves non-disclosed SVPs exposed to poaching, and the 2025-26 turnover cluster removes the executives who held the China supply chain, the legal fights and the AI org.
plan.comparison_set: Microsoft (Nadella FY2025 reported pay $96.5m) and Alphabet (Pichai 2025 reported pay $10.9m but a 2026 target award of $210m and a 1,348,607-share PSU vesting in February 2026) as pay benchmarks; Apple's own 2011 Cook handover as the base rate for an internal succession.
plan.counter_evidence: Apple's own account calls every 2025-26 change a planned transition; Siri AI did ship by WWDC26; Ternus is a 25-year insider with the hardware depth the role now needs; Cook's tenure produced a 2,162% cumulative TSR and 92% say-on-pay.
plan.visual: Team assessment matrix across Cook, Ternus, Parekh and Khan, with the education and career tables and an evidence box on the AI reorganisation.
plan.prohibited: strong team, deep bench as an assertion, world-class, well positioned, experienced team, huge market, any sentence about how the report was written

rows.finding: John Ternus became Apple CEO and a director effective 2026-09-01, with Tim Cook moving to Executive Chair; the appointment was made by the board on 2026-04-17 and disclosed in an 8-K filed 2026-04-20.
rows.mechanism: A planned internal succession from COO-era operator to the hardware engineering chief, preserving continuity of the product organisation while separating the chair and CEO roles.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft and Alphabet both still combine chair/CEO or founder control; Apple's split chair/CEO is the cleaner governance form among the three.
rows.weakens: Ternus has no disclosed experience running services, legal or government affairs — the functions where Apple's margin and regulatory risk now sit.
rows.implication: Succession risk is largely retired for 2026-27; governance continuity supports a multi-year holding, but the CEO's learning curve in services and policy is a real risk to price.
rows.confidence: high — primary 8-K and proxy
rows.follow_up: What operating scope outside hardware has Ternus run, and what retention award did he receive as CEO-designate?

rows.finding: Apple named Johny Srouji Chief Hardware Officer effective 2026-04-20, a newly created role combining Hardware Technologies (his remit since 2015) with Hardware Engineering, which Ternus had led.
rows.mechanism: Retention by expanded remit: the executive reported in December 2025 to be considering leaving was given the company's largest engineering organisation, concentrating silicon and hardware execution under one person.
rows.benchmark: Peer platform companies split silicon and hardware across separate leaders (Microsoft: silicon and devices under different SVPs); Apple is consolidating.
rows.weakens: The December 2025 departure report (S131) is superseded; key-person concentration replaces flight risk as the relevant exposure.
rows.implication: Positive for near-term execution and retention; negative for succession depth — no successor to the consolidated hardware role is disclosed.
rows.confidence: high — near-primary release plus independent coverage; SEC 8-K names only Ternus
rows.follow_up: Who is Srouji's number two, and what retention equity was granted to him outside the proxy's NEO table?

rows.finding: AI was reorganised on 2025-12-01: Giannandrea stepped down to advise before retiring in spring 2026; Amar Subramanya became VP of AI reporting to Craig Federighi, with Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety in Software, and other AI functions moved to Khan and Cue.
rows.mechanism: Accountability for models, product and commercial terms is split across three executives, so no single named owner of the AI P&L appears in any filing.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft has a named EVP of AI and a chief scientist; Alphabet has a CEO of Google DeepMind — both with disclosed, single-point AI accountability.
rows.weakens: The reorganisation shows active management, and Siri AI shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, so the structure has delivered something.
rows.implication: The AI bench is the weakest part of the team case; a holding case should not pay for an AI option until ownership and P&L accountability are named.
rows.confidence: high for the reorganisation; medium for its consequences
rows.follow_up: Who signs off the AI roadmap and budget — Federighi, Subramanya, Cue or the CEO?

rows.finding: Cook's 2025 target compensation was $59m ($3m salary, $6m target cash, $50m equity, 75% performance-based); other named executives target about $23m; there are no employment contracts and no change-of-control payments.
rows.mechanism: Retention runs through unvested time-based RSUs over roughly four and a half years rather than contractual protection, making turnover expensive for executives and cheap for shareholders.
rows.benchmark: Nadella $96.5m (Microsoft FY2025); Pichai $10.9m reported for 2025 with a $210m 2026 target equity award (Alphabet).
rows.weakens: SVP pay for Federighi, Cue, Srouji and Joswiak is not disclosed because they are not Section 16 officers, so the incentive structure of the operating bench is invisible.
rows.implication: Pay is defensible at 92% say-on-pay and aligned through equity, but the disclosure gap limits how far investors can underwrite retention of the technical bench.
rows.confidence: high — proxy and peer proxies
rows.follow_up: What 2026 equity awards went to non-NEO SVPs, and how much is unvested at each?

rows.finding: Apple changed CFO (2025-01-01), COO (2025), general counsel (2026-03-01), AI leadership (2025-12-01), environment leadership (2025-12-04) and CEO (2026-09-01) within about eighteen months.
rows.mechanism: A coordinated generational handover of the executive team, with two internal promotions (Parekh, Khan) and one external hire (Newstead) covering the regulatory load.
rows.benchmark: Large-cap peers typically turn over one or two named executives in an eighteen-month window; Apple's six is a cluster, even if each is planned.
rows.weakens: The outgoing general counsel stayed on government affairs until late 2026, which signals continuity rather than rupture but also the weight of live DOJ and DMA cases.
rows.implication: Bench depth is real (internal successors) but the institutional memory in legal and AI left at the moment regulatory and AI risk peaked.
rows.confidence: high for dates; medium for interpretation
rows.follow_up: Why did the general counsel change at the peak of the antitrust cycle, and who now owns the DOJ and DMA relationships?

rows.finding: Apple's proxy discloses no degrees for any named executive; only Ternus's 1997 Penn engineering degree is established from a university record.
rows.mechanism: Apple's disclosure practice emphasises tenure and scope over credentials, leaving the CEO's technical formation evidenced mainly by his career.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft, Alphabet and Samsung proxies and bios disclose degrees for named executives as a matter of course.
rows.weakens: The gap is a disclosure choice, not evidence of weak qualification; Ternus's 25 years in Apple hardware engineering is stronger evidence than a degree.
rows.implication: The people case cannot be fully verified from filings; confidence in the team's technical depth rests on operating history rather than credentials.
rows.confidence: high — verified absence in the proxy
rows.follow_up: Can Apple IR or the leadership pages supply degrees and prior employers for Parekh, Khan, O'Brien, Newstead and Subramanya?

rows.finding: The June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin included 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS; TrendForce projects 4Q26 conventional DRAM contract prices +10-15% QoQ and NAND +15-20%, with DRAM tight into 2027.
rows.mechanism: A cost shock hits a hardware line priced months ahead: Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, so the gross margin absorbs the increase before any price offset arrives.
rows.benchmark: iPhone 18 Pro BOM +38% YoY with memory 34% of BOM against ~10% a year earlier; 200bp of gross margin = $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of trailing $8.72.
rows.weakens: Q4 guidance of 47-48% reported already assumes part of the increase, and memory price growth is moderating from the 146% first-quarter 2026 jump; services at 76.3% margin cushion the blend.
rows.implication: A 46% gross margin takes FY2027 EPS to about $9.3 and, at 29x, fair value to $270 - the entry price becomes the base case, not the bear case.
rows.confidence: high on the cost data, medium on the pass-through because Apple's price elasticity is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: What gross margin does management guide for the December 2026 quarter, and how much FY2027 memory is contracted at fixed prices?

rows.finding: The trial record put the Google payment at $20bn in 2022, 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and about 15% of operating income at near-pure margin; the district court remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments, and the D.C. Circuit appeal No. 26-5023 with a DOJ cross-appeal seeking a ban is live into 2027.
rows.mechanism: A rent with almost no marginal cost is capitalised in the services multiple; a ban removes operating income and de-rates the line that carries most of the terminal value.
rows.benchmark: A ban is -10% to -13% of EPS and, at 30-35x, -$35 to -$45 a share; a lower rate is the more likely outcome and is worth less than the market's implied perpetuity.
rows.weakens: The payment survived the district court remedy, Apple has filed in support of it, and appellate courts defer on remedies; the 2022 figure may understate or overstate the 2026 rate.
rows.implication: Price a 20-25% probability of loss into any entry; do not pay a services multiple on the full toll.
rows.confidence: medium: the legal record is high-confidence, the outcome and the payment's current size are not
rows.follow_up: What is the current annual payment and term, and when is the D.C. Circuit argument scheduled?

rows.finding: From 2026-10-01 Apple's EU terms charge 26% on in-app purchase, 20% on alternative payment, 15% on link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission; Europe was 26.7% of nine-month FY2026 revenue.
rows.mechanism: Regulated take-rate compression on the highest-margin line transfers rent to developers and alternative storefronts and lowers switching costs out of the App Store.
rows.benchmark: EU band of 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere; each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of trailing operating income.
rows.weakens: Apple retains 26% on in-app purchase; EU App Store revenue is not disclosed and the direct hit may be 1-2% of operating income.
rows.implication: The EU amount is manageable; the template is not. Underwrite services growth at 10-12%, not 15%, and treat a US move to a 5-15% band as the bear case.
rows.confidence: medium: the fee schedule is high-confidence, the revenue exposure is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: How much EU App Store commission revenue is at stake, and how fast are developers migrating to external distribution?

rows.finding: Apple trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median and a 31.0x four-year mean, while the DCF is $212 at a 9.0% cost of equity and $193 at 9.5%.
rows.mechanism: Almost all of the value is terminal, so the discount rate and the exit multiple dominate: each 50bp on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%.
rows.benchmark: Reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.5%, to the 24.6x FY2022 trough 38%; the 52-week low of $243.42 is a 29.4% drawdown.
rows.weakens: Forward 35.2x equals the twelve-month average of 35.7x, and quality franchises have held premium multiples through a 4.93% ten-year Treasury.
rows.implication: Zero position at $344.63; a starter only at $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% across 27-34x exits.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the timing of any re-rating
rows.follow_up: What would the ten-year yield have to do for a 7.0% cost of equity to be defensible, and how sticky is the passive bid?

rows.finding: China shipments fell 10% YoY in Q3 2026 on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%; Apple gained 4.8 points of share in the quarter, and IDC expects the decline to widen to 20% in H2 2026.
rows.mechanism: A shrinking unit pool with a fixed premium layer means revenue growth comes from price and share, both of which reverse when demand is pulled forward.
rows.benchmark: Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue and 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue; Apple grew 30% in the nine months against a market down 4.3% in Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: Apple gained share and the iPhone 18 Pro launch sold 23.5% more than its predecessor; the two trackers disagree by 1.7 points on Apple's Q3 share, so the data are noisy.
rows.implication: Do not capitalise the 30% China growth; a 20% China decline is about 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS.
rows.confidence: medium-high on the direction, medium on the magnitude because the trackers disagree
rows.follow_up: What share of the China growth was pull-forward ahead of Apple's H2 2026 price rises?

rows.finding: Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14 on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capex fell to $6.80bn; no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation.
rows.mechanism: Rented intelligence is operating expense with no asset behind it: the marginal AI dollar is a margin cost, and the supplier also owns Android, so renewal terms carry the bargaining power.
rows.benchmark: A $1bn licence is 0.6% of trailing operating income; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would be several times that and would land in the 76.3% services margin.
rows.weakens: Apple keeps distribution, personal context and Private Cloud Compute, and a better assistant may sell handsets even if Apple does not own the model.
rows.implication: Treat AI as a cost line, not a moat; the upgrade cycle must show up in units and ASP before it is worth paying for.
rows.confidence: low-to-medium: the licence price is reported, not confirmed, and the AI P&L structure is an absence of disclosure
rows.follow_up: What are the Gemini renewal terms, and who signs off the AI budget?

rows.finding: Trailing free cash flow of $136.7bn includes $14.1bn from a rise in other liabilities; normalised FCF is $122.6-125.1bn, while intangibles rose $12.1bn in nine months and inventory is $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end.
rows.mechanism: Working-capital accruals and acquisitions convert into free cash flow without being earnings; inventory build is the channel through which a demand miss becomes a write-down.
rows.benchmark: Conversion of 0.95-0.97x normalised against 1.06x headline, still ahead of Microsoft at 0.50x; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of trailing operating income.
rows.weakens: Apple's cash conversion is genuinely better than peers and the liability swing may be a timing item that reverses as memory is pre-bought.
rows.implication: Use the normalised $122.6-125.1bn for valuation; a 30% lower FCF of $95.7bn no longer covers the $82.2bn buyback plus dividends.
rows.confidence: medium: the swing is filed, its cause is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: What is acquired for $12.1bn of net intangibles, and what sits in the $13.5bn rise in other non-current liabilities?

FY2025 returned $106.1bn, 107% of $98.8bn FCF but 93% of the $114.6bn normalised for the Irish tax payment.
rows.mechanism: Key-person and board-refresh risk affects the roadmap rather than the near-term cash flow; capital return is sustainable on normalised cash but not on the depressed FY2025 figure.
rows.benchmark: 92% say-on-pay, no dual-class stock, internal CFO and COO promotions; underlying FY2025 EPS growth of about 10.6% once the prior year's $10.2bn tax charge is added back, not the 22.7% headline.
rows.weakens: Srouji was promoted and retained, the CEO transition was planned over two years, and the payout ratio is a tax artefact.
rows.implication: Carry as a low-level monitor, not a thesis risk; anchor EPS growth on 8-11% operating growth plus the buyback, not the headline.
rows.confidence: high on the records, medium on the retention outcome because no succession is disclosed
rows.follow_up: When do Levinson and Sugar leave the board, and what retention award keeps Srouji through the 2028 silicon roadmap?

plan.decision_question: At what entry price do the memory, search-payment, DMA and China risks still leave a long-only fund a 9% three-year return, and which signpost would invalidate that entry?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple is a high-quality compounder whose price already capitalises a peak margin and a contested services annuity, so the risks that matter destroy the multiple rather than the balance sheet, and none of them is yet priced at $344.63.
plan.why_different: This is the only section that prices the left tail and the multiple: it separates fatal risks from execution risks, stress-tests the base case against smaller markets, lower FCF and higher discount rates, and gives each risk a dated signpost.
plan.mechanism: Each risk transmits to value through one of two channels: a cost shock against a 48.7% gross margin that applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, or a legal remedy against two near-pure-margin services tolls, and a 39.5x multiple capitalises both at a 2.5% earnings yield so either shock is amplified by the exit multiple.
plan.comparison_set: Peer median 20.2x P/E against Apple's 39.5x; Apple's own four-year mean 31.0x and FY2022 trough 24.6x; the $243.42 52-week low (-29.4%); Samsung's mobile division losing KRW0.8tn and Xiaomi at an 8.5% handset margin show what the memory shock does to weaker hardware models.
plan.counter_evidence: Apple grew iPhone revenue 22.4% through a 16.7% industry unit decline, gained 4.8 points of China share to 19.5% in Q3 2026, holds $62.2bn of net cash, and the district court remedy preserved Google's payments; the multiple has held above 34x for two years.
plan.visual: risk-matrix of nine risks with probability, impact, level, timing, signpost and mitigation, plus a danger card on the gross-margin risk
plan.prohibited: generic risk lists, 'risks are manageable', unquantified probabilities, a risk without an early-warning signpost, repeating the thesis without stress-testing it

user_data_requests.database: PACER — U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey, docket for United States v. Apple Inc., No. 2:24-cv-04055
user_data_requests.query: Docket entries and orders after June 2025: the ruling on Apple's motion to dismiss, the current scheduling order and trial date, and any order defining the remedy theories that remain in the case.
user_data_requests.why: The timing and scope of a US remedy against App Store and device-interoperability rules are the largest long-dated regulatory tail in the investment case; Apple's filings disclose the case but not the schedule or which claims survived dismissal.
user_data_requests.how: Log in to PACER, open the D.N.J. docket 2:24-cv-04055, download the docket sheet and the motion-to-dismiss and scheduling orders, and attach them.

user_data_requests.database: European Commission DMA case register — DMA.100206 (Apple new business terms) and the Article 6(4) non-compliance proceeding
user_data_requests.query: Any formal decision, commitment decision or closure of the Article 6(4) and Article 5(4) proceedings accepting Apple's 18 August 2026 EU business terms; the non-confidential decision text and the effective fee schedule.
user_data_requests.why: It determines whether the 26%/20%/15%/5% EU fee schedule is a binding settlement or an interim step, and therefore whether EU App Store take-rate erosion is settled or still exposed to further Commission action and fines.
user_data_requests.how: Search the Commission's DMA case register for DMA.100206 and the Apple non-compliance cases, download the latest decision and press release, and attach them.

user_data_requests.database: IDC Worldwide Quarterly Mobile Phone Tracker (regional pivot) or Canalys/Omdia regional smartphone dataset — paid subscription
user_data_requests.query: Smartphone market value in USD and unit shipments by region (Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, Rest of Asia-Pacific) for 2023-2026, with the premium segment (wholesale ASP $600+) split by vendor.
user_data_requests.why: Free releases give global market value ($613B for 2026) and China units only. Without the regional pivot I cannot size the regional TAM or compute Apple's share of each regional market, so the regional growth table relies on Apple's own segment revenue as a proxy and the durability conclusion is weaker for Americas, Europe, Japan and Rest of Asia-Pacific.
user_data_requests.how: Export the regional market-value pivot from the IDC tracker (or the equivalent Canalys/Omdia workbook) and attach the Excel or PDF to the case file.

user_data_requests.database: PACER — US v. Google LLC, D.D.C. No. 1:20-cv-03010 (remedies record and trial exhibits on the Apple default-search agreement)
user_data_requests.query: The current Apple–Google Safari default-search agreement terms: the revenue share (36% of Safari search advertising in the 2022 record), the annual amount paid to Apple for the most recent year, and the renewal/termination terms under Judge Mehta's 2025-12-05 final judgment.
user_data_requests.why: Apple discloses no search-licensing revenue. The only public figure is the 2022 payment of $20B, which is 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue and 12.9% of operating income. Whether the 2026 run-rate is $20B or $30B changes the size of the largest single repricing risk in the business model section by half.
user_data_requests.how: Download the final judgment and the revenue-share exhibits from the D.D.C. docket on PACER (fee per page), or use the Department of Justice antitrust division's public case page for US v. Google, which posts the opinions and trial exhibits without a login.

user_data_requests.database: USPTO Patent Center and PatentsView (patent search and grant counts)
user_data_requests.query: For Apple Inc. (assignee): granted and pending US patents filed 2023-2026 in foldable hinges/displays, on-device model compression and optical health sensing, with patent numbers, filing and grant dates and status; plus Apple's US grant count for 2025 and 2026.
user_data_requests.why: The technology section's patent table rests on an aggregate grant count (2,722 in 2025, down 12%) and could not cite a single verified patent number or a granted-versus-pending mix. Without it, freedom-to-operate risk in foldable hinges and health sensing cannot be assessed, which is the one part of the moat argument left at low confidence.
user_data_requests.how: PatentsView's current API needs a key (free registration at search.patentsview.org); alternatively export a Patent Center search by assignee "Apple Inc." for CPC codes on hinges (E05D), displays and PPG sensing, 2023-2026, as CSV.

user_data_requests.database: Apple Investor Relations leadership and governance biographies (investor.apple.com/leadership-and-governance and apple.com/leadership)
user_data_requests.query: Degrees, prior employers and start dates for Craig Federighi, Eddy Cue, Johny Srouji, Sabih Khan, Kevan Parekh, Deirdre O'Brien, Jennifer Newstead, Amar Subramanya and John Ternus.
user_data_requests.why: Apple's proxy discloses no university degrees for any named executive and no pay or ownership for its technology leaders, so six of seven executive education cells and the prior-career records of the AI, software and silicon leaders cannot be verified from filings. Filling them determines whether the bench really has AI and cloud depth, which is the core of the team judgement.
user_data_requests.how: Open investor.apple.com/leadership-and-governance, open each executive's bio, and save the pages as PDF or paste the bio text (about 12 profiles).

user_data_requests.database: Bloomberg, FactSet or LSEG consensus (subscription terminal)
user_data_requests.query: AAPL consensus revenue, EPS and free cash flow for FY2027 and FY2028, the consensus 12-month price target, and trailing/forward P/E and EV/EBIT for Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and Xiaomi (1810.HK) as of 2026-10-30
user_data_requests.why: The valuation section states Apple's forward consensus as "not disclosed" because no free source in this run carried it, and the two named global handset peers could not be valued at all: they file no US GAAP accounts. Without the estimates the DCF's 9%-to-5% growth fade cannot be checked against the street, and the peer premium is measured against US platform names only, which understates or overstates Apple's premium depending on Samsung's and Xiaomi's multiples.
user_data_requests.how: Export the consensus summary page (revenue, EPS, FCF, target price) for AAPL and the valuation multiples screen for 005930.KS and 1810.HK, dated 2026-10-30, as a PDF or spreadsheet.

user_data_requests.database: CIRP (Consumer Intelligence Research Partners) US iPhone upgrade and installed-base reports
user_data_requests.query: iPhone upgrade rate by model year for 2024, 2025 and 2026, and the share of iPhone buyers upgrading from a device three or more years old
user_data_requests.why: It is the one datum that separates the two readings of the 27.6% ASP rise: cost recovery at higher prices, or genuine upgrade demand that supports FY2027 iPhone revenue. Apple discloses no upgrade rate and no unit volumes, so without a panel series the durability of the price-led growth cannot be tested.
user_data_requests.how: Subscribe to or request CIRP's quarterly US iPhone upgrade reports (cirp.com), or any equivalent panel (Counterpoint's installed-base tracker). A single quarterly series covering 2024-2026 is enough.

user_data_requests.query: Apple (AAPL): FY2027 and FY2028 consensus EPS, revenue, gross margin and free cash flow, plus the mean 12-month price target and number of covering analysts, as of 2026-10-30.
user_data_requests.why: The report's FY2027E EPS of $9.79 is implied from a 35.2x market-data multiple, and the $338-355 target range comes from four retail aggregators with no disclosed methodology. A licensed feed would confirm or move the fair-value range and the $270 entry ladder.
user_data_requests.how: Export the consensus summary page for AAPL from your LSEG Workspace or Visible Alpha subscription and attach it to the request.

notes.note: Your 22 May 2026 Google date is the opening brief, not the appeal: Google appealed the 2025-12-05 final judgment in Jan-Feb 2026 and filed its D.C. Circuit brief on 2026-05-22. Your App Store take-rate row says 15-30% globally. From 2026-10-01 Apple's EU terms are 26% in-app purchase, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission for alternative marketplaces or web distribution, so the EU band is 5-26% and falling. Worth a footnote where you compare take rates.

The pricing table now has a separate row: App Store (EU, from 2026-10-01) — 26% in-app purchase, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission, i.e. an EU band of 5-26% against 15-30% outside the EU, cited to your S77 (Apple newsroom, 2026-08-18) and S78 (Commission DMA decision, 2025-04-23). I left the 15-30% row labelled "ex-EU" so the two do not read as one global rate.

Corrected. Dropped the claim that Google appealed on 22 May 2026; the section now says Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default deal at 12 months, and that Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 2026-05-22 challenges that judgment (the brief, not the notice of appeal). A dated fact for the competitive section: Apple's newest foldable-hinge family, pending US20240147644A1 (filed 2023-10-06, published 2024-05-02), is co-assigned with Hangzhou Amphenol Phoenix Telecom Parts, the supplier, not solely Apple's. Patent verification changes one moat input for the risk section. Supplier-concentration plus shared IP, not a clean patent moat.

Two reconciliations. The $270 entry is a single-point bet: 27.6x $9.79, but 29.4x the $9.19 low end of the FY2027 EPS band and 26.8x the $10.08 high end. In multiples the ladder is entry $254-278, fair value $267-292, sale $414-454 (44-48x forward): tranches at $278/$266/$254 hold 27-28x whatever FY2027 delivers; a 6% lower EPS path cuts the 9.9% three-year return at $270 to 7.6%. A 30% revenue fall on through-cycle margins (44.1% gross, opex held) gives $4.68 EPS, not $5.95 at the 43% incremental margin; at 24.6x that is $115, not $242.

Your 10-Q count is now disclosed in the exit share-count row (14,609m outstanding, 0.7% lower, $5,034bn on that basis). The $440 sale trigger sits inside your $414-454 band, so the sale side reconciles. 1.name: Completeness sweep
1.notes: Completeness sweep against the section standards and the lens checklist. Met: company identity and single-class cap table with exact counts and float; entity map with ownership; dated timeline (27 events, all YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD); team education and career tables with an explicit \"not disclosed\" record for six of seven executives and a reference-check target list; product inventory, technology comparison and moat table; TAM/SAM/SOM with a bottom-up cross-check ($581B vs IDC's $613B, 5% apart); regional table with barriers and competitors; status quo and a substitutes row in the competition table; unit economics, pricing and take-rate table; five-year financial statements, returns and working-capital table with a normalised-FCF bridge; four valuation methods plus a sensitivity grid; exit routes, precedent realisations and an entry/exit return table; dated regulatory record table; weighted score table with position sizing; scenario and analog tables. Components all present and populated (verdict, briefing, efficiency, one-question, takeaways, kpi, timeline, evidence x4, quad, info, risk-matrix, scenarios, analogs, sensitivity). The tool's rule check on version 1 returned no findings; my own N2/N3 spot checks found no unlabelled company-only claim and no unattributed material figure. Gaps that became items: the bull-case collision, the patent table, the sign error, the length ceiling. Not raised because explicitly and adequately stated in the report: the unverifiable BlackRock 13G/A (2023-12-31), the missing regional market values (three of five regions \"not published\": paywalled, U3 open), no named AI P&L owner, no degrees for six executives, no disclosure of the Google payment by Apple.

2.name: Claim verification
2.notes: Claim verification, claim by claim. Verified against primary filings: revenue, segment mix, gross and operating margin, EPS and share count (S5, S6); the 50.1% June-quarter margin with 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of $2.02 EPS (S17); net cash $62,173M (S6); buyback and dividend history FY2021-FY2025 (S1-S5); share count 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02, insiders 9,079,765 shares, Vanguard 9.63% (S11); Ninth Circuit 2025-12-11 finding on the 27% link-out commission (S69); Mehta final judgment 2025-12-05 allowing non-exclusive payments (S76, S101); EU fee schedule from 2026-10-01 (S77, S78); Ternus appointment 2026-04-20 and Srouji as Chief Hardware Officer (S56, S133, S141). Independent and cross-checked: IDC shipments -16.7%, $613bn value, $581 ASP against Omdia's $565 (S84, S88); China Q3 2026 -10% Counterpoint against -15.4% IDC (S139, S140); TrendForce memory +146% 1Q26 and 4Q26 contract increases (S68, S136); Xiaomi 8.5% handset margin and Samsung MX KRW0.6tn loss (S90, S91, S75). Labelled as company or reported: 2.5bn installed base (earnings call, S73 — labelled as estimate throughout the business-model table), Gemini licence at ~$1bn (reported, unconfirmed, S111/S122), $1.4tn App Store ecosystem (Apple, S83), Siri and Private Cloud Compute (Apple Newsroom, S113). The $20bn search payment is a litigated 2022 estimate, not an Apple disclosure, and is labelled as such in the ESG and risk sections. No stale claim older than its purpose requires: the 2022 payment figure is the most recent public figure and is dated; S118 (TPU use, 2024) is dated and still the only disclosure. Confidence grades on the register are respected in the text except for the three aggregator comparisons raised above.

3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes: Missing-competitor challenge, working outward from the report's own text. Checked and adequately covered: Samsung (share and loss-making MX division), Huawei (China share, HarmonyOS 51M units, CNY192.3bn R&D), Xiaomi (8.5% handset margin), Google as both rival (Pixel, Android, Gemini) and supplier, Lenovo/HP/Dell in PCs, Spotify in music, Alphabet in advertising, the status quo of longer device life, and the regulatory substitute of DMA-enabled distribution. Geographic check: China covered; India covered as supply and demand; Japan, Europe and the Americas are thin on local rivals but the vendors named there are the global set, so no separate gap. Academic and spin-out check: no university or lab programme can replicate an installed base at this scale, so nothing to add. Supply-side concentration (TSMC as the single 2nm source) is named only indirectly through the Taiwan Strait risk; it is a dependency rather than a competitor, and the risk section does flag the 2nm supply stop, so it is not raised as an item. The technology section's own weakness (a rented frontier layer) is already conceded, which is why the open-weight omission matters: the report argues Apple could have built rather than rented but never tests the cheaper third route.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes: Product/market-fit questions as put to the section owners. 1) What is the single hardest thing about selling this product now? Answer from the evidence: re-pricing a $1,199 handset into a unit market falling 16.7% while the cost of the bill of materials rises 38% — the report makes this case well but measures demand only after the fact. 2) Who is the budget owner? Consumer, or carrier instalment plan, or developer and subscriber inside services; the memo names all three, evidences none of the channel split. 3) Typical sales cycle? Annual September launch, carrier-controlled channel in Japan, no enterprise cycle discussed; adequate for a consumer business, but the claim that the procurement cycle follows the launch is unevidenced. 4) Why is adoption not faster? Answered well: Siri shipped 23 months after Apple Intelligence and only as an English beta, so the AI upgrade reason arrived late; foldable at $2,550+ ASP is a new price point. 5) What do the lost deals say? Partly answered — China unit share behind Huawei, Xiaomi winning on price-performance, Samsung on foldable head start — but no switching data out of iOS, which is the number that would make the installed-base argument testable. The memo is stronger on why the franchise holds than on what would make a buyer refuse, which is the pass's main finding.

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes: Stress-test arithmetic, key number by key number. (1) Gross margin 50.1% to 47-48%: 200bp = $9.35bn of gross profit on $466.8bn, $0.52 of EPS after a 17.3% tax rate on 14.75bn shares, 6.0% of $8.72 — the report's figure checks. At 46% ($4.66bn more), EPS $9.79 falls to $9.26, and 29x gives $269 — the entry price is exactly the 46% case, which is why the entry and the margin assumption must be read together. (2) Losing the $20bn payment: 20 × 0.827 / 14.75 = $1.12 of EPS, 12.9% of $8.72 — checks; on a near-pure-margin basis before tax it is $20bn of operating income, 12.9% of $154.9bn, consistent. If the 2026 payment is 25% larger at $25bn, the hit is 16.1% of trailing EPS — not thesis-breaking at a Watchlist rating, but it widens the bear. (3) Revenue 30% lower: at 43% incremental the report gets operating income $95bn and EPS $5.4 (checks: 466.8 × 0.7 = 326.8, a $140.1bn fall, × 0.43 = $60.2bn, leaving $94.7bn; × 0.827 / 14.75 = $5.31). With operating expense held flat the fall passes through at roughly the 33% margin, operating income about $108bn, EPS about $6.05 — the report's stress is the flattering version. (4) Free cash flow 30% lower: $125.1bn × 0.7 = $87.6bn, inside the stated $85.8-89.1bn range, 57.4x on $5,029.6bn — checks; it covers the $82.2bn trailing buyback and not the $97.9bn of buybacks plus dividends. (5) Multiple reversion: 31.0/39.5 = -21.5%, 24.6/39.5 = -37.7% — checks, and the exit section's three-year returns from $270 (5.0-13.3% across 27x-34x exits on FY2029E EPS of $11.45) are consistent with its own assumptions. (6) Probability-weighted value: 0.25 × 357 + 0.50 × 284 + 0.25 × 241 = $291.5, -15.4% on $344.63, and +8.0% at $270 against the tabulated +7.8% — rounding, acceptable. (7) Sum of the parts: services EBIT $62.7bn at 23x = $1,442bn, hardware $92.1bn at 12x = $1,105bn, plus $62.2bn net cash = $2,609bn, $177 a share on 14.72bn shares — checks; the 28x/18x upper case gives $238. (8) Own-history 31.0x on $9.79 = $303 — checks, but inherits the unexplained EPS. Does the thesis survive a 30% worse number? Yes, and asymmetrically: the recommendation is Watchlist with zero position, so a worse number reinforces it; the dangerous error is on the upside, where the 27.5% twelve-month return is the evidence against the discipline and the report concedes it. What the memo has not stress-tested is the entry ladder itself, which is a single-point bet on $9.79 — item 2 above.

items.issue: The memo runs two different bull cases and the executive briefing quotes the weaker one as if it were the upside. The executive briefing and scoring say "the bull case $277, 20% below the market"; the thesis scenario table and the 25/50/25 weighting use a bull of $357 at 35x FY2027 EPS of $10.20, which is +4% on the price. A reader of the briefing concludes the upside case is 20% underwater, while the thesis's own bull case is a positive return and is what the probability-weighted $291.5 depends on. The funding section's "even the bull case ... is worth $277" compounds it.
items.action: Name the two objects distinctly in every section: the DCF bull ($277 at an 8.5% discount rate) and the scenario/multiple bull ($357 at 35x FY2027 EPS). Rebuild the executive briefing, the scoring takeaway and the funding conclusion on the scenario range, since that is what the recommendation and the weighting use, and state plainly that the bull case is roughly flat to +4%, not -20%.

items.issue: The patent table carries no patent number, no filing or grant date and only "not verified" for status, on an aggregate 2025 grant count of 2,722. The section states this as a limitation and a data request is open, but the technology standard requires a patent table with numbers, jurisdiction, dates and legal status, and the moat table's "difficulty" scores for foldable hinges and health sensing rest on an unverified portfolio.
items.action: Either cite three to five verified patents (number, assignee, filing date, grant date, status) in hinges, display lamination and PPG health sensing, or mark the moat-table difficulty scores that depend on them as judgement with low confidence, so the reader can see which moat claims are evidenced.
items.evidence_request: Granted and pending US patents for Apple Inc. 2023-2026 in foldable hinges (CPC E05D), displays and optical health sensing, with numbers, dates and status, plus 2026 grant counts.

items.issue: The regime sentence reads "down 8.3% over one month against 0.9% for the SPY". The register's own relative figure (Apple +3.5% against the S&P at +4.4 points of relative performance) implies the SPY fell about 0.9% over the month, and the same sentence calls technology the laggard, so the index figure is sign-flipped.
items.action: Correct the SPY one-month move to -0.9% so the regime paragraph is internally consistent with the leadership figures in the funding section.

items.issue: Ten of the fourteen sections sit between 8,930 and 8,991 characters against a 9,000-character refusal limit. There is no room to add the evidence the Important items below require without deleting something, and an edit that overruns will be refused outright.
items.action: Trim each affected section by 400-700 characters of restatement (the repeated 39.5x/35.2x and 50.1%-refund sentences appear in five sections) before adding the new evidence, so each fix fits.

items.issue: The anchor forecast of the whole valuation, FY2027 EPS of $9.79, has no shown derivation and no source that can produce it. S71 (S&P Global) is an iPhone-revenue preview carrying $56.4bn for the quarter, $252.4bn for FY2026 and $277.4bn for FY2027; the financials section nevertheless cites it for "consensus of $252.4B for FY2026 (+20.4% on FY2025) and $277.4B for FY2027 (+9.9%)" as if it were company revenue, which would put FY2026 revenue below FY2025 and contradicts the same section's $477bn revenue forecast. Separately, $9.79 appears as "implied FY2027 EPS" in the funding table, as the base-case numerator ($284 at 29x) in the thesis and scoring, and as the denominator of the $440 sell trigger, while the open data request records consensus EPS as not obtained. A trailing filing (S6) cannot source a forecast, and no bridge from TTM EPS of $8.72 to $9.79 (+12.3%) is given anywhere.
items.action: Show the bridge: TTM net income and diluted shares to FY2027 EPS, with each assumption (revenue growth, gross margin 47-48%, operating margin 33%, tax 17.5%, share count after buyback) and tag the derived figures as the report's own estimate rather than consensus. Correct the financials sentence so $252.4bn and $277.4bn are labelled iPhone revenue consensus, not company revenue, and state company-level consensus revenue and EPS as not disclosed if that is the case.
items.evidence_request: Primary consensus for AAPL revenue, diluted EPS and free cash flow for FY2027 and FY2028, dated 2026-10-30, to replace or corroborate the $9.79 estimate; and confirmation of the FY2026 iPhone consensus of $252.4bn.

items.issue: Three load-bearing comparisons rest on low- or medium-confidence aggregators, and the memo's central claim of non-consensus pricing depends on the weakest of them. Apple's 35.2x forward comes from FinanceCharts (S97, medium), the S&P 500's 18.09x from Trendonify (S146, medium) and the "sell side's median target of $338-355" from Tickernerd (S142, low) and TickFlow (S144, low) — two retail aggregator pages. The premium to the index (95%) and the "the sell side sees fair value where this analysis sees overvaluation" sentence are both conclusions a committee will test first.
items.action: State the source basis and confidence beside the index multiple and the street target, or replace them with a primary consensus feed. If the street target cannot be corroborated, downgrade it from "the sell side's median" to "two aggregator estimates" and remove it from the executive briefing's non-consensus argument.
items.evidence_request: Primary consensus 12-month price target and index forward P/E from a licensed feed (the open request covers AAPL consensus but not the index multiple).

items.issue: The Google payment is expressed on two bases without a label: "18.3% of services revenue and 15% of operating income" is the FY2025 denominator, while the business-model section uses 16.6% and 12.9% on trailing figures. A reader comparing sections sees four different percentages for one cash flow.
items.action: Give the basis in the executive briefing card and in the ESG section ("18.3% of FY2025 services revenue; 16.6% on trailing") and keep one basis for the sensitivity arithmetic.

items.issue: "Index role: largest in the peer set; the weight itself is not publicly disclosed in the sources here" — index weights are published daily by the index providers, so the sentence describes the register's gap as a market fact and weakens an otherwise strong liquidity paragraph.
items.action: Either cite the published S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 weights, or drop the weight and keep the point that passive ownership is structural.

items.issue: Four substitutes a committee partner would name first are absent. The competition table lists eight rivals but no app-distribution substitute (Epic Games, DMA-enabled alternative storefronts), no assistant substitute (OpenAI/ChatGPT, which the report itself cites in the xAI suit context), no Microsoft, and no open-weight model that could commoditise the Gemini licence the technology section prices at $1bn a year. Epic is the counterparty to the contempt finding quoted in the ESG section and does not appear as a competitor anywhere.
items.action: Add to the competition table and map each to Apple's profit pool: Epic Games and the alternative storefronts enabled by the DMA (the litigant whose contempt finding already cost Apple the 27% link-out commission, and the direct substitute for App Store distribution in a region that is 26.7% of revenue); OpenAI (ChatGPT as the assistant users open instead of Siri, and a consumer-hardware entrant with a design team drawn from Apple); Microsoft (Copilot against Siri and Windows on ARM against the Mac, with a distribution base Apple cannot match); open-weight models (Llama, DeepSeek, Mistral) which are the credible commoditisation route for the licensed Gemini layer; and Tencent/WeChat mini-programmes as the Chinese substitute for app distribution, which is more relevant to the China profit pool than another handset vendor.
items.evidence_request: Share of EU iOS digital transactions that moved to alternative marketplaces or web distribution since 2026-10-01, and any published figure for ChatGPT or Copilot usage among iPhone owners, to size the assistant-substitution threat.

items.issue: The China share claim is reported selectively across the two trackers in the register. The competition and market sections quote Huawei on both counts (21.3% Counterpoint, 21.1% IDC) but Apple only on Counterpoint's 19.5%; IDC has Apple at 17.8%, which is 3.3 points behind Huawei rather than 1.8. The sentence "Apple took 19.5%, second" is therefore load-bearing on a single tracker while the reader is shown the other tracker's rival figure next to it.
items.action: Quote both trackers for Apple and Huawei in the same sentence, or state explicitly which count the "second, up 4.8 points" claim uses and why, and carry Apple's 17.8% IDC figure into the weaknesses row and the risk matrix so the China gain is not presented as tracker-independent.
items.evidence_request: Counterpoint's and IDC's own Apple share for Q3 2026 alongside Huawei's, ideally from the primary notes rather than the secondary write-ups.

items.issue: Honor appears in the market section's China competitor list and in the "top six vendors hold 96%" sentence but is missing from the competition table, and Transsion, the emerging-market leader named in the regional table, has no row either. The table reads as complete when two named rivals are absent.
items.action: Add Honor to the competitor table (it holds top-six China share and appears in the market table's vendor list) or state that the table is limited to the five largest global vendors plus Apple's litigation counterparties.

items.issue: The hardest thing about this sale is a 27.6% average price increase into a market whose units are falling 16.7%, and the memo prices the outcome without the evidence that would predict it. There is no upgrade or replacement-cycle figure, no sell-through or activation data for the iPhone 18 and Duo launch, no trade-in or financing attach, and no lost-deal evidence on elasticity; the demand question is deferred in five sections to the 2026-11-02 print. "Price-led growth is the most reversible kind" is asserted but never measured against a base rate.
items.action: Add, in the market and business-model sections, the evidence an operator would want before accepting $1,199-1,299 pricing: the installed-base upgrade or replacement rate and its trend, any published sell-through or activation data for the iPhone 18 line, and the lease or trade-in attach. Where none is public, say so and name the December-quarter unit disclosure or carrier activation data that would settle it, and state explicitly that the demand test is unresolvable before 2026-11-02 rather than deferring to it.
items.evidence_request: iPhone replacement or upgrade rate (or installed-base churn) for 2024-2026, and any third-party sell-through or activation estimates for the September 2026 launch in the US, Europe and China.

items.issue: The Klarna Apple Upgrade programme is listed as a launched partnership with no economics, while it is precisely the mechanism that could make a $1,199 handset affordable and is therefore part of the pricing-power argument. Who carries residual value and credit risk under the lease is not stated.
items.action: Either quantify the residual-value and credit risk borne by Apple under the Klarna lease, and who the lessee's counterparty is, or drop the phrase "Apple Upgrade device leasing" from the partner table and keep the partner listing to scope only.

items.issue: The $48.2 per-active-device services line divides services revenue by 2.5bn devices, including free-tier users, so it is an average monetisation rate, not attach. The services thesis (12-14% growth) needs paid-subscription penetration and churn, neither of which appears in any section.
items.action: Split the per-device services figure into what is disclosed (total services revenue per active device) and what is not (paid-attach rate), and say which would settle it.

items.issue: "The budget owner is the consumer or carrier financing plan" is asserted without evidence of how much of the installed base is bought on carrier instalment, and the 40% direct / 60% indirect split is given without saying which channel carries the retail price. Enterprise and education buying, where the budget owner is a procurement function rather than a consumer, is not costed at all.

items.issue: Two market capitalisations and two trailing multiples coexist. 5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes: Stress-test arithmetic checked. Build to $9.79: $520.8bn revenue (iPhone consensus $277.4bn + $243.4bn, +9.2% on $477.1bn), 48.0% gross margin = $250.0bn, less $80.0bn opex = $170.1bn operating income (32.7%), plus $1.0bn other, taxed at 17.3% = $141.5bn over 14,450M shares = $9.79. Band: 46% gives $9.19, 49% gives $10.08; 100bp is $0.30 of EPS; 200bp off margin takes EPS to $9.27 and $270 to 29.1x; a 12.9% search-payment cut on top gives $8.07 and $270 to 33.5x against the 31.0x four-year mean. Thesis survives a 30% worse number: on $4.10-4.68 of stress EPS at 24.6-29x the value is $101-136, at or below the $133 DCF bear, and the memo already states that this is a permanent-loss tail rather than a trading drawdown. Every changed-section paragraph ends with at least one source tag and every table has a Source column. Spot checks: $5,071.2bn = $344.63 x 14,715M; 35.2x = 344.63/9.79; 39.1x is EV/NOPAT ($5,009.0bn/$128.1bn), consistent with the $5,009.1bn enterprise value in the same paragraph though not labelled as EV; the FY2027 build ties ($520.8bn x 48.0% = $250.0bn gross profit, less $80.0bn opex, plus $1.0bn other, at 17.3% tax on 14,450M = $9.79). The competitor set read in this review holds up: Huawei and Samsung in handsets, Google in models, chips and distribution, Xiaomi in China, Microsoft and Alphabet in services margins (S49, S15), HP and Dell on hardware multiples (S103-S106), with Samsung's DX operating loss and Xiaomi's margin squeeze used as substitutes evidence (S75, S90, S91). The open gaps are geographic and data-specific rather than missing firms: no regional market-value pivot (IDC/Canalys, filed as a user request), so regional share is proxied by Apple's segment revenue; no licensed consensus for the two Korean/Chinese handset peers, stated in funding_valuation. Substitutes are covered at the platform level (licensed assistant, alternative app stores, external payment links) and the second-hand/refurbished market is absent but not decision-relevant at a 39.3x multiple on new-device gross profit. The three verified patent records (S148-S150, one co-assigned with Amphenol) close the R1 objection that the patent table rested on an unverified aggregate.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes: Product/market fit. The five questions are answered in the memo, and the answers are consistent across sections. Hardest thing about selling: price-led growth into a shrinking unit market (IDC -16.7% in 2026, S84) with memory at 34% of the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials (S99) - the memo says so explicitly rather than claiming volume demand. Budget owner: the consumer, paid before the cost is incurred (cash conversion cycle -56.8 days, S5/S6), so there is no acquisition-cost payback to compute. Sales cycle: none at retail, carrier and channel mediated; the binding constraint is the replacement cycle, not a procurement process. Why adoption is not faster: the flagship feature is a licensed model shipped as an English beta 23 months after Apple Intelligence (S111, S113), and the upgrade rate is not disclosed anywhere - the memo says the 27% implied ASP rise is memory pass-through and Pro mix \"not evidence of an upgrade cycle\", and the CIRP panel request (U8) is the datum that would settle it. Lost deals: China, where Apple is at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3% on Counterpoint (S96) and 17.8% against 21.1% on IDC (S140), framed as a shrinking pool rather than a share loss - with the market down 10-15.4% in Q3 2026, that framing is defensible but worth watching. No customer concentration risk exists (index and retail holders, largest 9.63%), and the distribution question is regulatory rather than commercial: the EU fee schedule from 2026-10-01 and the link-out remand.

Valuation: $284 = 29 x $9.79; $241 = 24.6 x $9.79; $357 = 35 x $10.20; weighted $291.5 = 0.25 x 357 + 0.5 x 284 + 0.25 x 241; -15.4% at $344.63 (0.25 x 3.6 + 0.5 x -17.6 + 0.25 x -30.1) and +7.8% at $270 (0.25 x 32 + 0.5 x 5 + 0.25 x -11) both check; $270/9.79 = 27.6x, $440 = 45 x 9.79, and $440 is 27.7% above the price and 23.2% above the $357 bull. Multiples: 39.3x = 5,071.2/128.93; 40.5x = 5,071.2/125.1 (39.8-41.4x across the band); 2.5% FCF yield; EV $5,009.0bn. Exit table reproduces exactly (27x/31x/34x on FY2029E EPS of $11.45 plus $3.55 of dividends: -3.2%/1.3%/4.5% from $344.63 and 5.0%/9.9%/13.3% from $270); a 6% lower earnings path gives 7.7%/yr from $270. Earnings: FY2027 build ties to $9.79, and each 100bp of gross margin is $0.30. Stress: revenue -30% = $326.8bn; at 44.5% gross margin and $72.3bn opex, operating income $73.1bn, EPS $4.10, a 58.5% decremental margin; at the 43.0% up-cycle rate, $94.6bn and $5.4; FCF -30% = $85.8-89.1bn, 56.9-59.1x, which covers the $82.2bn buyback but not $97.9bn of buyback plus dividends; the balance sheet survives on $62.2bn of net cash. Kelly: on 25/50/25 of +32%/+5%/-11%, argmax E[log(1+f.r)] sits near 4.4x the fund, so \"about 5x\" is fair and 39% was indefensible - the rebuilt block is consistent with the 5% cap and the 0.75-1.0%/2.5-3.0% tranches, and the 1.5% maximum loss at the cap (5% x 30%) is right. Thesis survives 30% worse: at $4.10 EPS and 29x the value is $119, at or below the $133 DCF bear, and the recommendation is already zero position with a conditional ladder, so a worse number strengthens rather than overturns it.

# Apple Inc.: Investment research report
Rating: Watchlist
Composite score: 6.0
Data as of: 2026-10-31

## Executive Briefing

Apple closed at $344.63 on 30 October 2026, a $5,072bn market capitalisation and a 27.5% total return over twelve months; the last reported period is the June quarter, with Q4 FY2026 results due on 2 November 2026, so the price contains no post-results adjustment. The market it trades in is near its high: the S&P 500 at 7,580.07 is up 10.7% year to date and 3.4% below its record, the Nasdaq is 8.2% below its high, the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93%. Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month while the SPY fell 0.9% — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.97 times net income, 0.95 times at the low end of the normalised band, on capex of 2.2% of revenue; it holds $62,173M of net cash and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48% [S6, S17].

The price is the problem. At 39.3 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings against 18.7 times for the S&P 500 (FactSet, 2026-10-23), the shares discount a 7.0% cost of equity or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth; the DCF at 9.0% is $212, its 8.5% discount-rate bull is $277 (20% below the close), the sum of the parts is $177-238, and the base scenario is $284, 18% below the close. The recommendation rests on the base case and on the 25/50/25 probability-weighted value of $291.5, 15% below the price — not on either bull. The scenario bull is $357 at 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20, a 25% branch with a +4% return. The market is capitalising a peak margin and a peak multiple at the same time; the retail aggregator targets of $338-355, unverified, sit at the spot price, so the Street sees fair value where this analysis sees overvaluation [S7, S97, S156, S142, S144].

Two facts would change the call. A gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it; an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear toward the discounted-cash-flow floor. The one question below decides which of the two the next twelve months delivers.

Positioning follows from that: zero today, a conditional staged entry below the base case, and a sell discipline tied to the multiple and to services growth. The first tranche at $270 requires the 2026-11-02 guide to hold FY2027 EPS at $9.27 or better and gross margin at 47%; if it holds, the second tranche is $245; if it fails, the first moves to $235 and the second to $210. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and the December-quarter guide on 2 November 2026, two days after this version. The follow-up diligence is threefold: the working-capital and intangibles note in that filing, a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, and the D.C. Circuit briefing and decision [S6, S7].

## Company Overview

Apple is legally and structurally clean enough to hold for years — one share class, one registrant, no VIE and a genuinely unblocked exit — but its governance has barely refreshed in a decade and two of seven independents sit at Apple's own age-75 ceiling, so the holding should be underwritten on cash generation and clean title rather than on board quality. Apple Inc. is a California corporation incorporated on 1977-01-03, listed on Nasdaq under AAPL in US dollars. At 2026-01-02 it had 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding against 50,400,000,000 authorised, all of a single class of $0.00001 par common stock with one vote per share. There is no dual-class structure, no VIE, no nominee shareholder and no contractual control chain — verified in the balance sheet and the 2026 proxy, not assumed. Float is effectively the whole company: directors and officers hold 9,079,765 shares, or 0.06%, leaving 99.94%. Vanguard (9.63%) and BlackRock (7.10%) are the only disclosed 5% holders — and BlackRock's figure rests on a Schedule 13G/A reflecting holdings at 2023-12-31, so the 2026 register is partly unknown.
