The structure that mattered economically was profit allocation, not ownership: Irish branches operated under tax opinions issued in 1991 and 2007, which the Commission treated as state aid on 2016-08-30. The General Court annulled that decision on 2020-07-15, the Court of Justice set the annulment aside on 2024-09-10, and Apple booked a one-time $10.2bn net charge in Q4 FY2024 — $15.8bn payable to Ireland from escrow, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit. Irish law had already closed the opinions from January 2015. Two consequences follow: the tax rate is now policy-driven rather than engineered, at 24.1% in FY2024 and 15.6% in FY2025 with no filing supporting a return to the pre-2015 structure; and the entity map carries no enforceability premium, because the legal risk attached to it is regulatory rather than structural — a materially better position than a contractually controlled China VIE. [S5]

### Business model: one platform, one rent, one budget owner

Apple sells integrated hardware to consumers, small businesses, education, enterprise and government, then monetises the installed base through Services. FY2025 net sales were $416,161m, split $307,003m products and $109,158m services, with 40% direct and 60% indirect distribution. The end user is usually the buyer, but the budget owner for the highest-margin line is the developer and the subscriber: Services earned a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products. Growth comes from installed-base expansion and price/mix, not unit share — Apple states it holds a minority share of global smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 iPhone was 53.9% of revenue against 51.2% a year earlier and Services 25.2%, so concentration is rising again rather than falling. [S5, S17]

### Governance: senior, stable, slow to refresh

Eight directors stood in 2026: seven independent plus the CEO. Independent tenure averages 12.0 years — Levinson 26 years and chair since 2000, Jung 18, Sugar 16, Wagner 12, Lozano and Gorsky 5, Austin 2 — and two of the seven (Levinson, 75; Sugar, 77) are at or past the company's own guideline that directors generally may not stand for re-election after 75. Committees are conventional and fully independent: Audit under Sugar (nine meetings in 2025), People and Compensation under Jung, Nominating under Wagner; 92% of votes cast supported say-on-pay in 2025. From 2026-09-01 the structure shifts in a way that matters: Ternus joins as CEO and Cook becomes Executive Chair, taking non-independent directors to two of nine (77.8%) and replacing an independent chair with a lead independent director. [S11, S56]

### A clean structure is not a clean earnings record

The forensic problem is optical, not legal. FY2025 returned $106.1bn — $90.7bn of buybacks and $15.4bn of dividends — against free cash flow of $98.8bn, or 107% of it, while diluted EPS rose 22.7% against an 8.0% rise in operating income and the effective tax rate fell to 15.6% from 24.1%. Diluted shares fell 6.9%, from 15,812,547,000 in FY2023 to 14,714,676,000 in Q3 FY2026, and $263.2bn of buybacks over three years bought the arithmetic. That is how a mature hardware company reports high-teens EPS growth; it is also what stops working the year the buyback slows. Counter-evidence is genuine: Q3 FY2026 revenue grew 16% and gross margin reached 50.1%, so FY2026 is not an optical year; no audited FY2026 accounts had been filed on 2026-10-31. [S5, S17]

### Where the judgement breaks, and what to settle

Three events would change the call: a structural remedy in the DOJ monopolisation suit or the DMA Article 6(4) file that reaches commission economics would compress the 75.4% services margin; a board that keeps the executive-chair arrangement past 2027 would entrench a post-CEO chair; and a buyback slowdown would expose the underlying operating growth rate. Confidence is high on identity, ownership and capital-return facts and medium on the board's appetite for refresh, because its own age guideline is already being waived for two members. Diligence should settle whether that waiver was formal and who chairs the board after 2027; whether BlackRock's stake has moved since 2023; what share of Services revenue depends on US third-party payment rules; and the FY2026 buyback pace under the $100bn authorisation of 2025-05-01. ## Technology & Product

Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate: sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and December 2026 is the first test. [S112]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context and Private Cloud Compute. On 2025-12-01 Foundation Models, ML research and AI Safety passed under software chief Craig Federighi as John Giannandrea stepped down: Apple bought what it could not ship and reorganised the rest. [S111, S122, S127]

**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.**

Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]

### The AI bill lands in R&D, not capex

Rented intelligence sits in operating expense, not on the balance sheet: R&D rose a third in nine months while capital spending fell. Free cash flow stays intact and the buyback continues. The marginal AI dollar has no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android.

Apple's revenue compounded 3.3% from FY2021 to FY2025 ($365.8B to $416.2B) and then accelerated to 16% in the first nine months of FY2026, with iPhone revenue up 22% [S5, S6].

Value capture, not unit share, is the franchise an investor is buying [S94, S92, S84, S5, S6, S88].

### The 27.6% price rise is cost pass-through, and Apple is pricing above it

The increase is not demand-led. IDC attributes the 27.6% ASP rise to a memory shock, with NAND and DRAM up more than 300% and passed into shelf prices, and TrendForce shows the cost landing on Apple directly: the iPhone 18 Pro 256GB bill of materials rose 38% year on year, memory reaching 34% of the BOM in Q3 2026 against one-tenth a year earlier. Apple then raised Pro and Pro Max list prices by $100 and held the standard iPhone 18 to spring 2027. What supports willingness to pay is sell-through at those prices: Counterpoint recorded iPhone 18 Pro sales up 23.5% in the first three weeks in China, and Apple's installed base reached an all-time high in the June 2026 quarter. What weakens it: Apple discloses no upgrade rate or unit volumes, so an upgrade-cycle claim rests on third-party panels, and IDC attributes part of China's Q3 strength to buyers pulling purchases forward ahead of Apple's own second-half increases, with the market possibly down 20% in H2 2026. On IDC's unit base Apple's implied revenue per iPhone rose from $832 in FY2025 to $1,101 annualised in 2026, 32% against the market's 27.6%; on the higher 261M unit estimate for FY2026 the rise is 21%. Apple is pricing above the market average, but the magnitude rests on a unit count it does not publish: the gain is cost recovery plus Pro mix, not proof of an upgrade super-cycle. A consumer-panel upgrade rate would settle it and is not available here [S84, S99, S112, S96, S17, S87, S74].

Three pools can add revenue to 2030, and only one is large enough to change the trajectory. Foldables: Apple enters in H2 2026, and IDC expects more than 17M foldable iPhones by 2027 at an ASP above $2,550, 40% of a category worth more than $45.7B. Services: $120.5B trailing twelve months to June 2026, up 14.1% in nine months at a 76.3% gross margin, against a $1.34T advertising pool in 2026 and an App Store ecosystem Apple says carried $149B of digital goods and services in 2025. Wearables and PC: a 2.4% CAGR market to 2030 with smartwatches shrinking 3.7% in 2026 while glasses grow 18.1%, and Apple took 18.2% of combined PC and tablet units in Q2 2026. The non-phone pools, $33.7B of Mac and $35.7B of wearables in FY2025, are too small to carry group growth alone [S84, S6, S17, S89, S83, S85, S152, S5].

## Business Model

Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.9% gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.3% gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. Consensus puts iPhone revenue at $252.4bn for FY2026 and $277.4bn for FY2027, a 9.9% step that assumes the price-and-mix cycle repeats without unit growth. [S5, S6, S71]

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

### The cost side has turned, and the multiple is buying a margin

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% a year earlier, and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%, and Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed, and the FY2027 EPS of $9.79 that the $284 base case and the $270 entry divide by requires 48.0%, with each 100 basis points worth $0.30 of that EPS. The risk runs both ways: Apple has passed component cycles through before by raising prices and shifting to Pro models, and Greater China grew 30% in the nine months, so margin could hold above 47% rather than break below it, in which case the earnings band and the entry price move up together. At $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the market capitalisation is $5,071.2bn on 14,715M diluted shares — 39.3x trailing net income of $128,930M, or 39.5x on the $8.72 sum-of-quarters diluted EPS — and that price already assumes the annuity survives intact and that memory costs are passed through. The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value: that justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. [S6, S7, S17, S68]

**The services annuity is what the multiple buys, and it is a smaller share of revenue than it was a year ago.**

Services produced $120,478M of trailing-twelve-month revenue — 25.8% of the total but 40.3% of gross profit and 2.1x company R&D — while its revenue share fell to 25.2% in the nine months to 27 June 2026 as iPhone revenue grew 22.4% against services growth of 14.1% (S5, S6, S17). Two tolls inside that line, the App Store commission and the Safari search licence worth 16.6% of services revenue on a 2022 court figure, are both under active legal challenge (S69, S70).

### The downside is larger than the up-cycle margin implies

The 30% revenue-fall stress cannot be run at 43%. The operating story that supports 39.3x is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, with iPhone up 21.7% and Greater China up 22.4%, and the September quarter is guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it, from 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price and mix in a shrinking unit market while its cost base rises; Samsung's mobile division lost money for the same reason. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities — $10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter — against a $2.5bn three-year average. Netting the line to those levels gives normalised FCF of $122.6-127.3bn, $125.1bn central: 0.95-0.99x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and 40.5x P/FCF on the $5,071.2bn market value. The $122.6bn floor treats the build as deferred consideration for $13.3bn of gross intangibles added. Shareholders have received $438.6bn of repurchases and $75.0bn of dividends in the five fiscal years to FY2025; no equity has been raised [S5, S6, S1].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.1bn (nine months actual $364.4bn plus the guided $112.7bn fourth quarter), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin and a 17.5% tax rate. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212; the market price is reached near a 7.1% discount rate. The two bulls are not the same animal. The DCF bull at an 8.5% cost of equity, a 35% margin and 14% first-year growth is worth $277 — 20% below the price — because it still discounts at 3.6 points above the 4.93% risk-free rate. The $357 that the thesis weights as its bull is a multiple-based target: 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20, today's 35.2x forward multiple held on earnings 4.2% above the $9.79 base. The $20bn Google search payment survives as a renegotiation rather than a ban, but it is on appeal. The dated catalysts are the 2026-11-02 fourth-quarter release, the May 2027 buyback authorisation and the D.C. Circuit's search-remedy decision expected in 2027. The conclusion is a price range, not a point: own Apple below the high-$200s, or on evidence that FY2027 EPS is tracking above $10.20; at $344.63 the market has paid for the bull. The sell-side targets I can see — $338-355 across four retail aggregators, TickFlow $339.35 from 50 analysts and vcpscanner $340.88 from 112 — are unverified and cluster at the price rather than at intrinsic value [S5, S7, S70, S97, S101, S142, S144, S157, S158].

The counter-case deserves its weight. The discount rate is a judgement: at the low end of the range the base DCF reaches the market price, and quality franchises have held premium multiples for years. What I will not concede is a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, already at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value.

## Development Strategy

Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model. In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple spent $34.04bn on research and development (+33%), $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn) and $62.1bn buying back its own shares, while services grew 14% to $91.73bn at a 76.3% gross margin. The allocation is unambiguous: the balance sheet funds shareholders, the income statement funds AI. [S6]

### Capital returns come before capital projects

FY2025 set the pattern — $89.3bn of buybacks, $15.4bn of dividends, a new $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.26, against $34.55bn of R&D, up 10%. R&D is now growing three times faster than that, yet none of the increase goes into owned infrastructure. Returning cash while renting intelligence keeps return on equity high and removes the risk of stranded datacentres, but it also means Apple has no AI asset that a competitor cannot rent on similar terms. If features fail to lift average selling price, the R&D step-up is a pure margin cost, and the buyback is what keeps earnings per share intact. The investor gets a capital-return story with an AI expense line, not an AI investment cycle. [S5]

### Tariff insurance is being bought with margin

Apple assembled 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, up from 36 million, taking India to 25% of the 220-230 million made globally; Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron now build every iPhone 17 model there, including the Pro and Pro Max. The strategy is insurance against tariffs and China concentration, and it is working on volume. It is not free: assembly and components still cost more in India than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expired on 2026-03-31, with Apple and peers lobbying New Delhi for a further round. India is also becoming a demand market — sales above $9bn, six stores and Apple Pay planned for 2026. The hedge is real; the margin benefit is not yet. [S115]

### Services funds the strategy; regulation taxes it

Services is the profit engine, and its growth is concentrated where regulation bites: advertising and cloud services drove the 14% increase in the nine months to 2026-06-27, at a gross margin 1.5 times the company average. The Digital Markets Act makes that position contestable. By 2026-03-22 Apple had received 56 interoperability requests under Article 6(7), closing 43 of them and keeping 27 closures confidential, while continuing to challenge the obligations. Each request is engineering time and a potential loss of default status, the mechanism by which services margins are defended. Apple's response has been to comply narrowly and litigate broadly. [S6, S119]

### The AI layer is a partnership, not a programme

The defining strategic choice of the cycle was made on 2026-01-12, when Google confirmed a multi-year deal to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year. Apple paired that with rented Google TPU capacity for its own foundation models rather than building training clusters. The logic is defensible: ship a competitive assistant on time, keep the interface, personal context and the Private Cloud Compute boundary, and let a rival absorb frontier training costs. The price is strategic: the supplier also owns Android, and Apple's own research, while still credible, sits behind a rented frontier. Platform control is preserved at the layer users see; it is ceded at the layer that determines capability. The agreement was confirmed under Tim Cook, who moved to Executive Chairman on 2026-09-01 when John Ternus became chief executive, so execution now sits with Ternus and Federighi's software organisation rather than the negotiators: the contract is continuous, the signatory is not. A supplier that also owns Android has seen Apple slip once, which makes renewal terms the thing to watch — a licence priced per device or per query turns the AI bill into a services-margin item rather than an R&D line. ### The talent question is the weak link

The partnership was necessary partly because the in-house programme lost people: through 2025 Apple's AI executives and researchers left, mostly for Meta, which paid to recruit them. The leadership answer is now dated: on 2025-12-01 John Giannandrea, senior vice president for Machine Learning and AI Strategy, stepped down ahead of retirement, Amar Subramanya joined as vice president of AI, and Foundation Models, ML research and AI Safety and Evaluation moved into Software Engineering under Craig Federighi, with the rest going to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue. Headcount-related expense is one of the two drivers Apple cites for the R&D increase, so the company is paying more for a team that is smaller at the top than it was two years ago. Apple still publishes competitive inference research, which argues against the strongest version of the decline story, but a research organisation folded into a software group while its flagship assistant runs on a licensed model is a programme in transition, not a moat under construction. [S121, S127]

### Second curves: health and foldables are adjacencies; Vision is not yet one

Health is the most defensible adjacency because it is regulated and sticky: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny, giving owners a reason to upgrade and not to leave. The foldable Duo is the other extension, priced above the Pro Max and manufactured with a hinge that depends on AI-matched assembly and 3D printing rather than on scale alone. Vision Pro has no disclosed revenue, sits inside Wearables and has no confirmed successor: a research option, not a growth curve. The test of an adjacency is whether it earns its capital; health and foldables plausibly do, and the headset does not yet.

The strategy converts AI into growth through the installed base rather than through the model: a better assistant sells phones and protects high-margin services, and those services pay for the R&D the assistant requires. What must be true within twelve months is narrow and checkable. The December 2026 quarter has to show that higher prices did not break demand; Siri has to leave beta and hold quality in languages beyond English; services growth has to stay in double digits against DMA remedies; and gross margin has to absorb memory inflation without the non-recurring tariff refunds that flattered 2026. If all four hold, the company has bought time and the partnership is a bridge. If two fail, the AI expense is funding a feature that does not defend the price.

The signposts that would show the strategy failing are specific: a discount or a lower-capacity model to hold iPhone volume, a second slip in Siri availability, a fall in services growth below the rate of the installed base, or disclosure of a large multi-year model licence whose cost is not offset by hardware price. None of these is visible in the filings reviewed. The strategic risk is not that Apple loses the AI race on capability — it is that the race turns out not to be the thing that sells phones, in which case Apple wins the hardware cycle and the AI spending was a cost of staying in the conversation.

## Risk Assessment

Apple is a high-quality compounder whose price already capitalises a peak margin and a contested services annuity, so the risks that matter destroy the multiple, not the balance sheet, and none is priced at $344.63. At that price on 2026-10-30 the shares trade at 39.3x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median, and the base DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212. ### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The 50.1% gross margin carried 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS; because that margin applies to $466.8bn of revenue, one point is $4.7bn of operating income. Memory prices rose 146% in Q1 2026 versus 2025; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts Q4 DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter and NAND 15-20% higher; the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38%, memory at 34% against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin, 200bp below the 48% top of the base range, takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to $9.27 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $269 — the entry price, not a discount. [S17, S6, S99, S136]

**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, and 39.3x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, together a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The trial record put the payment at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy preserved non-exclusive payments; the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 brief asks the D.C. Circuit to strike it, and Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, with the DOJ's cross-appeal, stays live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value. The EU fee schedule from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ: Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit. A 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### The growth swing factors are AI and China

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14 on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year. Apple rents the capability and books the bill in operating expense; no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation, and X Corp. and xAI's suit survived dismissal. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case holds while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across 2.5bn devices would land in the 76.3% services margin, and whether a licensed assistant sells $1,199 handsets is the swing factor. China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war: Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%. Greater China was 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue; IDC sees the decline widening to 20% in H2 2026, and a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds India — 25% of iPhones, incentives expired 2026-03-31, costs above China's — and Section 301 duties replacing the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk, and the entry ladder assumes the base EPS

At 39.3x, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and 40.5x trailing free cash flow of $125.1bn (39.8-41.4x across the $122.6-127.3bn band, on $5,071.2bn) makes the multiple the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.1%, reversion to the 24.6x FY2022 trough 37.4%. Each 50bp on the cost of equity moves the DCF 15-18%; the ten-year is 4.93% against a 7.0% implied return. A 30% revenue fall leaves $326.8bn; on the 43.0% nine-month incremental operating margin it leaves $94.6bn of operating income and $5.4 of EPS, but that is an up-cycle margin. On the FY2021-FY2025 average gross margin of 44.5%, with $72.3bn of operating expense held flat, gross profit is $145.3bn, operating income $73.0bn and EPS $4.10 at the 17.3% tax rate on 14.75bn diluted shares — a 58% decremental margin, not 43%; a 10% cost cut lifts EPS to $4.50, and the FY2016-FY2025 average margin of 41.4% gives $3.54. At 29x that is $103-131, at or below the $133 DCF bear. A market 50% smaller is revenue 35% lower and EPS $3.51, $70-88 at 20-25x. Free cash flow 30% lower is $85.8-89.1bn, 56.9-59.1x, covering the $82.2bn trailing buyback but not $97.9bn of buybacks and dividends; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not. The entry ladder is the same single-point bet: 0.75-1.0% at $270 is 27.6x only on FY2027 EPS of $9.79. A 46% gross margin takes EPS to $9.27 and $270 to 29.1x; a search cut of 12.9% takes $9.79 to $8.53 and, with the margin, to $8.07, so $270 becomes 31.7x to 33.5x against the 31.0x four-year mean and $245 becomes 28.7x to 30.4x. The same 27.6x is $223-235 on $8.07-8.53. The ladder needs a condition, not a new number: $270 only if the 2026-11-02 guide holds FY2027 EPS at $9.27 or better and December gross margin at 47%; otherwise the first tranche belongs at $235 and the second at $210, with the 5% cap unchanged. [S10, S97, S6, S5, S151, S70]

### Governance, unknowns and the call

Governance and key-person risk are monitors. Cook is Executive Chair and Ternus CEO under a nine-director board. Srouji's 2025-12-06 departure report is superseded by his 2026-04-20 promotion to Chief Hardware Officer with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, which concentrates rather than removes the dependency. Cash quality is smaller than it looked: the $13,531M non-current liability build against $13,270M of gross intangibles added reads as deferred consideration, but net of a $4,128M current-liability fall it is $9,403M, inside the $10,016M line; if unpaid, free cash flow is $123.2bn, inside the $122.6-127.3bn band. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption stopping 2nm supply, and an appellate remedy treating the Gemini default as the next search payment. The downside is a de-rating, not insolvency, so position size carries the risk; open diligence is the December-quarter margin guide, the 10-K working-capital note, the appellate schedule and the Gemini renewal terms. None changes the call: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if December confirms the margin trough and EPS at $9.27 or better. [S134, S133, S141, S11, S5, S6]

## Investment Potential & Thesis

Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base and services annuity are real, and FY2026 is strong: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. What is in dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,072bn market capitalisation, 39.3 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.7 times forward. The decision is not whether Apple is a good business — it is — but whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S156].

Three valuation methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; the DCF bull case at an 8.5% discount rate and a 35% operating margin gives $277; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year average multiple of 31.0 times implies $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth in net operating profit after tax. Those assumptions make the price exactly fair rather than cheap; the base rate is modest, with revenue compounding 3.3% a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value; this report sees 18% overvaluation: retail aggregator targets are $338-355, unverified, flat to +3% from the close [S142, S144]. Consensus expects iPhone revenue of $252.4bn in FY2026 and $277.4bn in FY2027 and capitalises the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin. The disagreement is specific: that margin included two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned (the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38%, memory 34% of it), and our base case underwrites 47-48%. A 46% margin, which a full memory pass-through implies, takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value to $270 at 29 times — the entry price below, not a discount to it. The non-consensus view is that the market is capitalising a peak margin and multiple at once.

Three scenarios weighted 25/50/25 put the probability-weighted value at $291.5, 15% below the price, and the recommendation rests on that weighted value and the $284 base case, not on the bull. The scenario bull ($357, 25%) — distinct from the $277 DCF bull above — assumes the AI and foldable cycle extends iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate: 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the search payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline, with intrinsic value of $212-264. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as the DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF bear as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 without a break-up: the asset survived, but the overhang ran three years and the settlement did not re-rate the stock — the cloud did, a decade later. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007, peaked near $250bn and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record, 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not [S143, S145, S147]. The rule they teach is that at a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.3x against 201), owns silicon and a services annuity Nokia never had, and holds $62.2bn of net cash; the analogy is about duration and multiple, not extinction.

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price, not narrative. The first tranche of 0.75-1.0% is $270 only on a condition: the 2026-11-02 guide must hold FY2027 EPS at $9.27 or better and gross margin at 47%. At 27.6 times, $270 is a discount only on the $9.79 base EPS; on $9.27 it is 29.1 times, and on $8.07-8.53, after a 12.9% search-payment cut, 31.7-33.5 times, above the 31.0x mean. Those lower cases imply $223-235, so if the guide holds the second tranche is $245; if it fails the first moves to $235 and the second to $210. The position reaches its 5% cap below $225 or if FY2027 EPS growth tracks above 12%. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $242 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety, and the ladder prices the EPS bridge rather than a single point. The counter-evidence is the stock's own record: 27.5% in the twelve months to 30 October 2026; a sale at 35 times forward would have missed it. The open diligence is the appellate outcome on the search payment and a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, neither of which the register holds. Sell above 45 times forward earnings ($440), or if two consecutive quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a services structure that removes the search payment [S6, S7].

## Exit Strategy Analysis

Apple's only exit is the public market and its own buyback, and at $344.63 the shares already discount the scenario bull. No peer is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,071.2bn market value (14,715m diluted shares at $344.63) — so realisation depends on the multiple another investor will pay. With dividend and gross buyback yielding 1.9% and earnings per share compounding at 8-9%, the arithmetic is adequate only while the 39.3x multiple holds; if it reverts toward the four-year average of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to 1.3% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, and sell at $440 and above — 45x FY2027E EPS of $9.79 — not at the $357 scenario bull [S7, S11, S6, S97].

The discipline has been wrong before. Apple has compounded while the technology sector fell in the last month, and a fund that sold on valuation last year would have forgone most of that gain; multiples of this quality have held through a high long-bond yield that most models said would compress them. That argues for modest size and buying weakness, not to abandon the arithmetic: the exit route is liquid, the cash return is real, and the only thing between today's price and the required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on multiple reversion. The open question is the Google payment's share of services revenue and when the appeal is decided; neither is publicly disclosed; both set the floor under the services multiple.

## ESG Assessment

Apple's regulatory exposure, not its ESG record, is what can change a long-only case. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn and Services revenue $109.2bn at a 75.4% gross margin, so App Store commissions and the Google default-search payment sit inside the profit pool carrying the premium multiple [S5]. Fines are not the mechanism; remedies and fee schedules are. Bear case: a 10-15% operating-income tail from losing or repricing search placement and a structurally lower App Store take rate over 2026-2028. A dollar of commission or default rent carries almost no marginal cost, so losing it hits operating income faster than revenue.

### The EU fine is small; the fee schedule is not

On 2025-04-23 the European Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA anti-steering obligation, 0.1% of FY2025 net sales. The material part is the fee schedule: from 2026-10-01 Apple's unified EU terms charge 26% on in-app purchase (down from 30%), 20% on alternative payments, 15% on link-outs and 5% on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web. Apple calls the terms a settlement; EU developer groups contest them. Apple does not disclose EU App Store revenue; at a 75.4% Services margin, each $1bn of commission lost equals $0.75bn of gross profit, and the take rate falls permanently [S78, S77, S5].

### The $20 billion Google payment is the largest policy-sensitive cash flow

Apple does not disclose the Google default-search payment, but the US v. Google trial record put it at $20bn in 2022, or 36% of Google's Safari search revenue: a litigated estimate, not an Apple disclosure. That is 18.3% of FY2025 Services revenue and, if near-pure margin, 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's final judgment of 2025-12-05 preserved non-exclusive payments, banned exclusivity and capped default deals at 12 months; the DOJ and states cross-appealed in February 2026 seeking a payment ban. A lower negotiated rate is more likely than zero, because the payment is worth more as Apple profit than as Google cost; either way it compresses Services growth, and an appellate decision is likely in 2027 [S80, S76, S5].

### US courts are already narrowing the App Store take rate

On 2025-12-11 the Ninth Circuit affirmed that Apple willfully violated the Epic injunction, upheld the steering remedy and limited any fee on linked transactions to Apple's costs; the Supreme Court granted certiorari on 2026-06-30. The DOJ and 16 states and DC have sued Apple for monopolization of "performance smartphones" and "smartphones" since 2024-03-21, seeking equitable relief, not damages; pre-trial litigation has no trial date in Apple's 2026 filings. A willful-violation finding raises the odds of stricter remedies and weakens management's "substantial defenses" posture. US courts can reset App Store economics before the DOJ case reaches trial [S79, S81, S6].

### Tariffs have flipped from cost to refund, not to a new margin level

Q3 FY2026 revenue was $109.4bn and gross margin 50.1%, including 2 percentage points from tariff refunds; EPS of $2.02 included $0.11 from refunds. The underlying margin is 48.1%, against 46.9% for FY2025, when products gross margin fell on tariff costs. The refund follows the Supreme Court's 2026-02-20 ruling striking down certain IEEPA tariffs; Section 232 semiconductor results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariffs on Apple products, but Section 301 duties have since been imposed and more remain possible. For valuation, normalise the margin rather than extrapolate the refund: underwrite 47-48%, not 50% [S17, S5, S6].

### Governance is sound, but the chair is now the former CEO

Governance is not the discount, but the structure changed on 2026-09-01: Tim Cook became Executive Chair, John Ternus became CEO and a ninth director, and Arthur Levinson became Lead Independent Director. The chair is the former CEO, not independent; the independent check now rests on the lead director. The board also waived its guideline against re-election after age 75 for Levinson (75) and Audit Chair Ron Sugar (77), both re-elected in 2026, so refreshment lags the rule. Offsetting that, there is no dual-class stock, four of the 2026 directors were women, the Audit Committee owns privacy and cybersecurity, related-party transactions above $120,000 need its approval, and the 2026 executive-pay vote passed. The gaps are labour and disclosure: 166,000 employees at 2025-09-27, a 10-K concession that supplier code violations "occur from time to time", and no audit metrics; climate claims are unverified. None has changed demand, so ESG is a tail-risk and discount-rate input, not a revenue driver [S56, S11, S138].

## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation

The composite score describes a good company at a poor price rather than a mediocre one: the quality dimensions score high and the price-related ones low, as the weighted table below shows. That split is the recommendation: Watchlist with a staged entry, not Buy, because the price already pays for the quality, and not Avoid, because the franchise would still compound through most of the downside scenarios.

The composite score is 6.0 out of 10. Valuation scores 2 of 10 and carries the largest weight, 20%. At $344.63 the shares trade at 39.3 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.7 times forward (FactSet, 2026-10-23) and a peer median of 20.2 times; the trailing multiple is 10.8% above Apple's own twelve-month average of 35.66 times [S97, S156]. The DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212, the DCF bull case $277, the sum of the parts $177-238, and the scenario bull is $357 at 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20; the recommendation rests on the $284 base case and the 25/50/25 weighted $291.5, not on either bull, because the market price is matched only at a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. The retail aggregator targets of $338-355, unverified, offer flat to +3%, so there is no analyst catalyst to close the gap either.

The quality block is where the score earns its keep. Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Earnings quality scores 7 and the balance sheet 9: normalised free cash flow of $125.1bn, the midpoint of a $122.6-127.3bn band, converts at 0.97 times net income and 0.95 times at the band floor, against 0.50 at Microsoft and 0.08 at Alphabet; net cash is $62,173M, and only $12.4bn of debt matures within a year [S6, S17]. The deduction on earnings quality is deliberate: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, and the FY2026 10-K must settle whether the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities is an unpaid intangible purchase, in which case free cash flow is $123.2bn and the multiple 41.2 times.

Growth and regulation both score low, and together they explain why the recommendation is not merely to wait for a cheaper multiple. Revenue growth has been price and mix rather than volume, so the growth dimension cannot carry the multiple. Regulation is the largest single threat to the services multiple, through the search payment and the European fee schedule, and the catalyst calendar is event-dense and mostly adversarial.
